O Kaṇva, that which snorts like a she-ass or like a sow—
drive it away from her.
He who approaches a woman who is clothed in a woollen garment— may he swallow a red-hot stone.
Having snatched away her garment,
he shall drive her away even to the furthest distance.
That which is auspicious, that which is propitious,
and that which is vigorous along with nourishment—
may Agni establish those in our home.
May Gārhapatya restrain this for you. This, O gods, is Savitṛ;
this, O gods, is Bṛhaspati.
O All-Gods, you have prepared this dwelling for yourselves.
The divine Agni has gone forth around [the sacrifice].
The destroyer of demons and the dispeller of disease,
he drives away all enemies and burns up the Rākṣasas forever.
These men have led the cow around;
they have carried the fire around;
they have established glory among the gods.
Who would dare to challenge this [power] here?
In you is sensory power, in you is luster; may you be the lord of dharma.
You are superior to your rivals;
your splendor is full of milk.
O Aśvins, hear this invocation of yours.
Your kingdom is established in heaven;
may you be long-lived, a slayer of rivals, and superior to your enemies.
You are a bull with sharp horns,
like the ocean whose waters are inexhaustible;
you possess a thousandfold power.
Your two arms are the lords of cattle;
and whatever rival,
adversary, or enemy seeks to slay you—
O fierce one, having taken away the prosperity of all of them, hold it fast;
you are the controller whose intentions are true.
Seeking the truth and the dharma,
having crossed over all calamities,
increase the prosperity of your rivals.
Let offerings come together for you;
let the bride-price be bestowed upon you;
let the sovereign lady milk forth nourishment for you.
May the great peoples desire you;
may the vast kingdom desire you;
splendor has been placed upon your face.
May you be dear to the gods;
upon you the cows are established.
In you is sensory power, in you is splendor.
The sacrifice is entrusted to you;
let the gods come to your call;
you are dear to Bṛhaspati.
May Agni and Soma, the two purifiers,
the goddess Virāj, and the milk-rich one—
may all these protect [us] without weariness.
May your kingdom not be subject to reproach.
Like fire consuming grass, burn it away; like a flood breaking down a bank, destroy it.
Seize the fortune of your rivals,
as one seizes a lotus from the water;
seize it like a horse seizing its chariot.
Like a lion, seize the man; like an elephant, crush the reeds;
uproot the fortune of our rivals.
May Kaśyapa perform for you that sacred formulation (brahman) which is praised by the gods,
which is pleasing, and which is unfailing.
Bring this khadira wood;
then bring the shaft;
and bring this leaf as well.
— Bṛhaspati gave you those fuel-sticks gathered by the gods, which take away the strength of the draft-oxen.
Place them into this well-composed fire that shines like the sun; through these,
may you become superior.
Tear away the fortune of our rivals;
moreover, take away their vital essence.
O Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus!
The seers and those who are the creators of beings,
and the gods, have poured forth for you prosperity, sovereign power, and vigor.
You are a Vasu, named Indra; may you be long-lived for a hundred autumns.
Bhatt. [long-lived]
Like Indra among the gods, speak with brilliance to the people;
let this kingdom expand with cattle and horses.
This kingdom [is established] with food, with energy, with sap.
Let the six wide expanses bow down unto him; let the seven hotṛ-priests, being of one mind, strike down the enemies.
May these kings slay their enemies with arrows; may these kings strike down others in battle;
may these kings overcome hostile armies.
I am Brahmā; I strike down all adversaries.
This kingdom is possessed of wisdom, filled with heroes, victorious, and fierce;
this kingdom resounds with the noise of the drum and is wondrous in its splendor.
Let others bring tribute to this kingdom;
I shall serve the gods with an oblation,
whether there be war for you or peace.
Whether it be through an offense against the gods or through one against the ancestors—
whatever has caused the cows to suffer,
for that I offer an oblation to the gods.
Whatever cruelty is in your mind, whatever in your speech, whether from sin against the gods or against the ancestors—
wash that away like water, as you do with a bad dream.
Then, joyful and well-disposed, come together!
Like the rush of waters, crush the enemies;
coming together, rushing toward every direction, come together!
United in a single vow, distribute the wealth; may the gods, together with your domestic priest, extend your kingdom.
May your kingdom be harmonious and your minds be in accord.
The animals are well-disposed and multiform;
I am the Brahman for you who are well-disposed.
May the gods, being well-disposed, come to this my invocation.
Just as the waters flow together toward the ocean bringing splendor,
even so, O gods, [bestow] sovereignty upon my kingdom.
Bring together prosperity;
may your kingdom be united with cattle, with cows, and with horses, and united with food, with vigor, and with essence.
Through me, as Brahmā, may you, foremost among horses, be ever more prosperous and fierce;
may he be many, youthful, crushing, and bold.
The youth is many and worthy of his fathers;
speaking truth, moving through the assembly, and taking hold of friendship, may they reach old age in companionship.
May nobility, splendor, and sovereignty come together here; may sensory power, in harmony with the cattle, assemble here.
Shaking off those who are displeasing and those whom we hate—
May this kingdom always expand.
May this kingdom be possessed of arrows, rich in heroes, victorious, fierce; may this kingdom be rich in cattle and increased by the sacred word (*brahman*).
This kingdom has its enemies slain; it is victorious, overcoming rivals, crushing them—
this kingdom is firm and fierce.
Sāḍhāmitra, the subduer of adversaries, has conquered all hostile armies with his victorious aid,
by means of the amulet made of udumbara wood.
May Savitṛ, the Ordainer, grant increase to all my cattle in my pen for one who desires prosperity.
May this Agni of the household be the lord of our cattle;
may the amulet, made of udumbara wood, be a bull.
May she unite me with nourishment;
may she, who possesses manure and bears fruit, provide for us the ancestral offering and refreshing food in our home.
May Dhātṛ bestow nourishment upon me through the splendor of the udumbara tree,
and whatever [nourishment] there is from bipeds and quadrupeds.
Whatever foods and whatever flavors there are, I grasp the abundance of them all,
wearing this amulet made of udumbara wood.
I have grasped the nourishment of cattle—
of those that are four-footed and two-footed— and whatever grain there is;
the milk of cattle and the sap of plants.
May Bṛhaspati and Savitṛ bestow [them] upon me.
May I be the lord of cattle; may the Lord of Prosperity bestow prosperity upon me.
May the udumbara gem bestow riches upon me;
may the udumbara gem come near to me.
With progeny and with wealth,
may the jewel, gladdened by Indra,
come to me together with splendor.
The divine jewel, slayer of rivals, winner of wealth, for the winning of wealth;
[the master] of cattle, food, and abundance.
May he bestow abundance upon the cattle.
O Lord of the Forest, just as you were born in the beginning together with prosperity, [so may you grant it to us].
May Sarasvatī bestow upon me the increase of wealth;
may Sarasvatī bring wealth to me.
May Sinīvālī bring abundance of milk and grain,
as well as this amulet made of udumbara wood.
You are the lord of jewels, you are the bull; in you the Lord of Prosperity has produced abundance.
In you are all these strengths and riches.
O Udumbara, may you overcome for us hostility from afar, as well as lack of intelligence and hunger.
You are the leader; [may you lead] us to leadership.
Consecrated, sprinkle me with splendor! You are brilliance; bestow brilliance upon me.
You are wealth; grant wealth to me.
You are nourishment; unite me with nourishment.
As one who performs domestic sacrifices, make me the master of the house.
O you who are made of udumbara wood, bestow wealth upon us.
Bestow all heroism; for the increase of wealth, I fasten you on myself.
This is the amulet made of udumbara wood.
The hero is bound for the sake of the hero;
may he make our gain honey-sweet and bestow upon us wealth consisting of all-heroic sons.
Section 1.
May we attain the benevolent favor of King Bhaga,
whom men invoke in many ways; performing his work, he chooses Bhaga as his portion.
May she make us fortunate among the people.
Awakening in the east, may we behold the goddess Uṣas as she shines forth.
May the radiant Aditi come toward us, bringing wealth along with Bhaga; may Bhaga bestow upon us prosperity today for our well-being.
Lead us toward the path of the gods here; may auspicious favor come to us hitherward,
and may we be united with fortune.
Through Bhaga may I speak the inspired word; may I, full of luster, utter the honey-sweet Sarasvatī.
Through Bhaga’s gift, may this [speech] come to me.
So that, full of splendor, I may address the assembly.
May Bhaga protect me among the cattle; may Bhaga protect me among the grain.
May Bhaga not be among the dice;
may Bhaga protect me with splendor.
May Bhaga protect me in the evening.
May Bhaga protect me during the night;
may Bhaga come to me in the morning as we lie down to rest.
May Bhaga protect me in the morning; may Bhaga protect me at midday;
may we [attain] Bhaga in the afternoon.
Like a garment we put on,
we take Bhaga from the gods, Bhaga from men.
From heaven, from earth, and from the intermediate space, I choose fortune;
O Agni, may it delight in me.
May he protect me with splendor.
Choosing Bhaga, they carry the bride; setting forth, they seek gain; indeed, they invoke Bhaga.
Through Bhaga, this has come to me;
all that is well-being and auspicious riches.
Through Bhaga, we have attained the gods.
He who clothes himself in all these worlds goes forth bestowing riches in many ways; may he grant us that which is most excellent.
May Vāta, Bhaga, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Agni, and the Lady of the Field be easy for us to invoke;
may she who is golden-eyed, far-seeing, and beholder of men [be so].
Come to us, joining with all [of them].
Rise up, O divine Sūrya, together with good fortune!
"With the vigor of the bull together with the wind, together with the maker of space"—this is one verse.
"With the golden one"—this is another. (6)
May the bull protect you with the rays;
may the steed protect you with the swift ones;
may Vāyu protect you with the sacred word.
May Indra protect you with his powers;
may Soma protect you with the plants;
may the Sun protect you with the constellations.
May the moon with the months, the slayer of Vṛtra,
and the wind protect you with his breath.
Three heavens, three earths.
The three intermediate spaces, the four oceans,
the threefold hymn, and the threefold waters— they say these protect you with the threefold and by means of the threefold.
I ordain for you three heavens, three oceans, three suns, three Vaiṣṭapas,
three Mātariśvans, and three suns as your guardians;
I sprinkle you with clarified butter.
O Agni, increasing [him] with clarified butter—
may the deceivers not harm the breath of Agni, of the Moon, and of the Sun.
Let not the deceivers harm your out-breath, nor your in-breath, nor your vigor, O radiant ones who possess all knowledge.
The gods,
like us, have united Agni with divine breath; Vāta is joined with breath.
By means of the vital breath, the gods generated the sun, which faces in every direction; by means of life-span, they generated the life-sustainer of those who grant life.
—O long-lived one, live! Do not die!
Live by means of the vital breath; do not fall under the power of death, you who possess a self.
The treasure deposited by the gods,
which Indra discovered by the paths traveled by the deities—
the waters guarded that gold with their threefold protections.
May they protect you with the threefold [hymns], with the threefold [powers]. The thirty-three deities and the three heroic powers, being well-disposed, have guarded you within the waters.
Whatever gold is upon this moon,
with that may he perform heroic deeds.
O gods who are eleven in heaven...
O gods, may you accept this oblation!
O gods who are eleven in the intermediate space... (see 1b) PS_10,8.2.
O gods who are eleven upon the earth,
you gods, enjoy this oblation!
[May it be] free from rivals in the east.

may Savitṛ protect me from the south, and the Lord of Might (Śacīpati) from the north.
May the Ādityas protect me from heaven; may the fires protect me from the earth;
may Indra and Agni protect me from the east.
May the Aśvins grant protection on all sides;
may the inviolable Jātavedas guard us from the transverse direction;
may the creators of beings be my armor on every side.
Those fires that have entered within the waters—
Mroka, Manohā, Khana, Nirdāha,
Ātmadūṣin, and Tanadūṣin— [may they depart].
I release this upon them;
I release sin and I release falsehood for the sake of truth.
I cast away bad dreams. May Vasiṣṭha and Arundhatī protect me; may the sacrificial grass-bundle of Prajāpati and the hair of Bṛhaspati protect me.
Unfailing sight, well-hearing ears, and unimpaired out-breath and in-breath—may my heart not abandon me until old age; may I not suffer harm in my middle years.
May the waters cleanse me from evil-doing.
Whatever misdeeds we have committed,
may we go forth purified in our bodies from them;
may Vaiśvānara purify us with his rays.
May Vāta, impetuous with the vital breath, purify me with salutations;
may Heaven and Earth, rich in milk, observers of the cosmic order, and worthy of sacrifice, purify me with their milk.
May the fires of the household purify me; may the bold ones invoked by the gods purify me;
may the Śakvarī verses whose backs are laden with Soma purify me.
The purifying ones, the swift-flowing;
he who is the Purifier, may he cleanse me with the great [hymns], O divine Savitṛ!
Like the highest heaven above,
may the *brahmasava* purify me;
may the *rājasava* purify me.
A hundred purifiers are spread out crosswise;
with them may the god Savitṛ purify me.
And may the hundred purifiers purify me.

May the giver again obtain life and auspiciousness here today.
O gods, we have gone to heaven; we have gone to the light of heaven;
we have gone to the light. We have gone to the light.
You are Mahendra, the Supreme Lord,
the good friend whose face is turned in every direction;
may we not be separated from your sight.
Rising today with wondrous splendor,
strike down my rivals;
as the sun strikes them with its rays, so do thou strike them down.
With this night, I have slain your darkness; let it go to the lowest darkness.
I turn according to the turning of the sun.

with the power of Indra, and with the splendor of Soma.

of such-and-such a descendant,

Having sat down, having joined [the victim] with a bad dream, I place him within the gaping mouth of Death.
Whoever— whether our own kin or a stranger— seeks to strike us down as an enemy,

— may they carry away these sins from here:
whatever piśāca, yātudhāna, or flesh-eater seeks to kill me.

may Indra and Agni pierce him through the heart.
Whoever seeks to destroy my sacred knowledge, my austerity, and my supreme strength—

May Indra and Agni both cast away that which is useless for him—
[that] which [harms] my thread and which [harms] my offspring.

may Indra and Agni find his weapon among the gods.

may Indra and Agni spread a magic spell (*kṛtyā*) within his house.

may Heaven and Earth burn him down.

O Agni, and those who cause me distress— slay their dearest one.

I am the bull for you who desire the bull.
I place the embryo within the womb; if, though protected by the gods,

May Dhātṛ, Sinīvālī, and Varuṇānī bestow that upon you; may Indrāṇī grant a male child.

may the gods, with Indra as their chief,
destroy your clan.
Viśara is the mother of Vijṛmbha; Īṣu is the father of Dhanu;
the Ādityas are the sons of Ādityā.
May they cause the destruction of your bowstring, your arrows,
your arm-rest, and your two arms.
From the apāṣṭha, from the horn, and from the tortoise,
I destroy your poison;
[so too] that which is in the alavatī and the ruru-deer's head.
And also for that one whose mouth is iron—
for the arrow of the goddess Parjanya-retas— pay homage!
The plant which Atris, Aṅgirases, and Gotamas know— by that [plant] Bharadvāja and Kaṇva [know it].
He destroys your dissolution—
[that power] which has driven you away from women and which has mounted upon men.
That which is weary, thoroughly exhausted, and sinewy—
that we fashion for you;
like the wind, I cause it to fall away like a cloud.
The consumption that they have placed upon your body,
that heavy burden we make light by means of our speech and this verse.
Therefore,
by that utterance of truth, I shall cause your body to fall apart, so that the man may not be true to his word.
One should always recite:
"The *viṣkandha*, the *apaśara*, the *viśara*, and the *puṣṭyāmaya* [are driven away]."
Jambha, Hanugrābha, and Śaṅkha—
these we drive away with the goat.
Prosperity indeed be yours, O plants!
I have bestowed [these] for the sake of medicine—
[the plants] that seek wealth, that seek old age, and that carry man across.
This plant, produced by the gods, is a protector of the self and a source of long life;
with it, granted by Indra, I [protect myself].
I shall destroy your decay—
whether it be from indolence, or from a covering, or from the wearing of leaves.
With the arrow from my great bow, I destroy your Viśara;
fly away together with Viṣkandha!
Together with the blue jay,
with the kikidivi bird, vanish along with the rush of the wind and the whirlwind.
You are Jaṅgiḍa; you are the protector Jaṅgiḍa; you are Jaṅgiḍa. [Protect] our bipeds and quadrupeds.
May Jaṅgiḍa protect everything!
May the eighty-three Gṛtsyas and the hundred makers of sorcery [be overcome].
May Jaṅgiḍa render all [enemies] devoid of splendor and devoid of strength;
may it render the artificial poison (nāḍa) tasteless.
The seven tasteless decays have departed; O Jaṅgiḍa, drive away the malady as an archer shoots his arrow.
This very Jaṅgiḍa is the destroyer of sorcery, the destroyer of enemies, and moreover, it is powerful.
May he prolong our lives;
may that greatness of Jaṅgiḍa protect us on every side.
By means of which he has overcome Viṣkandha and Saṃskandha, [and] vital force with vital force—
the gods, having seen it, brought it forth.
He is established upon the ground;
him indeed, the ancient Brahmans know as Aṅgiras.
Neither the ancient plants nor those that are new shall overcome you; the fierce Jaṅgiḍa is your dispeller.
O Blessed One,
you who possess immeasurable power, the *jaṅgiḍa* plant is a protector, most auspicious, and a source of horses.
In former times, Upendra bestowed heroic power upon you who were fierce;
O Lord of the Forest, you are indeed fierce.
Indra has bestowed vigor upon you;
driving away all diseases, O herb, slay the demons.
The bodiless, the dismembered, the phlegmatic, the disease of nourishment,
the *takman* that lasts through all autumns.
May the jaṅgiḍa plant render it sapless.
Pronouncing the name of Indra, the seers bestowed the jaṅgiḍa.
May that Jaṅgiḍa protect us, which the gods fashioned in the beginning as a medicine to destroy Viṣkandha.
Dhanapāla is like wealth;
he whom the gods and the brahmins made their protection against the enemy.
O thousand-eyed one, [ward off] those who have come with evil intent, with terrible eyes, having committed wicked deeds.
Destroy [the enemy] through awakening;
you are the all-encompassing Jaṅgiḍa.
Protect me from heaven; protect me from earth.
From the atmosphere, from the plants,
from what has been and from what is yet to be— let Jaṅgiḍa protect us from every direction.
Whatever harms have been wrought by the gods,
whatever have been brought forth or have settled within— may Viśvabheṣaja [the All-healer] overcome them all.
May Jaṅgiḍa render them tasteless.
O Earth, receive this which has been brought;
it is the churned body of clarified butter.
Guard this cow of this donor upon the sacrificial grass so that she may remain there;
and they call you the wife of Varuṇa.
And so they call you Aditi, the one of all forms;
upon the jarāyu, I offer the oblation-bearer Agni into the Āghāra— into this, I offer his greatness.
He stretched out a thousand threads;
he attained ten sets of Agniṣṭomas.
The gods cause him who gives a cow with her calf and still in the membrane to ascend to heaven; those still in the membrane, they cause to ascend to heaven.
By this [mantra] has been given a well-milking cow that bestows vigor;
may she milk for him an inexhaustible stream of a hundredfold [blessings],
which is his in the world of the highest heaven.
The cow dwelling together with her previous calf— whatever other calf she has and whatever placenta there is—
that is the third flesh that has been transformed.
That which the gods call the afterbirth;
drive it away with might, O thou who hast grown strong, and bestow upon him superior renown.
O Indra, protect this man with great protection— unite him with progeny, with body, and with strength.
May he be difficult to overcome from below and manifoldly from above.
All the gods behold her as she approaches;
may that offering which is auspicious and directed toward all sides become for me a means of crossing over.
Making the first-calf cow, still bearing her afterbirth, into a self-sustaining offering, he bestows her upon the Brahman;
may she milk for him an inexhaustible stream in a hundred ways.
In that world, in the future age,
may he who gives us a well-milking cow— the calf, the afterbirth, the fresh milk, and the first-pressed cream— [attain this].
May the gods prolong his life; may he ascend to the world of those who have performed good deeds.
[He has] climbed over the caul, over the afterbirth, by means of battle.
The living one gave this [earth] first:
"May she, pleasant, helpful, and auspicious, enter for us; do not harm us with your divine heat."

I accept this auspicious, well-made, and beneficial garment that brings prosperity, which is ready for use and comes to me; it is clothed in the splendor of clarified butter and dwells in the atmosphere.
The gods, humans, asuras, and the great seers—
these five deities drink this forth:
Indra, Tvaṣṭṛ, Varuṇa, Mitra, and Agni.
They have all granted this to me; through this, living here, may you extend my life.
Kaśyapa, Jamadagni, and Vasiṣṭha.
The seers won this [earth] for us in the beginning:
Bharadvāja, Gotama, and Atri. May Viśvāmitra extend the life of the one who gives this pleasant [gift].
O fortunate one, give strength to the gods, strength to human beings,
and strength to the ancestors, O inviolable cow.
Bestow vigor; enter into me!
Those herbs which were born for the gods three ages ago.
I think indeed that there are a hundred and seven abodes of the tawny ones;
O mothers, a hundred are your abodes.
A thousand are your sprouts;
therefore, a hundred times over, do you make this man of mine free from disease.
Flowering, bearing fruit, fruitful and even fruitless—
you are like mares, ever victorious.
The creepers are those that bring us across. O divine Mothers, when I address you as "the plants" (oṣadhīḥ).
Driving away curses and scattering the demon from here,
Niṣkṛti is the name of your mother.
Niṣkṛti is indeed your father;
you are winged rivers, for whatever is diseased, Niṣkṛti heals it.
The aśvattha tree is your seat;
the parṇa leaf is made your dwelling. You shall indeed be sharers in cattle.
That you may restore the man to life;
when I, seeking strength, take these plants into my hand.
May the self-disease perish like one who has long seized life;
may the vigor of the plants [be ours].
Like cows from the cow-pen, they rush forth— those women desiring to win wealth, while your man wins their very selves.
When the plants have gathered together like kings in an assembly,
he is called a wise physician.
The dispeller of demons and the driver away of disease;
[the cow] rich in horses, rich in Soma, strengthening, and full of vigor.
"I have known all the plants; may they carry me across from here," [he says],
having passed beyond all obstacles.
Like a thief breaking into a pen, he has stepped upon them; the plants have driven out whatever blemish was in the body.
O medicinal herbs, you who creep limb by limb and joint by joint— drive away the consumption from that person.
Fierce as one who sits in the midst,
let one of you protect another; let each of you assist the other.
The plants, being in agreement,
have favored this speech of mine as they descended to the trackless place.
The plants protect him from the day;
the man whom we reach while he is alive shall not come to harm.
The many herbs that have Soma as their king, possessing a hundredfold vision,
impelled by Bṛhaspati— may they [protect us].
May they release us from distress—
those that bear fruit and those that are fruitless,
those that are sheathed and those that are hairy.
May those [waters], impelled by Bṛhaspati, release us from distress— the life-giving, non-harming ones.
I bind upon you this herb,
which shall bring back your life-span and drive away the malevolent spirits.
Time is a horse with seven reins;
he is thousand-eyed, undecaying, and rich in seed.
Upon him mount the wise who are possessed of inspired insight.
His wheels are all the worlds.
This Time carries seven wheels;
its hubs are seven, and the axle is indeed immortality.
He has illuminated all these worlds; he moves as Time, the first god indeed.
A full jar is placed upon Time.
We indeed behold him who exists as many;
he faces toward all these worlds.
They call him Time in the highest heaven.
Being that very one, he brought forth the worlds; being that very one, he went around the worlds;
being their father, he became their son.
Therefore, indeed, there is no other splendor higher than this.
Time generated that heaven; Time [generated] this earth as well.
In due time, what has been and what is to be remains as the desired oblation;
Time created prosperity.
In time the sun shines;
indeed, time [governs] all beings;
through time the eye perceives.
In time the mind, in time the vital breath, and in time the name are composed;
through time all rejoice.
When he has arrived, these subjects [are protected]: at the proper time [is] austerity, at the proper time [is] the eldest [Veda],
and at the proper time is the Brahman concentrated.
Time indeed is the lord of all,
who was the father of Prajāpati; by him it was impelled, by him it was born.
That [Brahman] is established in him;
Time, having become Brahman,
sustains Parameṣṭhin.
Time created progeny; in the beginning, Time created Prajāpati;
Kaśyapa was born from Time as the Self-existent One.
From Time, austerity was born;
from Time, the waters came into being; from Time, the sacred word, austerity, and the directions arose.
In due time the sun rises; in due time it sets again;
in due time the wind blows.
In time the great earth and the great sky are established;
time indeed is both what has been and what is to be.
Puraḥ brought forth his son;
from Kāla the Ṛg-verses came into being, and from Kāla the Yajus was born.
Time has sent forth the sacrifice as an imperishable portion for the gods;
in Time dwell the Gandharvas and Apsarases.
At the proper time, the worlds are composed;
at the proper time, this divine Aṅgiras and Atharvan preside over them.
Having conquered this world and the highest world, as well as the meritorious worlds and the meritorious supports,
by means of the Brahman, all worlds.
That supreme god, Time, indeed moves on.
Seven are his, the seven seers are his arrow-makers, and twelve are his [spokes].
Indra and Agni cast down the dart and the great belly;
Mitra and Varuṇa [cast down] Indra-rāśi.
You two cut away what was cast off;
impelled by the fierce Indra, it became the father of the Brāhmaṇas.
A non-Brāhmaṇa should not eat this,
nor should he bring it into his own home;
it is as parched and dark as poison.
The heap of Indra lies in the lap of the wicked;
he lies here, guarding his own body—
he who eats this [food] without discernment.
In the midst of the threshing floor,
a great-bellied heap of grain has been fashioned;
or perhaps this becomes consumption (yakṣma).
Mahodara, who has a heap of food like Indra,
devours his prey in the presence of food like a horse eating the reeds of Śinī.
May he who offers the heap for Indra increase the threshing-floor grains;
may he take hold of the abundance of the threshing-floor.
And may it bring great merit to the cattle—
[the chariot] which Śunaḥśepa,
Indra, and Brahmaṇaspati drew.
The seers made that auspicious for us, for the sake of life;
the parched *tṛḍha* vegetable lay there.
The beast was given;
those who ate the offered oblation lie there groaning in pain.
From the oxen with speckled hooves, carrying their loads and drawing their yokes,
from the sweat born of the labor of the plowman.
The heap of Indra was born from whatever sweat of the blacksmith rises,
heated from his body.
Like thirsty cows reaching for water, he attains the heap [of grain] belonging to Indra;
when the Lord of the Plow reaches the plowman.
With his staff he strikes those who are full of wrath;
whatever is indeed base or ancestral has been placed within the heap of Indra.
O woman, urge on the mortar and pestle; prepare the winnowing basket and the two sieves for the sake of the son, O Gotamī.
May he make the heap of grain full of sweetness.
O singer, bring this winnowing basket; come with the mortar and pestle and the cooking pot.
May our sons today, on this auspicious day, consume the honeyed stalk of Soma pressed by us.
This Agni has come as a messenger sent forth by us.
May he make all our food free from poison; O Brahman, drive away the undigested, the unprepared, the indigestion, the bile, and the phlegm as they are impelled.
O sweet drink, O honeyed drink, O food— O food,
come to us with auspicious protections, you who are auspicious.
Becoming a lion, he slaughters cattle; becoming fire, [he consumes] grain;
he is an uncreated mass of Indra.
And it goes even to the enemy.
The hundred-jointed, unshakable,
thousand-leaved, victorious [plant].
The Darbha grass which is a formidable herb— this I bind upon you for the sake of long life.
They do not shave his hair.
He strikes his breast with a blow,
for he grants protection with a blade of darbha grass whose leaf has not been torn away.
O herb, your tuft is in heaven; you are established upon the earth. By you, who possess a thousand stalks—
We increase our lifespan. You have pierced through the three heavens and these three earths.
With that [power], I cut down the tongues and the words of all those who are ill-disposed toward me.
You are the Conqueror.
I am the powerful one;
having both become powerful,
may we overcome our rivals.
Overpower our assailant; overpower those who attack us in battle;
overpower all the evil-hearted ones.
O friend, make many [good things] for me with the Darbha grass, born of the gods,
which eternally supports the heavens.
Therefore, may I win food together with my own people, and may I win it for myself.
O Darbha, make me dear to the Brahmin and the Kshatriya.
To the Śūdra and to the Ārya,
to whomever we desire,
and to every one who perceives clearly.
He who, being born, made firm the earth, who propped up the mid-air and the sky—
he whom no evil found while he was bearing [the world].
This Darbha grass of ours is a supporter of heaven;
it is a slayer of rivals, possessing a hundred stalks and being powerful.
It was the first among plants to come into being.
May this *darbha* protect us on every side; with it may I overcome the armies of those who attack us.
It is worth a thousand, possessing a hundred stalks, and full of sap.
Agni is the consecration (rājasūya) of the waters and the plants;
may this darbha grass protect us on every side; may the divine amulet unite us with long life.
Drawn forth from ghee, rich in honey, full of milk,
a firm support of the earth, unshakable and immovable; driving away rivals and casting them down.
O Darbha, with great majesty and great power, you shall surpass the earth with your vigor;
you sit upon the sacrificial altar, beautiful at the rite.
The seers have brought you, the purifier;
purify us from our misdeeds.
Sharp is the king, the overcomer.
The slayer of demons, the observer of all people,
the brilliance of the gods, this fierce strength—
this I bind upon you for old age and for well-being.
By means of the darbha-grass, perform heroic deeds;
bearing the darbha within yourself, do not waver.
Surpassing others in splendor, you shall stand firm upon the path.
Shine like the sun toward the four quarters!
May the earth, the giver of life, rise up;
may the wind blow coolly upon her.
May the Earth, possessing her proper season, receive the seed, causing it to take root and rise up with a thousand shoots.
May Indra, whose horses are bay, [protect] this.
Agni, indeed, has red horses;
the Aśvins have donkey-horses;
they have yoked the goddess Agriculture.
May you hold the leather thong auspiciously; raise the goad auspiciously;
may the ploughshare heat itself auspiciously.
May the plough bring us prosperity; let it yoke the draft-animals, stretch out the yokes,
and sow the seed here in the prepared field.
So may Dhātṛ, so may Bhaga, so may the Aśvins act; so may the goddess Sarasvatī.
The plants have ripened with good fruit, never failing;
this [is the work] of Indra, Varuṇa, and Vāyu.
O Aśvins, may you extend this speech of mine!
Dhātṛ, Pūṣan, and Bṛhaspati have brought about prosperity together.
The gods who have found the light of heaven [performed] agriculture.
She who is auspicious like a fortunate woman, beautiful in her form at the assembly, is worthy of admiration.
May she carry us across to the honeyed stalk.
May the abundance of food, the abundance of men, and the abundance of cattle resort to you here.
Let intense rains fall for our prosperity,
for greatness, and for growth;
let Parjanya stand pouring down his bounty.
Together with the *pṛṣṭhya* [stotra], the Sun goes forth,
generating joy,
driving away all enemies.
Open wide, O Earth, O serpent; spread out your wing and become broad.
May the grain grow auspiciously.
O goats, drive away those who cause harm;
bestow greatness upon us.
Let not the snare-catcher injure you; let him not injure us.
May your plow not tear asunder; may your fierce and enraged [weapons] not harm even the slightest part of our bodies.
The increase of wealth, O Śuna and Sīra, and also that which is the fortune of the furrow; the Goddess,
the Ocean, and Sinīvālī.
Impel our agriculture;
impel these five directions, O Vāta.
May heavy rains fall upon the threshing floor as if upon the Sātvatas;
may the plowman happily follow after his draft animals.
May the plowshare, breaking through, enter the earth;
may Śuna and Sīra, strengthened by our oblation, make the grains auspicious for us.
O Aśvins, that luminous [power] which has carried us across the darkness— to grant us that nourishment, do you two bestow it upon us.
These waters are indeed called "upward-supported," namely the plants and the trees;
Agni is their overlord.
Whoever knows these upward-supported waters and Agni as their overlord—
Just as these [rays] stand up toward him, so do they stand up toward him who knows this; he becomes the overlord of his own people and of others. PS_11,16.1
These waters that are splashing are indeed called *praskadvarīḥ*;
their overlord is Āditya.
Whoever knows these splashing waters and Āditya as their overlord—
Just as these [waters] rush forth when he rises,
even so do they rush forth when he descends;
he is the overlord...
These waters are indeed called *takvarīs*;
of these, the earth is the sovereign mistress.
Verily, he who knows these *takvarī* waters and the earth as their sovereign mistress—
Just as these [insects], being driven away from this [place], go screeching, even so do those who hate him, being driven away by him, go;
he is the overlord. […]
These waters that flow are indeed called Vaśinīḥ; Varuṇa is their overlord.
Whoever knows these waters as Vaśinīḥ and Varuṇa as their overlord—
Just as one takes control of the flow of these [rivers] as they rush along,
even so does the sovereign take control of his enemies. (…)
These cows are indeed the waters named Ūrj;
Tvaṣṭṛ is their overlord.
Verily, he who knows these waters as Ūrj and Tvaṣṭṛ as their overlord [attains his desire].
He becomes vigorous and radiant;
he obtains a thousand cattle and becomes a sovereign lord. (…)
These waters, which are ghee, are indeed named "splendor" (varcas);
Pūṣan is their overlord.
Verily, he who knows these waters as splendor and Pūṣan as their overlord [attains splendor].
He becomes radiant and glorious,
and even his face shines, though it is not anointed;
he becomes a sovereign lord.
These waters which are honey are indeed called "vital force" (ojas);
Indra is their overlord.
Whoever knows these waters as vital force and Indra as their overlord—
He becomes vigorous, powerful, and possessed of the senses;
as a sovereign, he receives the honey-mixture (madhuparka) in the royal assembly. (…)
These waters, namely the hailstones, are indeed called "Fierce";
the Maruts are their overlords.
Whoever knows these fierce waters and the Maruts as their overlords—
"He becomes fierce and powerful;
they call him the host of Maruts, the sovereign lord. (See 1e PS_11,16.8)
These waters that rain down are indeed named "Maha";
Parjanya is their overlord.
Whoever knows these waters as Maha and Parjanya as their overlord—
He becomes great and has many friends;
moreover, his own people rejoice, saying, "This one is ours.
Therefore, everyone exults when it rains.
These waters called *atimanyā* are indeed *surā*;
the Aśvins are their lords.
Whoever knows these waters as surpassing and the Aśvins as their overlord surpasses his rivals; his rivals do not surpass him.
Therefore, one who is intoxicated surpasses another who is intoxicated.
The Lord is … // These waters that are in the furrow are indeed named "the familiar ones" (paricita);
Yama is their overlord.
Or whoever knows these well-known waters with Yama as their overlord—both his own people and the subjects submit to him;
he becomes their overlord. (…)
These waters, namely women, are indeed called *rantayaḥ*; desire is their overlord.
Whoever knows these waters as *rantayaḥ* and desire as their overlord—
They take delight in this; he becomes delightful, like a lover, the sovereign of women. These waters are indeed called "the all-sustainers" (viśvabhṛtaḥ), for they are the person (puruṣa).
Death is their overlord.
Whoever knows these waters as the all-sustaining ones, with Death as their overlord, becomes the sustainer of the universe; the universe sustains him.

Three fires are maintained in his house: the Dakṣiṇāgni, the Gārhapatya, and the Āhavanīya. Four precious things come to him: a gold ornament, a bronze vessel, a mule, and an elephant as his lord. (…)

Of these very waters, the Himavat is the udder, Soma is the calf, and Parameṣṭhin is the overlord. Whoever knows these waters— the Himavat as the udder, Soma as the calf, and Parameṣṭhin as the overlord—
becomes a Parameṣṭhin and attains the state of Parameṣṭhin.
He who knows this becomes the sovereign of his own people and of others.
Thus ends the eleventh section, the sixteenth lesson,
the eleventh chapter.
May Agni drive away the fever from here; may Soma, the pressing-stones, and the Maruts of purified strength;
may the altar, the sacrificial grass, and the brightly blazing fuel-drifts do so as well.
May the Rakṣasas be blown away by that [wind].
This one, who is the glowing fever,
makes all forms turn yellow.
To that Aruṇa, to the tawny one,
to the fever with burning wealth, let there be homage!
O Takman, seek out one who has a companion.
Being self-controlled, be gracious to us; now come to where your home is, among the Dasyus who have been struck down.
The man who is harsh, like a crumbling ruin, and ruddy— [may] Takman,
[possessing] all-pervading power, [drive him] down.
Drive him far away downward;
having directed my mind, I send him down to the disease.
The slayer of Muṣṭiha of Śakambhara; go again to the Mahāvṛṣas,
to the Mahāvṛṣas and the Mūjavats.
Go away, O fever; having departed, abide elsewhere.
We declare these observances to the fever, or rather, these belong to another's field.
The Mūjavants are his home; the Mahāvṛṣas are his home.
Since you were born, you have been the subduer of fever.
O Takman,
you who dwell among the Bālhikas, you serpent, you who cause disease and deformity— drive away in great numbers!
Seek out the female servant who is rebellious;
strike her with the thunderbolt!
Go to the mountain, for you are born of the mountain.
On the mountain is your buffalo home;
O Prapharvī, desire a female slave,
and shake her off like a fever.
You who are cold and you who are burning,
along with Kāsā and Āvīviya—
terrible, O Takman, are your weapons.
With these, do thou encompass us.
O Takman, together with thy brother Balāsa, and with thy sister Kāsikā—
May he perish through his own rival,
the Pāmna; may he perish from the Gandhāris and the Mūjavats.
From the people of Kāśī and Magadha,
we entrust the fever to [them], as if it were a beloved treasure.
We declare these observances for the fever: neither from the Arkavindas, nor from the Arvidālas, nor from the Annadī, nor from the Vartakāvatī.
Or these other fields:
"The thousand-eyed immortal does not delight in another's field."
The fever has indeed arisen;
it will go away along with Balihikā.
Go hence to the Mūjavat mountains.
Or even further than that; let them not come upon us from there again.
Therefore, O Takman, I speak thus to you.
Move only for another, in the highest transcendence,
so that you do not come to an end for us.
So that you do not cause us grief; just as this vast earth,
though already full-grown, has received her embryo.
Thus I place the embryo within you;
for that purpose I invoke you for protection—
from the mountain, from the womb of heaven.
From limb to limb it is gathered;
the seed of every god has been placed upon the two blades like a feather.
May Viṣṇu prepare the womb; [the handle] of Mehendale, Henning Memorial Volume, 12,3.2. PS_12,3.2. viṣṇur yoniṃ kalpayatu.
May Tvaṣṭṛ fashion the forms;
may Prajāpati pour [the seed];
may Dhātṛ place the embryo within you.
Bestow a fetus, O Sinīvālī; bestow a fetus, O Sarasvatī;
you two, O Aśvins, place a fetus in her.
May you two bear the lotus-wreath.
May King Varuṇa place the embryo within you; may the god Bṛhaspati place the embryo within you.
May Indra and Agni place the embryo within you;
may Dhātṛ place the embryo within you.
You are the embryo of the plants.
The embryo of the trees,
the embryo of all that exists—
O Agni, place that embryo here within us.
That by which plants become pregnant, that by which animals become pregnant—
the embryo of those embryos.
By that, may you become pregnant.
We loosen your knot;
may Dhātṛ bestow a fetus upon you.
Let the son ascend to his womb;
let him be born toward his birth,
for he has indeed been born through greatness.
He has come together unto the womb;
now, like Soma for consumption, let the embryo settle in its proper season.
O Creator, with your most excellent form,
place a male child within the two labia of this noble woman.
For birth in the tenth month; with the most excellent form, O Savitṛ...
With the most excellent [form] of Viṣṇu... With the most excellent [form] of Tvaṣṭṛ...
With the most excellent form of Bhaga—
Place a male child within the womb of this woman,
so that she may give birth in the tenth month.
O Skanda, preside over it; display your heroism; place the seed within the womb—a vigorous one, full of virility.
We lead you forth for the sake of progeny.
Whatever King Varuṇa knows, and whatever the divine Bṛhaspati knows—
Drink that which Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, knows as the maker of embryos;
O you who possess the Bṛhat-sāman, open wide!
May your embryo rest in the womb;
may the gods grant you a son who drinks Soma and possesses both [sets of] teeth.
I approach you with the seasonal rite of Soma, so that you may conceive;
from this, let a son be born to you.
O Agni, be born from the Aśvattha tree for this sovereignty and for vigor, so that you may perform heroic deeds.
He who climbs the trees from the Ugrāpatika [tree].
O Agni, we generate you, who, though dwelling among the trees, endure all oppression.
Drive away my rivals, both those already born and those yet to be born, from the climbing aśvattha tree.
The fire-sticks were made from the wood of the *vṛkṣa* tree;
from them was born for Agni that fire with its formidable jaws.
I place that immortal Jātavedas, once born, within me— the purifying Agni— for my protection.
The pure one, the invincible.
Stretch forth your bow, put on your armor;
slay the enemies; I perform heroic deeds for you.
May those who are your rivals here be overcome;
may you alone be the bull.
May you be the bull among your kinsmen.
We make him one who overcomes rivals, the slayer of enemies, a sovereign ruler,
and a lord of cattle.
The ocean is the eldest of waters;
Indra is the slayer of Vṛtra among the gods.
We make you a tiger, a lion.
Subdue those who attack you, as Indra subdued the Dasyus;
like a fierce wind, scatter your rivals.
Let them wither away like wood from a forest fire;
you have surrounded them on all sides from Agni. Cut them down; let them wither away!
Strike them down; do not leave any remaining. Having slain all your rivals, become the sole bull.
Be thou fierce, be thou strong; be thou the one who causes separation; be thou the first against those who attack us.
Strike down our rivals.
Bhaṭṭa: [He conquers] those with rivals; [he is] without a rival, a slayer of rivals—like Indra, unharmed and imperishable.
May all your rivals be trampled beneath your feet;
may your rivals, their roots dug up, wither away.
I summon Agni out from their bodies;
with an oblation I restore their vital breaths,
and thus they are made free from sin.
We prepare this oblation for you, O Sovereign, which increases, which overcomes, and which destroys your rivals.
They were defeated by their rivals: "Whatever man, whether one of our own kin or a stranger, seeks to harm us..."
Like one who clears away the sacrificial fuel,
you shall leave nothing remaining of him.
"Without a rival"— these two [verses].
PS 10.8.4–5 are repeated at PS 12.6.5 (…) // PS 10.8.5 is repeated at PS 12.6.6:
(6) "By you, formerly, the Atharvans..."
O herb, you have slain the Rākṣasas;
with you Kaśyapa slew them, with you Kṛṇva and Agastya.
By you we drive away the Apsarases and the Gandharvas; O goat-horned one, O goat, drive away the Rakṣas.
Destroy them all with your fragrance!
Let the Apsarases go to the river,
like a wind blowing toward the intermediate region.
Gulgulu, Pīlā, Naladī, Aukṣagandhī, and Pramandinī—
wherein the immortals dwell within the waters.
In the ocean are Turū, Nīlī, Turvaśī, and Puṇḍarīkā;
go there, O Apsarases,
for you have been awakened.
Where the golden swing of the Gandharvas is fastened in heaven...
The meeting of the Gandharvas and Apsarases is called Ānarta.
Where there are *aśvattha* trees, *nyagrodha* trees, great golden [trees], and crested [trees]...
(see 4cd PS_12,7.7)
Wherever your green and white dice,
the *āghāṭas* and *kakaryas*, speak together—
there go away, O Apsarases!
You have awakened!
This is [the teaching] of the Gandharva Vīrucchikhaṇḍin, the lord of the Apsarases.
May it split his testicles and may his penis fall away.
This herb has come, a potent plant among plants.
May the goat-horned, the non-kingly,
and the sharp-horned one drive them away!
O Apsarases, depart from here!
Wherever your homes are, O Gandharvas,
let the sharp-horned arāṭakī and the goat-horned plant drive you away!
O Apsarases, you know your husbands, the Gandharvas;
depart from this man.
O immortals, do not associate with the mortal!
Terrible are the weapons of Indra;
there are a hundred iron-edged spears.
With them, may he drive away the Gandharvas who are difficult to overcome and who consume the *avakā* plants; let him burn up those who consume the *avakā* plants.
O herb, drive away and lead far off all the Gandharvas who shine with splendor.

The Apsarases who move about restlessly, maddening, causing intense longing, making the sage naked, and rendering his laughter futile— Please note: The term *raghaṭaḥ* is interpreted here as "restless" or "moving about impetuously," based on the context of the verse. The text describes the seductive power of the celestial nymphs over the ascetic.
Ajaśṛṅgī has placed the wives of the Gandharvas in her womb;
making the man white,
she shines forth in all forms.
Like a white dog, like a monkey, and like a youth with all his hair intact,
he became a pleasing sight to behold.
The Gandharva dwells with the woman;
him we drive away from here.
He who indeed desires a barren cow for the gods—him we drive away from here.
Or he who cooks for himself the most excellent oblation—
such a one is bound by the noose of Death,
and by that of the gods and of Yama.
They call her Dakṣiṇā, Sūryā, and Aditi;
fashioning her as the uniform cow of speech,
the seven seers established this speech.
Sarasvatī, being fashioned, may she be gracious.
They call this cow-like speech "vaśā"; three *vaśās* are established together in the place of assembly.
Of these, I offer one with my mind into the fire;
may the Lord of Beings make that sweet for us.
May Savitṛ make this sweet for us.
O Agni, knowing the sacred ordinances, offer this sweet oblation for us, which the progenitor of cattle has created;
may Bhūtapati make that [oblation] sweet for us.
This is the third [offering] for Vaśinī; O Vaśā, I offer you for greatness. As an embryo you have entered [the womb]; desiring, go to the desiring gods.
May the desires of the sacrificer come true.
This cow, who brings forth strength with her waters, has been established; in her Indra and Varuṇa have taken delight.
Strength and weakness attend one another; this [cow] has arrived, and the wise animal has entered into manly vigor. The barren cow has brought forth the ancient, wise one.
The barren cow gave birth to the bull that touches the heavens;
the barren cow gave birth to the young one at the time of distribution; the barren cow gave birth to the winner of riches.
That sprinkling water which fell from the sacrificial grass on the right side of the altar,
full of power— therefrom the cow, having come into being, bellowed forth.
Her girth became like a coat of mail;
homage to your greatness and to your eye!
O Vaśa-bull, I perform that with my mind.
Drunk by the gods through auspicious paths,
do not harm us with your divine heat.
The bull has leaped upon the cow.
Who knows that embryo today as it rests upon the threads, and how many times he has fashioned it?
He alone has encompassed form;
he alone is called by the name "King";
he alone is the lord of form, and he alone is form itself.
Form is the one [deity] among those who perform good deeds;
Prajāpati, Parameṣṭhin,
Mṛtyu, Viśvānara, and Svar.
The possessors of the Sarasvatī were born from this sacrifice, from the cow;
they belong to him whose house one would take [the fire] from.
The barren cow is an oblation prepared by the gods;
its place of rest is sought for her,
as for a daughter with a husband.
One should not step upon her even once, nor should there be a lame woman in his house;
she is like a barren cow or an ill-fated maiden.
One who understands through incapacity should not protect this [speech] from the Brahmins,
nor should he cause it to fade away.
One should not turn back a female ascetic;
one should not keep a cow that is barren among someone's cattle.
Since gods and humans alike followed her will through sacred prayer (*brahman*),
she therefore became known as Vaśā.
Bringing [all] under her control, this mistress has arrived; the auspicious one, beholding the place, has come forth,
being born toward the sacrifice for the sake of the non-desired.
Measuring out the proportions of the sacrifice,
the Maruts, accompanied by Indra, have taken possession of the fourth part according to their will.
The fourth is under the control of the Ādityas and the Rudras; the fourth is under the control of the Vasus.
The Ādityas are the sharers of the fourth.
The sages know the barren cow;
moreover, one of her forms is the path, and four have been fashioned as the quarters.
The barren cow beheld the path to the back of the firmament for those who find the light; the Ādityas followed after her.
And the ascetic seers,
fashioning the *yajus* of the Ādityas and Aṅgirases at every step, [attained success].
Following the *vaśā* cows, they went along chanting;
therefore, this *sāman* is called the *aiḍa*.
The *vaśā*, the *iḍā*, and *vaśānumati* [are its forms].
They call Sarasvatī the cow;
they consider Virāj to be the cow; Vāc is the cow, and Pṛthivī is the cow.
Vaśā is the commander, Sinīvālī,
Vaśā Uṣas, and Vaśā Nirṛti;
through Vaśā, death entered.
The cow entered into death;
Agni is speech, water is the eye,
the mind is the wind— the cow is the controller.
Who knows her body— that [body] by which she went forth alone,
she who was in harmony with the eye and the mind?
The seers, possessed of wisdom, behold her with their hearts.
She is the sovereign mistress of offspring and of cattle;
she is the royal cow, whose creation is beyond measure.
Who knows the udder of the barren cow? Who knows the inner membrane and the outer membrane? Who knows her teats?
Who knows what she yields?
I know her udder; I know her amnion and her placenta.
I know her breasts, and I also know what she yields.
I would not protect her— Bhatta says "I would not protect her"— nor her.
I would surely give it to him;
for I know her breasts, the milk, the amnion, and the placenta.
The skin is her womb, the afterbirth her garment, the placenta her white cloth, and the umbilical cord her turban;
may she, self-controlled, suckle her mother until old age.
He was fashioned by the Brahmās, for he is his kinsman. (PS 12.11.9, Anuvāka 1)
Now I shall proclaim the heroic deeds of Indra,
those which the wielder of the thunderbolt performed for the first time: he slew the serpent and released the waters.
He split open the flanks of the mountains;
he slew the serpent as it lay coiled upon the mountain.
Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned for him the thunderbolt that roars like heaven.
Like lowing cows, the flowing waters have gone straight down to the ocean;
acting like a bull, he chose the Soma.
At the Trikadruka festivals he drank of the pressed juice;
Maghavan took up his missile, the thunderbolt, and slew him, the first-born of the dragons.
When you, O Indra, slew the first-born of the serpents, you destroyed the illusions of the deceivers along with their magic;
then you brought forth the sun, the sky, and the dawn.
At that time, you truly did not know the enemy.
Indra slew Vṛtra, the worst of Vṛtras, the shoulderless one, with his great thunderbolt, his mighty weapon.
Like a serpent struck by a thunderbolt,
he lies prostrate upon the earth;
for like a drunken warrior, he has challenged one who is not a fighter.
But he did not withstand the great hero, the oppressor, the one with the residue; Indra’s enemy, though crushing his own weapons, was shattered by their impact.
Footless and handless, he challenged Indra; upon the mountain ridge, Indra struck him with his thunderbolt.
He who was a eunuch became a match for the bull.
Vṛtra lay scattered in many places;
like a breached embankment, the waters flow over him as he lies there, while the mind ascends above.
Even those whom Vṛtra had encompassed with his greatness, of them the serpent became one whose head lay at the feet.
Vṛtra’s son became one who looked downward.
Indra has hurled his weapon down upon her;
the mother is above, the son is below.
Dānu lies there like a cow with her calf.
The body was placed in the midst of the standing, unsheltered logs;
the waters flow over the lair of the wolf.
Indra’s enemy lay long in deep darkness;
the waters stood obstructed, with the Dāsa as their lord and the serpent as their guardian, like cattle held by a Paṇi.
The opening of the waters which was closed up,
that Vṛtra, having struck him down, Indra threw open. You then became the horse's tail-hair, O Indra.
When the one god struck you with the *sṛk* weapon,
you won the cattle; O hero, you won the Soma and released the seven rivers to flow.
Neither lightning nor thunder remained for him; even the celestial fire did not cast its flame upon him when Indra and the Dragon fought together.
And Maghavan has conquered others besides;
whom did you see as the avenger of the serpent, O Indra, when fear entered your heart after you had slain him?
Like a frightened hawk, he crossed the ninety-nine flowing rivers and the regions; Indra is the king of what has been traversed and what remains to be traversed.
Vajrabāhu [conquered] Śama and Śṛṅgin; he,
the king, rules over the peoples, encompassing them as the felly encompasses the spokes.
He who, as soon as born, was the first wise god and surpassed the gods by his power of will—
he at whose breath the two worlds trembled.
By the greatness of his manly power, O people, he is Indra—
he who steadied the earth as it was being shattered, and who brought to rest the agitated mountains.
He who measured out the wide mid-air, who propped up the sky— he, O people, is Indra; he who,
having slain the dragon, set the seven rivers flowing.
He who drove out the cows by unfastening Vala’s enclosure,
he who generated Agni between the two stones, the devourer in battles— he, O people, is Indra.
By whom all these shakings were made, who cast the Dāsa race down into the depths, and who,
like a gambler winning the stake, took it for himself.
The noble one nourishes them...
when they ask of that terrible one, "Where is he?",
and people say of him, "He does not exist."
That noble one bestows prosperities like a winner in a game; have faith in him who is the impeller of the weary and the helper of the emaciated.

He who is the protector of the imploring Brahman Kīri when he has set the pressing-stones in motion, he of the beautiful jaws, the protector of him for whom the Soma is pressed— (he is …). // PS_12,14.6
He whose horses, whose cattle, whose villages, and whose chariots are in every direction—
he who brought forth the sun and the dawn.
He who is the leader of the waters...
whom the two contending armies invoke, both the higher and the lower, and both kinds of enemies.
Even though they have mounted the same chariot,
they invoke [the gods] separately;
for without him, people do not achieve victory.
Him whom those fighting invoke for protection,
he who has become the counterpart of the universe,
he who shakes the unshakable— (he is...)."
He who has forever struck down all those who commit sin against me while remaining unawakened;
he who does not yield to the arrogance of the arrogant.
He who is the slayer of the Dasyu...
he who discovered Śambara dwelling on the mountains in the fortieth autumn.
He who slew the dragon as it was displaying its vigor,
the Dānu as it lay prostrate—
he who pursued Śambara while he was at Śaśibi... // PS_12,15.1 //
Or he who did not drink the pressed juice of the wolf, nor [protected] the many people sacrificing within the mountain— he who was not eager to attack him... // PS_12,15.2
He who, the bull of many rays, the mighty one, released the seven rivers to flow;
he whose arm wields the thunderbolt struck down Rauhiṇa.
As he ascends to heaven,
both heaven and earth bow down before him; even the mountains tremble before his might.
He who is the drinker of Soma, the one whose arm is the thunderbolt,
he who holds the thunderbolt in his hand—
he who protects the one pressing the juice and the one cooking the oblation.
He who [helps] with his aid the one who praises and the one who exerts himself, for whom prayer is a source of strength, for whom the Soma is,
and for whom this bounty is— O people, he is Indra.
O you who, even when provoked, grant strength to the one who presses and cooks [the oblation]— you indeed are truly real;
may we, O Indra, be ever dear to you.
May we, with brave sons, proclaim our wisdom at the assembly.
Having been born, he looked out from the lap of his parents; he knows not of any other progenitor than the earth.
Displaying his power as he exerts himself,
he has observed the ordinances of the gods; he, O people, is Indra—
the one who desires the Soma, the lord of the bay horses, among these [beings].
He at whose roar all the worlds tremble,
he who slew Śambara and Śuṣṇa—
he who is the sole hero, O people, he is Indra.
May Indra and Agni be auspicious to us with their protections;
may Indra and Varuṇa, to whom oblations are offered, be auspicious to us;
may Indra and Soma grant us well-being, prosperity, and health.
May Indra and Pūṣan be auspicious to us in the winning of booty;
may Bhaga be auspicious to us, may our praise be auspicious,
may Purandhi be auspicious to us, and may riches be auspicious.
May the praise of the true, well-guided one be auspicious for us;
may Aryaman, born of many, be auspicious to us.
May Dhātṛ be auspicious to us, and may Dhartṛ also be auspicious to us.
May the far-reaching [goddess] be auspicious to us with her self-sustaining powers;
may the two great worlds, heaven and earth, be auspicious; may the mountain be auspicious to us; and may the easy invocations of the gods be auspicious to us.
May Agni, whose face is light, be auspicious to us; may Mitra and Varuṇa and the Aśvins be auspicious;
may the good deeds of the doers of good be auspicious to us.
May the swift wind blow auspiciously for us.
May Heaven and Earth be auspicious to us at our first invocation; may the intermediate space be auspicious for us to behold.
May the plants and the forest trees be auspicious to us;
may the victorious Lord of the Atmosphere be auspicious to us;
may the god Indra with the Vasus be auspicious to us.
May Varuṇa, the one of auspicious praise, together with the Ādityas, grant us peace; may Rudra, the healer, together with the Rudras, grant us peace;
and may Tvaṣṭṛ, together with the divine wives (gnās), hear us here for our well-being.
May Soma be auspicious for us; may the sacred prayer be auspicious for us; may the pressing-stones be auspicious for us, and may the sacrifices be auspicious;
may the felling of the sacrificial posts be auspicious for us.
May the sacrificial grass be auspicious for us, and may the altar be auspicious.
May the sun, far-seeing, rise for our welfare, and may the four quarters of space be auspicious for us.
May the firm mountains be auspicious to us; may the rivers be auspicious to us, and may the waters be auspicious.
May Aditi be auspicious to us through her sacred ordinances.
May the Maruts, who are well-praised with hymns, be auspicious to us;
may Viṣṇu be auspicious to us, and may Pūṣan be auspicious to us; may the means of protection be auspicious to us, and may Vāyu be auspicious.
May the divine Savitṛ, our protector, be auspicious to us;
may the radiant dawns be auspicious to us;
may Parjanya be auspicious to our progeny.
May the Lord of the Field be auspicious to us; may he be the source of well-being.
May the lords of truth be auspicious to us; may our coursers be auspicious and our cattle be auspicious.
May the Ṛbhus, the skillful-handed doers of good deeds, be auspicious to us;
may the Fathers be auspicious to us in our invocations;
may the Viśvedevas, the gods, be auspicious to us.
May Sarasvatī, together with our prayers, be auspicious; may those who bring us gifts be auspicious, and may those who bestow rewards be auspicious;
may the celestial beings be auspicious to us, the terrestrial beings be auspicious to us, and the aquatic beings be auspicious to us.
May the god Aja Ekapād be auspicious to us; may Ahi Budhnya be auspicious, and may the ocean be auspicious. May the protector of the waters, the lord of the waters, be auspicious to us.
May Pṛśni, whose guardians are the gods, be auspicious for us.
May the Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus take pleasure in this newly performed prayer.
May the divine ones and the earthly ones hear us,
as well as those born of the cow who are worthy of sacrifice—
those who are the priests of the gods and worthy of worship.
O worshipful ones, immortal ones, knowers of the cosmic order (ṛta), may you grant us wide-striding space today. Do you all protect us always with your blessings. PS 12.17.5
May that be so, O Mitra and Varuṇa; may that be so, O Agni. May this recitation be auspicious and healing for us.
May we attain the path and a firm foundation.
Homage to the great, divine abode!
Agni moves, having entered into Agni;
he is the son of the seers, this sovereign ruler.
To him I offer an oblation of clarified butter;
may I not be deprived of my share among the gods. O Jātavedas, being yoked, carry [the offering] from the front.
O Agni, know this which is being performed;
you are the physician and the maker of the remedy.
Through you, may we obtain cattle, horses, and men.
So do thou, O Agni Jātavedas, being wise and most youthful, act with this oblation against whichever Piśāca has devoured him.
So that he may fall into his enclosures—
whoever has played against him or whoever has devoured him— so that he may fall into his enclosures.
So do thou, O Agni Jātavedas, acting in harmony with all the gods,
pierce his two eyes and pierce his heart.
Cut out his tongue; crush his teeth!
O Agni, most youthful one, crush back that Piśāca who has devoured him.
Whatever has been taken from him, whatever has been carried away, whatever has been brought to ruin, or whatever has been devoured by himself or by the Piśācas—
that, O Agni, do thou, being wise, bring back again.
You have sent forth the breath, the vital spirit, into this body.
Whosoever has deceived you in the drinking of water— whether in the rice-mash, the stirred drink, or in the licking of food— [may he be struck down].
Let the Piśācas depart from this person, along with their offspring; let him be free from disease.
Whoever has harmed you in milk or in meat—
May the Piśācas drive away that food and grain which ripens without being ploughed; may this person be free from disease, together with his offspring.
Whether it be raw, well-cooked, variegated, or thoroughly ripened—
whatever this Piśāca has harmed while eating, may the vigorous Indra strike that with his thunderbolt.
May the bold Soma split his head—
whichever flesh-eating demon or Piśāca has harmed you by day or by night upon your bed.
Therefore, O Agni, knowing this, burn him away and cast him into the lap of Destruction.
[This applies to those who act against] Soma, Indra, and King Varuṇa.
By the strength of Viṣṇu, by the impulse of Savitṛ,
by the office of Agni as Hotṛ, and by the sacred word of Jātavedas, the youngest [Agni], may I drive away the Piśācas.
O Agni Jātavedas, with your powers, slay the flesh-eating, blood-drinking Piśāca who steals the mind;
may this sacred prayer, accompanied by the sacrificial fee, be accepted as life.
So that he may live and become free from disease:
"May breath return to you; may life return; may sight return; may hearing return."
Strike away all our misfortunes; may we rejoice for a hundred winters with all our heroes intact.
Restore his mind to him again.
Again life, again strength—
O Agni, increase his out-breath and in-breath so that he may live.
O Sun, give back his sight;
O Wind, stir up his breath;
[give] his body its flesh.
O Agni, you yourself gather it together;
O Jātavedas, bring back what has been eaten and what has been carried away.
Fashion his limbs;
may he swell again like Soma, O Jātavedas.
May this stalk swell; O Agni, make it full of sap, pure,
and free from disease, so that it may live.
"May the Maruts sprinkle me," [this is] one verse (RV 5.53.10).
"With a sacred prayer I release Jātavedas,
Agni the Hotṛ, the ageless, who has won the chariot" (RV 10.8.6).
Knowing all the births of the gods, may Agni carry the oblation according to their respective portions.
Those male sorcerers...
Those women who are sorceresses—
powerful Indra, with his thunderbolt,
strikes them down headlong.
O Agni, with your great weapon, strike down the flesh-eating Piśāca whom we curse, who curses us, whom we hate, and who hates us.
Burn him up here as well, O Jātavedas—
he who has initiated it, or he whose it is, or the Apsaras, or he who performs it through secret agreement, the sorcerer.
The owl-demon, the bewildering one, whose demon is he—
him [I strike]...
He who has taken [it], or whose ancestral portion it was.
May the thief, the one afflicted by dogs, and those who split asunder— may the flesh-eating *piśāca* fall from the gambling-place, seeking to satisfy his craving for raw flesh.
The whirlwind that drives the owl-demon—
him who is driven by a man on a chariot...
The flesh-eater, the sorcerer, the slanderer, the *piśāca*—
with Vaiśvānara as his companion and with Sūrya, [drive] him away.
May Rudra, the archer, loosen the life-force of him who seeks tribute from us, or he who obstructs our agriculture, or he who curses us with sorcery.
May the sorcerers find no one to pity him;
may all directions be devoid of light for him.
May both worlds, heaven and earth, burn him down; O Jātavedas, consume him utterly here! May the luminous ones and those radiant realms that heat burn him.
O Agni, those bodies of yours which are ever-present— protect my vital organs with them on every side;
let not the sorcerers harm you, O Beholder of Men.
May the divine waters close the mouths of the Piśācas, so that they [may not harm] this body of mine.
May you fly again, invincible,
dwelling among flowers, dwelling among fruits, and ever protected by Indra.
May the piśācas always die; may not even one of them remain. May the yātudhānas who fall [be destroyed].
Day and night, perform the services;
may Night protect me from them,
and I entrust myself to the Day.
I bind this amulet upon you for long life and for splendor—

may we be masters of all heroic sons.
May we become possessors of all wealth as the dawns shine forth;
those who wish to harm my riches shall be thwarted by the name "śamyā."
May the night pass them away; may the night be a pleasant bed for us. Then no thief shall be found, and no enemy shall be found.
Auspicious art thou, O Night; like a mortar ground with flour, thou young woman, dost bear every form of the cow.
Endowed with sight, touching my limbs, touching my beauties—*mṛśatī* with *Lopez*; 10.128.4.
O Bhaṭṭa, you have released the golden, celestial, and immortal Adityas.
Lopez: [He sees] the divine golden disk of the sun;
Bhatt.: [he sees] the divine, golden-splendored sun-disk—[the one] who today comes as a thief.
PS_14,8.8: yo adya stena āyati.
May the night strike down the neck and the head of that mortal enemy who seeks to do harm.
Like one who approaches with his feet, like one who reaches out with his hands—
he who approaches as a thief.
Being crushed, he goes away; he goes away, indeed, he goes away;
he went away upon a dry stump.
Make the blind snake that stands in the smoke at night headless;
strike out both its eyes.
Strike the thief down upon the wooden post!
O Night, those oxen of yours that have sharp horns and swift paces—
With these, may he ferry us across all difficulties every day,
remaining unharmed night after night.
May we cross over with our own bodies;
may the enemies not cross over, like those without a boat in the deep.
Just as a grain of millet, having fallen away from of old,
is no longer found,
even so, O Night, cause [the enemy] to fall away.
Whoever seeks to harm us—
drive away the thief who steals clothes, the one who steals cattle or goats, and the robber.
