Born from you, O Rudra, she is most peaceful; for you have appeared to us with refreshing nourishment and healing remedies.
Drive away the consumptions from us, drive away distress, O Bhaga; dispel the diseases and drive away our ailments in all directions.
You, O Rudra, are the most excellent among the gods.
O you of mighty power, with fierce arms,
you have become one who rejoices with a most wrathful mind, O son of Rudra.
Do thou indeed send forth our heroes with healing remedies; O Maghavan, accompanied by the Maruts, become wide for us.
(Bhatt. reads *marutvam*).
Carry us across the distress to well-being;
drive away all threats from us.
For you, O Bull, are our most excellent beholder.
To this Rudra, the fierce, the bountiful,
the ruler of heroes, we offer our prayer, so that there may be well-being for our bipeds and well-being for our quadrupeds.
Where among them is the hand of Rudra that is gracious, full of healing,
and the remover of divine affliction?
Let consumption depart from us, let Destruction depart; let disease flee away like an army that has been released. Cast far away your ancient snares and abandon them!
Bhaṭṭāraka says:
"He has attained [it], he has abandoned [it]"; see Lelli PS 15,20.6:
"The Arhat bears the discarded bow."
The Worthy One gazes upon the golden, all-formed [sacrifice].
O Worthy One, you take pity on all this that moves; for you, Bhava, there is nothing distant and no place beyond your reach.
Immediately you behold the entire earth.
Homage be to you, O lightning; homage be to you, O thunder.
Homage be to your stone with which you cast toward the direction;
O fierce King of the gods, do not [strike us].
May our men suffer no harm;
we destroy the *rakṣas* and the diseases from us by means of sacred power (*brahman*).
O Brahmā, let us destroy whatever ailment is in the limbs,
as well as the darts of consumption and the sores.
We lead them away from here.
I lead you two away, O Paśupati, increasing you with clarified butter as an oblation.
"Against him whom we hate and him who hates us, you two shall make his dwelling;
speak over it, O Lords of Creatures!"
Wherever they struck my bipeds and quadrupeds at birth,
may that [sin] harm my mother.
That auspicious form of yours which is Rudra,
those healing powers of yours that exist,
and that life-sustaining form of yours—
With those [powers], may you two be gracious to us!
The observers of vows do not violate their sacred laws; enlivening truth, they speak at the assemblies.
He who has joined together both these worlds, heaven and earth, with his mind and heart— he is Prajāpati, the Lord of Creatures.
He protects well and rains down;
he knows the jewel-medicine brought forth from the gods.
Therefore, may you both be gracious to us— for our life, not for death,
and furthermore, for our safety.
The possessed ones sit together, joined for the sake of strength;
their power is vast.
It shines; it is a shining.
O you two great shining ones in the mid-air and likewise in heaven!
With those two, come toward us,
so that we may remain uninjured with all our heroes;
[may we be] with all our heroes, uninjured.
We have taken our stand upon the delighter,
so that wealth may not be thirsty for us,
whether it be in heaven or what moves in the waters.
I invoke Indra and Agni first; I call upon the auspicious Maruts;
I call upon all the auspicious gods.
May they protect this oblation for me!
O Agni, you, as a god, were the first to win immortality and divinity.
Your heart has gone to heaven;
O Jātavedas, bestow upon us those auspicious waters.
Fire moves within fire, having entered it.
This one is the son of the seers, the sovereign ruler;
for him I offer an oblation of clarified butter.
May I not be excluded from the portion of the gods.
O Jātavedas, those gods who abide in heaven, those on earth, and those in the broad mid-air;
those who are in the mountains, in the peaks, and within the waters—
O gods, ward off the thunderbolt!
O Jātavedas, make Mitra [the friend] with the quarters; make Mitra the wise overseer with the intermediate directions.
Do not harm us with your celestial fire,
that by which the Maruts go forth competing,
flashing and thundering.
Like a bull you come bellowing; O Parjanya, your chariot is terrifying—
may it indeed grant us protection.
The Maruts who spread forth lightning and thunder from the waters, for our sake, [grant] all-desired cultivation.
May he who, with bowless weapon, stretches his arrows— the lightning and the thunderbolt—
from the atmosphere, from the wind, and from heaven; may he [protect us].
Let there be homage to those Maruts for their vital power;
let them go by a path that is well-prepared, pleasant, and most auspicious.
O Indra, do not destroy our barley;
by means of this, we make him our friend.
Darbha is the foremost of plants.
He was born with a hundred stalks; sent by the gods,
this bull has come for our well-being, in harmony with the Maruts.
You are the weapon of the Asura Vṛṣākṣa;
I know you as such, and thus is the hope of Karṇa, the knower of all.
Do not go down toward her; let me guard her for twelve days.
My sword is of keen iron, well-sharpened by Indra and Agni.
"By that [means], drive away the consuming fire;
do not let it reach my cultivation— do not destroy my crop."
O Maruts, spare us from the small stones of heaven; [spare us] with your stones.
With a branch of the udumbara tree, we ward off the lightning that blinds the eyes;
O Maruts, have mercy on us!
With the bright stones of heaven,
with the branch of the udumbara tree, and with the eye of discernment.
We ward off the thunderbolt.
Step from one path to another, from mountain to mountain.
Resorting to the mountain, crush the trees, not the barley;
I bind you with a cord.
O you who are overcome by excessive beauty,
though you rest upon the mountain ridge, crush the grass, not the barley!
"Uśatī by name you are, Salindā by name;
go to another among these, go to him whom we hate!
[Follow] the distant enclosure.
Toward the distant one, following the consciousness;
toward the distant one, run away! From here we cause you to perish.
By means of the powerful Brahmā,
may the water of existence become the water of the water of existence.
Having become smaller than the smallest—
then come here, O lowest darkness!
Be pleasant, be auspicious!
Become more auspicious than the auspicious;
having become lighter than froth,
approach this sacrificial grain.
Homage be to you, O lightning; homage to you, O thunder!
Homage to you, O Agni, whose weapon is far-reaching; do not harm us, neither our bipeds nor our quadrupeds.
With power against power, we enclose you with power;
this is the great power of Indra.
From the earth you have ascended to heaven;
tread upon that which is not ploughed by the furrow.
O Indra, do not destroy our barley.
Those [waters] that rise from the ocean, those from springs and from rivers—
the serpent of lightning within them is exceedingly fierce.
"Drive away Saturn from here. Anuvāka 5. PS 15,23.13 (23).
(15) Kāṇḍa 16:
Homage to Antaka, to Death, here—
— May this man be together with his vital breath;
in the portion of the Sun, in the world of immortality, may his out-breaths and in-breaths find delight here.
Bhaga has lifted him up; Soma, rich in stalks, has lifted him up;
the Maruts, the gods, have lifted him up.
Up, O Indra and Agni, for well-being!
Here is your breath, O Asura; here is your life-force, here is your vitality, here is your mind.
We lift you up from the snares of Nirṛti by means of divine speech; step forth!
Do not fall down from here.
Releasing yourself from the fetter of death,
do not be cut off from this world, nor from the sight of Agni and Sūrya.
For you let Vāta Mātariśvan blow; for you let the immortal waters rain down;
may Sūrya shine auspiciously upon your body.
May Death have mercy on you; do not go forth from me!
O man, let there be for you an ascent and no descent; let it provide for you the skill and vigor of life.
Mount indeed this immortal, pleasant chariot; then, though aged, you shall speak at the assembly.
Let not your mind go there, nor let it be lost to view.
Do not be heedless toward the living; do not go to the ancestors. May all the gods protect you here.
Do not set your heart on those who have departed.
Those who lead [beings] to the far distance—ascend from the darkness to the light; come hither, O Bhaṭṭa!
We take hold of your hand.
The two dogs of Yama, Śyāma and Śabala, who guard the path—
come hither; do not hesitate.
Do not stay with averted mind; do not follow this path, for it is fearsome. I speak of that path by which you formerly led [him].
O man, do not fall into this darkness;
there is danger ahead, but safety behind you. May the fires that dwell within the waters protect you.
May the one whom men kindle protect you;
may Vaiśvānara Jātavedas protect you. May the lightning not strike you down from the sky along with its flash.
May the earth protect you; may the sky protect you;
and may both the sun and the moon protect you.
Let no flesh-eater seize you.
Move away from the place of collapse;
may the divine weapon protect you from the intermediate space,
and may both awakening and watchfulness protect you.
May he who is sleepless and he who is never heedless protect you;
may he who is a guardian protect you, and he who is ever-watchful.
May they protect you, may they guard you, and may they deliver you from distress.
Homage to them; to them, svāhā!
May Vāyu, Indra, Dhātṛ, and the protecting Savitṛ establish you among the living beings and in the ocean.
Let not the breath abandon your strength; we call after your life-force.
Let not the jaw-clencher nor the crushing grip find you; let not darkness find you.
Let not the tongue perish; how could it be [lost]? O Bhaṭṭa, let the Ādityas and the Vasus lift you up upon the sacrificial grass (barhis).
—O Indra and Agni, [come] for our well-being!
O gods, may this man remain right here; may he not go from here to the other world.
With this [mantra] of a thousandfold power,
we carry you across from death.
I have carried you up from death.
Let those who bestow vital strength blow together; let not women with disheveled hair blow upon you.
Let not the weeping, evil-voiced ones wail for you;
I have brought you back, I have found you; you have returned, renewed once more.
I have found every limb of yours, your entire sight, and your whole life.
Bhaṭṭa: "May Dyaus lift you up, may Pṛthivī lift you up, and may Prajāpati have grasped you. (PS 16.2.9)
The plants, whose king is Soma, have carried you up beyond death,
as far as your light has extended.
Away from you we drive away darkness;
away from you, death and destruction; away from you we cast down consumption.
Take hold of this nourishment of immortality;
may your life-span be unbroken until old age. I bring back to you the breath and the vitality.
O dust, do not come near me; do not overwhelm me. Come toward the light of the living, toward the world;
I bring you here for a hundred autumns.
I grant you a longer and more extended life;
may the nooses of death and the curses be released.
O Bhaṭṭa,
from the wind I have found your breath, and from the sun my eye around you.
Whatever mind is yours, I place that within you; perceive with your limbs, speak with your tongue when addressing,
and breathe through your breath among bipeds and quadrupeds.
Like a newborn fire, I blow upon you with my breath;
homage to your eye, O Death, homage to your vital breath have I rendered.
Bhaṭṭa: *tekaram* PS 16,3.4:
"May this one live, let him not die; we cause him to rise up."
I prepare a remedy for him; O Death, do not slay the man! [Grant him] life-sustaining power, free from affliction.
I [take] the living herb,
the protecting, the overcoming, the powerful, the Arundhatī.
I invoke him here for our safety and well-being.
Bhaṭṭa Huveṣman:
Speak for me; do not seize him!
Let him go; though he belongs to you, let him remain here with his full life-span.
O Bhava and Śarva, be gracious and grant us protection; drive away misfortune and bestow long life upon us.
May the weapon of the gods pass you by.
I have carried you across the dust; I have saved you from death. Having driven away the flesh-eating Agni from afar, I set up a boundary for you so that you may live.
Speak for him, O Death;
have mercy on him; let him go from here. (Bhatt.: let him go from here.)
Unharmed in every limb, with beautiful hair, may he enjoy his life-span through a hundred years until old age.
Is it by oneself, O hundred-year-old? That path of yours, O Death, which leads through the realm of dust, shall not be obstructed.
Therefore, protecting this path,
we fashion the sacred word (*brahman*) as armor for him.
I establish for you both out-breath and in-breath.
May they ward off old age and death, and grant long life and well-being;
I drive far away all the messengers of Yama who roam about, sent by Vaivasvata.
Far away, drive off the enemy, Nirṛti, the seizer, the flesh-eating demons, the Piśācas,
and every demon and evil being.
That we strike away like darkness.
O Agni, from the immortal, life-bestowing Jātavedas, I win for Manu your breath.
So that you may not suffer harm and may be immortal, being in harmony—I perform this for you; may it be fully accomplished for you.
May Heaven and Earth be auspicious for you.
May the two [fires] be placed upon the non-heating [altar];
may the sun shine auspiciously for you; O Bhaṭṭa, may the sun shine auspiciously for you; may the wind blow auspiciously for your heart.
May the auspicious waters flow toward you—
the celestial waters rich in milk;
may the plants be auspicious for you.
I have raised you up from the lower [world] toward the higher earth;
there may the two Ādityas protect you.
Both the sun and the moon;
that garment which is your covering,
and the lower fold you make for yourself—
We make that [ointment] auspicious for your body;
let it be smooth upon your touch.
O barber, with a sharp razor that is well-tempered and radiant, you shave the hair and beard.
Do not steal away his life with your gaping mouth; may rice and barley be auspicious for you—
those which are free from disease and full of sweetness.
These two drive away consumption; these two release one from distress—
whatever you eat and whatever you drink.
Grain from cultivation, milk,
whatever is edible and whatever is inedible— I make all that food for you, free from poison.
For the day and for the night— for both of them— we entrust you,
from the stingy ones who desire to devour.
Protect us on every side!
May you have a hundred, ten thousand, or even two, three, or four *ayuta*s of years;
may you live for two *yugas*, three, or four.
May Indra and Agni, and all the gods, grant their approval without resentment. For the autumn, for you, for the winter, for the spring.
We entrust you to the summer; may the rains be pleasant for you,
in which the plants flourish.
Death rules over bipeds; death rules over quadrupeds.
Therefore, from Death, the Lord, [I protect] you.
I lift you up; do not die!
You are unharmed; you shall not die. Do not fear.
Indeed, they do not perish there,
nor do they go to the lower realm;
everyone there lives.
The cow, the horse, the man, the beast—
wherever this sacred formula (brahman) is performed,
[there] the enclosing-stick is made for the sake of life.
May it protect you from the sorcery of your kinsmen and those related to you;
be unharmed, immortal, and long-lived.
O Bhaṭṭa, may Yama [protect] you; let not your vital breaths abandon your living body.
May all the gods sustain you with immortality.
May Paśupati be your advocate;
may Savitṛ grant you freedom from disease;
may breath enter into you for the sake of life.
May the gods release you from those one hundred and one deaths, and from those destructive powers that must be overcome.
From Agni Vaiśvānara. (PS 16.5.8) (Anuvāka 1)
I sprinkle the slayer of demons, the vigorous one; I approach for protection the most extensive friend.
Agni, kindled by sacred rites, sharpens his weapons.
May he protect us from harm by day and by night.
O Jātavedas, being well-kindled, touch with your flame those who have grown strong with iron fangs.
Seize the fools who worship false gods with your tongue; having devoured the flesh-eaters, place them in your mouth.
O you who possess both sets of teeth, set your fangs against both.
O Agni, as a destroyer sharpening both the lower and the higher [weapons],
go around the atmosphere.
With your jaws, crush the sorcerers!
O Agni, split open the skin of the sorcerer; let the destructive thunderbolt strike him down with its heat.
O Jātavedas, rend his joints asunder;
let the flesh-eating, flesh-craving [beast] tear him apart.
O Agni, fashioning your arrows with sacrifices—
Enveloping the word-thorns with thunderbolts,
pierce the sorcerers in their hearts with them; break their arms back against them.
O Agni Jātavedas, wherever you now see a sorcerer— whether he stands still, O Agni, or moves about, or flies through the mid-air— [seize him].
Piercing all with darkness,
sharpening [your weapons], O Jātavedas, strike down the sorcerer who has already begun his attack, and also the one who is still preparing, with your spears.
O Agni, blazing forth, strike down first; let the scavenging vultures, the spotted ones, devour the raw-eaters.
O Agni, declare here which one that is.
Whosoever is a sorcerer, whosoever hears this— seize him with your fuel, O Most Youthful One;
deliver him over to the eye of the one who beholds men.
With your sharp eye, O Agni, protect the sacrifice;
O wise one, lead it forward toward the Vasus,
blazing against the destructive Rakṣasas.
O thou who beholdest men, let not the sorcerers harm thee.
O beholder of men, look upon the Rakṣas among the people;
crush its three points.
O Agni, crush his ribs with your heat;
cut the root of the sorcerer into three pieces. Let the sorcerer go three times toward your snare.
O Agni Jātavedas, him who destroys the *ṛta* with falsehood,
strike him down before the very eyes of the singer, flashing forth with your flame.
O Agni, whatever curse a pair utters today, or whatever harshness of speech the bards produce, that which is born as a shower of arrows from the mind of wrath— [may it pass us by].
With that [weapon] pierce the Yātudhānas in the heart;
crush the Yātudhānas with heat; O Agni, crush the Rakṣas with your flame.
With your supreme radiance, crush the foolish gods;
crush those who thirst for life and burn with passion.
May the gods today crush the wicked.
May the curses released against him turn back upon him;
may the arrows of his own speech strike him in his vital organs; may the sorcerer fall into every snare.
From of old, O Agni, you have crushed the sorcerers;
the *rakṣas* have never conquered you in battles.
Burn down the flesh-eaters together with their roots.
May you not be released from the divine weapon of his! That sorcerer who smears himself with human flesh, or with the flesh of a horse or a beast;
O Agni, tear off with your heat the heads of those who bring the milk of the cow that must not be slain;
the milk of the cow belongs to the year.
May there be no sorcerer for him, O Agni, who looks upon men; whoever should seek to satisfy himself with the first-milked nectar,
pierce him in his vital organ from the front with your flame.
Let the sorcerers drink poison;
let the evil-doers be cut down for Aditi.
May the god Savitṛ cast them away, cast them far away.
May they conquer the supreme portion of the plants.
O Agni, protect us from below and from above; protect us from behind and from the front.
These unaging, most fiercely burning [flames] of thine— let them, glowing brightly, consume the one who speaks evil against thee—
from behind, from before, from below, and from above.
O Agni, as a poet protect us with your poetic wisdom; as an ageless friend, protect your friend so that he may reach old age.
O immortal Agni, you are our protector among mortals.
O Agni, bestow that eye upon the singer by which you may see the hoof-striking sorcerer,
with the Atharvan-like divine light.
Burn down the untruthful one who tramples upon the truth!
O Agni, O powerful one, we place you, the sage, as a fortress around us.
Day by day, Agni shines with great light, he of bold appearance, the slayer of those who are treacherous.
He makes all things manifest by his greatness;
he overcomes the godless, malevolent illusions;
he sharpens his two horns to gore the Rakṣasa.
The immortal Agni, with his bright radiance, drives away the demons;
he is pure, purifying, and worthy of praise.
O Agni, protect us from distress; O God, burn against those who seek to harm us with your most scorching, ageless flames.
O Jātavedas, those two horns of yours which are ageless, fiercely glowing, and sharpened by prayer—
with those two, [burn] the Kimīdin who attacks us with an evil heart.
O Jātavedas, cast down the sorcerer who comes against us;
O Indra, burn the destructive Rākṣasas with poison.
O Agni, with your bright glow and with flames whose tips are glowing, burn up the paired ones, O Agni.
O Yātudhānas and Kimīdins,
I sharpen you together with my inspired thoughts; remain watchful, O unerring sage!
O Agni, with your heat, crush the heat of the Yātudhāna and the Rakṣas on every side.
Shatter their strength and their valor!
O Indra,
crush the Sādānveyas with the foolish [missiles] that destroy the sorcerers (yātudhāna).
O Agni, let this pair of sorcerers, turned away from each other, lie prostrate, crushed by your heat.
May Bṛhaspati protect us from behind.
May Indra, from above, from below, and from the one who seeks to harm us— from the front and from the middle—
grant us, his friends, a wider space as our friend.
O Indra and Soma, burn up the Rakṣas; crush them and cast them down, O Bulls, you who increase the darkness!
Destroy that mindless one and consume him utterly.
Drive away the dead; sharpen your weapons against the devourers.
O Indra and Soma, let the evil against the one who utters evil be consumed by heat,
like a cauldron glowing with fire.
O Indra and Soma, bestow hatred upon the hater of Brahman, the flesh-eater with the terrible eye,
the Kimīdin who never ceases his hostility.
O Indra and Soma, cast the evildoers into the abyss.
Pierce them in the darkness where there is no support,
so that not even one of them shall rise up from here again; let that be your fierce and wrathful power for the sake of victory.
O Indra and Soma, drive away from heaven with those stones heated by fire— those ageless, heat-armed weapons— with which you strike down the devouring demons.
O Indra and Soma, pierce him with your thunderbolt; let him go forth without a sound. Cast down from heaven and from earth your weapon, the crusher of the one who speaks evil.
Fashion from the mountains that which sounds through the air,
with which you two consume the waxing demon;
O Indra and Soma, let it encompass you on every side.
This thought is like a girth upon a spirited horse; this oblation which I send forth to you with wisdom— O lords of men, quicken these prayers as if they were your own.
Remember us with your victorious impulses; strike down the malicious, treacherous Rākṣasas. O Indra and Soma, let there be no easy path for the evildoer.
Whoever would ever seek to harm me with malice;
whoever accuses me with false words while I am acting with a sincere mind.
May those who speak of non-existence be like water gathered in the hollow of one's hand; O Indra, let there be no speaker of what does not exist.
Bhaṭṭa: Those who, by their ways, sport with the one who proclaims the cooked offering, or those who defile the auspicious [sacrifice] with their own offerings; PS_16,9.8.
O Agni, may Soma deliver those who seek to harm our essence in our food, or place them in the lap of Destruction.

May he who is an enemy of horses, who is an enemy of cattle, or who is an enemy of our own bodies— may that thief, the perpetrator of theft, go to ruin; may he be utterly deprived of his body and his progeny.
May he be defeated in his own person and his offspring;
may he fall below all the three earths.
O gods, his glory withers away.
He who seeks to harm me by day and he who [seeks to harm me] by night—
true and false speech both touch the person who understands, so that it may be clearly discerned by him.
Of those two, that which is true, whichever is more upright—that indeed Soma protects; he strikes down the false.
Truly, Soma does not further the crooked.
He does not slay the Kṣatriya who holds [his word] falsely;
he slays the demon, he slays the one who speaks untruth;
both lie caught in the snare of Indra.
Whether I am one whose deity is false, or whether I have falsely presumed even the gods, O Agni— why, O Jātavedas, are you angry with us?
May those of deceitful speech fall into destruction!
May I die this very day if I am a sorcerer, or if I have consumed the vital breath of a man.
Bhaṭṭa:
And he who says to me in vain, "O sorcerer," may he be separated from his ten heroic sons. (PS 16.10.5)
Whoever says of me, "You are a sorcerer," or whoever, being pure, says of me, "I am a Rakshasa"—
may Indra slay him with his mighty weapon.
May she, the lowest of all creatures,
fall down— she who goes forth at night like an owl, hiding her body from the malicious one.
May she fall into the endless abyss;
may the pressing-stones strike down the Rākṣasas with their thumping sounds.
Spread out, O Maruts! Search among the people! Search among the people!
Seize the Rākṣasas, crush them down!
Those who fly about at night having become birds,
or those who have placed their hostility toward the divine sacrifice.
These very ones fly about as dog-demons;
seeking to deceive, they wish to deceive Indra, the undeceivable one— seeking to deceive the undeceivable one.
Śakra whets his weapon for the treacherous; he shall surely hurl his thunderbolt at the sorcerers. Cast down the stone from heaven!
O Indra, O Maghavan, sharpen that which has been sharpened by Soma;
strike down the demons with the mountain from the east, from the west, from below, and from above.
Indra became the destroyer of the sorcerers who plunder the oblations as they sought to attack; indeed,
Śakra was like an axe against them.
Just as one would split wood with a vessel, may he go forth and destroy the *rakṣas*—
the owl-demon and the screech-owl demon.
O Indra, crush the *śvayātu*, the *kokayātu*,
the *suparṇayātu*, and the *gṛdhrayātu* like a millstone;
destroy the *rakṣas*.
May the demon of those possessing sorcery not overcome us; drive away the pair of Kimīdins.
May the Earth protect us from earthly distress.
May the intermediate space protect us from the celestial realm.
O Indra, slay the male sorcerer and also the woman who exults in her magic power.
Let the Bhaṭṭas,
the Śāsadās, the Vigrīvas, and the Mūradevas weep;
let them not see the sun as it rises.
Look on, look around— O Indra and Soma, be watchful;
hurl your weapon at the Rākṣasas.
A thunderbolt for those who follow the path of sorcery.
(PS 16.11.5) Anuvāka 2.
Those plants that are tawny, those that are bright, those that are ruddy, and those that are speckled; those that are dark-grey and those that are black— [all these are the plants].
We speak clearly to all:
may they protect this man from the consumption sent by the gods.
Of those plants of which heaven is the father, earth the mother, and the ocean became the root,
the divine waters are the first.
May they drive away from every limb that consumption born of sin which belongs to you.
I invoke the plants that have not perished, those that spread out, those that stand firm, and those that grow with a single peak.
The sun-bright, the stalk-bearing, the many-branched— I summon for you these plants belonging to all the gods,
formidable, and life-sustaining for man.
Whatever conquering power you possess, O conquerors, and whatever heroism and strength is yours—
with that, [save] this man from this disease.
May the plants release the man— Jīvalā, Naghāriṣā,
and the Jīvantī plant as well.
I invoke Arundhatī, Unnayanī, Puṣpā, and Madhumatī;
may the wise ones come hither.
O lands, by my words,
so that we may deliver this man from distress.
The food of Agni, the embryo of the waters,
those which grow up ever anew.
May these herbs, brought hither, be steadfast, thousand-named, and healing;
the plants whose essence is water are free from cavities.
Shaking off misfortune, with sharp horns,
they release the bonds of Varuṇa; they are fierce, those who corrupt the poison.
Moreover, let those herbs come here which destroy strength, which destroy demons, and which corrupt malevolent spells. PS_16,12.10 (12)
May the plants be auspicious for you— those most powerful herbs that have been purchased and those that have been praised;
may Sarasvatī, the eldest of the waters, protect us.
Our cow, horse, man, and livestock—
may the root of these plants be honey-sweet, their tip honey-sweet, and their middle honey-sweet.
Sweet is their leaf, sweet is their flower; born from honey, they yield as food the enjoyment of nectar,
with clarified butter for their nourishment and the bull as their leader.
As many as there are, and however many these herbs are upon the earth— may they all be thousand-leaved for us.
May they release [us] from death and from distress.
The tiger-skin amulet, the protector among plants, is the guardian against curses.
May Trāyamāṇā, the protector from curses, drive away all diseases and all demons far from us.
Like the roar of lions from their chests, like the herbs [emerging] from fire, let the consumption of cattle and men be driven away by these gathered plants.
May the boat, having been brought across, come to the river's further bank.
Bhaṭṭa: "... these plants, being released from Agni Vaiśvānara... (PS 16,13.5).
Those plants that spread across the earth, whose king is the Lord of the Forest (Vanaspati), and those plants which I know— may they come hither.
And those whom I behold with my eye— those unknown ones we now recognize, and those among whom we perceive that which is gathered.
May all the herbs together heed my words— those that grow as the descendants of Aṅgiras.
The all-healing plants that grow upon the mountains and on level ground— may they be auspicious and bring us joy.
May the herbs be auspicious for the heart.
The Aśvattha tree, Darbha grass, and Soma— the king of plants— are the immortal oblation.
Rice and barley are the two immortal medicinal sons of Heaven;
you rise up while it thunders.
The plants cry out when Parjanya, O you whose mother is Pṛśni,
favors you with his seed.
By means of this nectar, we cause this person to cross over with strength; thus,
I prepare a remedy.
Just as a hundred-year-old boar knows the plants,
and the mongoose knows the medicinal herbs.
May those plants which the Gandharvas and the serpents know come here; those which belong to Suparṇa and the Aṅgirases.
Those which the divine Raghata-knowers know, those which the swans know, and those which all winged birds know— [those are the waters].
Those herbs which the deer know,
I invoke them for his protection.
Of as many herbs as there are...
The inviolable cows graze; as many as there are goats and sheep, so many are they, possessing all-healing remedies.
I bring you hither;
as much medicinal knowledge as physicians know among men.
May those herbs, as many as there are, which have been brought for you, grant protection—
those that possess flowers and those that bear fruit.
May those that bear fruit and those that are fruitless milk for him,
like mothers,
for his safety.
I have raised you up from the five-shale [balance], I have raised you up from the ten-shale,
and I have raised you up from the fetter of Yama.
I have brought them across with medicinal herbs.
Indra’s chariot is the first; the chariot of the gods is the next.
This is the third [station] of Varuṇa; the chariot of the serpents has reached the lowest point. May he not strike the pillar.
The *darbha* grass is the flame, the young sprout; it is the bridle of the horse, the bridle of the man,
the seat of the chariot, and the foundation of the worlds.
The poison of the snakes is sapless; even fierce water is [sapless].
O White One, strike them down with your foot, both from the front and from behind.
Like wood floating on water, like the sapless poison of serpents, or like fierce water— having submerged the *araṃghas* [demons], [may he overcome them].
Having emerged, he spoke again:
"Like wood floating upon water, like the sapless poison of snakes, or like fierce water."
The horse of the pāidva kills the kaṣarṇīla, as well as the white and black [leprosy];
the pāidva [kills] the variegated [leprosy] that has been attended to.
The Pṛdāku split the head of Ratharvyā, the offspring of the chariot-horse.
O Bhaṭṭapradākvā,
O Paidva, go forward as the first;
we follow after you.
O Bhaṭṭa, may the serpent drive us away from the path; O Bhaṭṭa, [drive away] the serpent that gives all,
by which we go.
From here was Paidva born;
here is his place of departure;
these are the tracks of the steed.
The unslayable one, rich in vigor— may he not open what is closed,
nor close what is opened.
In this field there are two snakes, a female and a male; both of them are sapless.
The snakes here are sapless.
Those who are near and those who are far away—
I strike the scorpion with a club and the approaching snake with a staff.
This is the remedy for both Aghāśva and Svaja (or Saja).
Indra, as the horse Pedu, held back for me the serpent who sought to do me harm;
we meditate upon the power of Pedu.
Of him who is firm and whose abode is firm—
these serpents (pradākavaḥ) sit behind him, shining brightly.
Bhaṭṭa: It is countered [by the following]:
"Those whose life-force is destroyed and whose poison is destroyed are slain by Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt. (PS 16,16.1)
Indra struck them down; we have struck them down.
The cross-striped snakes are slain, and the vipers are crushed to pieces.
O Kairātikā, O young maiden, destroy the white and black leprosy that has been fashioned like a ladle upon the *darbha* grass.
The friend digs for the remedy with golden spades upon the ridges of the mountains.
This young physician has arrived, the conqueror of the spotted snake, the invincible;
he is indeed the crusher of the *svaja* snake.
And for both [the hymns] concerning the scorpion:
"Indra and Mitra and Varuṇa have crushed the serpents (ahīn) for me. (PS 16.16.5) [Bhatt. reads *mehīn*].
May both Vāta and Parjanya [protect] us; Paidva has made my snakes powerless— the *ahīn*,
the *pṛdākūs*, and the female *pṛdākvis*.
And the Bhaṭṭas [offer] the Pradākūns and Pradākvas, the Svajas, the Tirashcirājīs,
the Kasarṇīlas, and those with ten fewer than a hundred.
Indra slew the first progenitor of you, O serpent, with ten [blows] from the ten fingers.
As they are being consumed,
what indeed might remain of them as their essence?
Bhaṭṭa says: "Of whom? Of these [demons].
For I have seized their heads, like a fisherman seizing a large fish."
Bhaṭṭa Pauñjaṣṭi,
having gone to the middle of the ocean, wiped away the poison of the serpent.
May the rivers carry away the poison of all serpents;
slain are the cross-streaked snakes.
The vipers have been crushed.
I choose the plants as one skillfully chooses fertile fields. *Bhaṭṭa* says: "The *pradākavaḥ*. 16.16.10 (16). *oṣadhīnām ahaṃ vṛṇa urvarīr iva sādhuyā*.
I lead you away like mares to the stall—
let your poison go out! Whatever poison is in the fire or in the sun...
Whatever stem-poison or creeping poison there is upon the earth among the plants— let it go out, let it depart from you to the outside! PS_16,17.2
Make it fall from limb after limb; avoid the heart; then [remove] whatever fiery potency belongs to your poison.
May that [oblation] go downward to you;
O Agni, protect Vimada, and lead him back again, O Jātavedas, so that he may live.
May we not fall into your wrath or into misfortunes; may the poisoner not slay our man.
Those born from fire, those born from plants, those of the serpents, and those born from clouds who have become lightnings; [all these are dismissed].
Their many offspring have been born in manifold ways;
let us worship those serpents with reverence.
Bhaṭṭa [says]: From all [of them], PS 16.17.5:
"You are a maiden named Taudī, or you are named Ghṛtācī."
With my foot beneath your feet, I seize you, the poison-destroyer. Far away has the poison gone; it has perished.
Poison was [neutralized] by poison even before it had reached him.
Agni drove the poison out from the serpent; Soma caused it to flow away.
It has gone after the biter; the serpent has become immortal.
Bhaṭṭa’s *Daṃṣṭrāra-mantra*, PS 16.17.7 (17),
Anuvāka 3.
From where were those two born? Which was that half? From which world, from which earth?
The two calves arose from the waters of Virāj.
I ask you both: by which [cow] were they milked?
O Bhaṭṭa, you who, having been deceived, caused that [being] to cry out with its greatness, making the water its womb as it lay upon its threefold support.
The calf of Virāj, the cow of plenty, lying down,
has made her bodies turn away into the secret cave.
Of those four great ones,
of which he releases the fourth as speech—
one who is wise through austerity should know this as Brahman.
In which one is joined, in which one [is joined];
from the *bṛhat* [sāman], the *sāmans* were fashioned out of the sixth, from the five.
From what was the *bṛhatī* fashioned,
and from what was the *bṛhatī* measured out?
Bhaṭṭa: From whence, indeed?
[From] the Great One (bṛhatī), who was fashioned from the measure of the mother, from the measure of the mother.
For from Māyā was Māyā born;
from Māyā Mātali was born;
the sky is above as the image of Vaiśvānara.
As far as Agni has spread out between heaven and earth,
from that distant sixth [day] the hymns go forth;
from here they go forth toward the sixth day.
O Kaśyapa, we six sages ask you this, for you indeed desire to join what is joined and what is fit;
they call Virāj the father of Brahman.
Bestow that upon us and our friends according to the seasons.
Just so, Bhaṭṭa,
following that [Vāk] which has departed, the sacrifices depart; as she stands near, they stand near her.
In her womb, at her birth, the Yakṣa moves;
she is the Virāj, O seers, in the highest heaven.
She breathes with the breath of all those who breathe.
The Virāj follows after the self-ruling Svarāj;
they behold the beautiful Virāj who touches everything, yet some do not behold her. (PS 16.18.9)
Who knows the pairing of Virāj? Who [knows] the seasons, and who her ritual arrangement?
Who knows her steps that have been milked in many ways?
Who is her foundation? How many are her dawns?
This very one is she who first shone forth;
she moves within the waters, having entered them.
The bride has won; she is the mother of new songs.
Within her are great majesties.
Adorned with meters, the two Dawns shine brightly.
They move together along a common womb;
the two wives of Sūrya move together, knowing,
conscious, undecaying, and possessing abundant seed.
Three have followed the path of *ṛta*; three heats have followed the seed. One quickens progeny; one [quickens] vigor.
One [quarter] protects the kingdom of those who seek the gods;
the seers, fashioning the wings of the sacrifice, established that which was the fourth as the Agniṣṭoma.
Bringing the Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, the Jagatī, the Anuṣṭubh,
and the Bṛhadarkī to the sacrificer, they bring him the light;
following the five dawns, there are five milkings.
The five seasons follow the cow of five names;
by the fifteenfold [stoma], the five directions have been fashioned.
They have one head; they look toward the single world.
Six beings were born as the first-born of *ṛta*;
indeed, the six *sāmans* carry the six-day rite.
They say there are six unions, six ploughs for every song; they call heaven and earth six, and six are the wide expanses.
"Six they call cold and six indeed hot months; tell us of the seasons, which one among them is the extra? (ŚS; Bhatt. reads *śītān* ... *uṣṇān* in PS 16,19.6).
Bhaṭṭa [says]: "The season... whichever is the most exceeding; seven wise Suparṇas have sat down, following the seven meters and the seven initiations. (PS 16.19.7)
There are seven oblations, seven kindling-sticks,
seven honeys, and indeed seven seasons;
the seven clarified butters have encompassed all that exists.
"Seven priests sacrifice in due season;
I have heard that they are the seven vultures.
Eight are the first-born abodes of Ṛta."
The eight divine officiating priests of Indra,
Aditi who has eight wombs and eight sons—
to her, on the eighth night, the oblation goes forth.
Thinking that this was for my own welfare, I have come here;
I am yours for friendship, being auspicious. May my service be to you, and may our sacrifice, shared by us as co-born, be auspicious.
He moves among all our creatures, fully cognizant;
for the young cow, while yielding her first milk, has yielded the entire, pure, desirable nectar for Indra.
Then he gratified the fourfold gods, humans, asuras, and sages in four ways:
eight for Indra and six for Yama.
The seven seers [beheld] the waters in seven ways;
they poured them out after those five: humans and plants.
Who indeed is the cow? Who is the sole seer? What is the Sāman? What are the blessings?
[He who] alone increases the consumption-disease upon the earth.
What indeed is that single season?
The one cow, the one [sacrificer], the one seer,
the one *sāman*, and the single blessings.
Consumption on earth is increased by one;
the single season does not exceed it.
Homage to Prāṇa!
He under whose control all this is,
who has become the Lord of all,
in whom everything is established.
Homage to you, O Prāṇa, for your roar; homage to you for your thunder;
homage be to you for your lightning.
Homage to you, O Prāṇa, who rains down!
When the season has arrived, O Prāṇa,
you roar toward the plants.
They are impregnated, they conceive, and then many are born,
when through the thunder, O Prāṇa—
The plants cry out;
then everything that exists upon the earth rejoices.
When the vital breath roars with rain and thunder,
then the cattle rejoice.
"Great indeed shall it be for us! Thus,
when the plants were rained upon,
they conversed together through their vital breath.
Life has indeed crossed over for us;
you have made us all fragrant.
Homage to you, O Prāṇa, who breathe!
Homage be to Apānata!
Homage to you who face westward; homage to you who face eastward.
To you, all this homage!
Homage be to you as you come; homage be to you as you depart.
Homage to you, Prāṇa, as you stand; homage to you as you sit. O Prāṇa, that body of yours which is dear—homage to it!
Or whatever is dearer than thyself, O Prāṇa,
and whatever medicine is thine— bestow that upon us so that we may live.
Prāṇa clothes himself with offspring;
like a father [clothes] his beloved son, he attends upon it.
Prāṇa is indeed the lord of all—both that which breathes and that which does not breathe. Prāṇa is death; prāṇa is immortality. Prāṇa is immortality.
The gods worship the vital breath;
the vital breath, indeed, places the speaker of truth in the highest world.
The vital breath is Virāj; the vital breath is the Director;
all worship the vital breath.
The vital breath is Agni, the Moon, and the Sun. (Bhatt.: Agni...)
They call Prāṇa Prajāpati; prāṇa and apāna are rice and barley,
and the ox is said to be prāṇa.
For barley is said to be the out-breath (prāṇa) placed therein, and rice is called the in-breath (apāna).
Bhaṭṭa [says]: "Endowed with the *upāna* breath, the person breathes out and breathes in within the womb. (PS 16.22.3)
When you, O Prāṇa, quicken him,
then he is born from you;
they call Prāṇa Mātariśvan.
Vāta is indeed called prāṇa;
in prāṇa is the past and the future, in prāṇa everything is contained.
May all the goddesses— the plants belonging to Atharvan, to Aṅgiras, to the gods, and those born of men— rejoice.
When you, O Prāṇa, quicken [it];
when Prāṇa has rained down rain upon the great earth.
The medicinal herbs rejoice,
as do all other plants that exist.
Bhaṭṭa: "May you rejoice!
O Prāṇa, he who knows this of yours, and in whom you are established—" (PS 16.22.7).
"Let all bring tribute to him in that highest world,
just as the vital breaths (prāṇas) bring tribute."
All these creatures belong to you;
thus let them bring tribute to him who has heard of you, and those who have heard [of you].
The inner embryo moves within the deities; having become manifest, he is born again.
He is the past, the present, the world, and the future.
The father has entered into the son with his powers.
Like a swan rising from the water, he does not strike at the one single foot.
O friend,
that calamity which he might uproot today or tomorrow shall surely not occur.
There would be neither night nor day; today it would not be so, nor would there be night or day. Nothing is perceived, for the eight-wheeled [wheel] with its single rim rolls on.
The thousand-syllabled one extends forward and behind;
with one half he has encompassed this entire universe.
What is that banner which constitutes his other half?
He who rules over this entire creation and over everything that moves,
[is superior] to others, O wielder of the swift bow.
To you, O Prāṇa, let there be homage.
Homage to him who rules over this entire birth and over all that moves.
May the tireless, wise vital breath protect me through the sacred word;
standing erect, it remains awake while others sleep.
Surely he does not fall like an animal;
no one has heard him sleeping while others were asleep.
Bhaṭṭa heard:
"O Prāṇa, do not turn away from me; do not be like one who has turned away from me;
you shall not become anyone other than me."
O Breath, as one who is bountiful, I bind you to me for the sake of life, like the embryo of the waters. PS_16,23.6 (23)
Section 4.
This thousandfold, brilliant bull, rich in milk, bearing all forms within his flanks,
bestows auspiciousness upon the donor who sacrifices, providing for him.
The son of Bṛhaspati has stretched out the thread of the dawns.
He who was the first image of the waters, the lord over all like the goddess Earth.
May Pṛthivī,
the mother of the calves and the mistress of the cows,
grant us prosperity even in a thousandfold nourishment.
A man who is pregnant, aged, and full of milk—Bhaṭṭa [says]:
"The bull bears the headless trunk (kabandha) of Vasu;
him [he carries] for Indra by way of the paths traveled by the gods."
May Agni Jātavedas carry the oblation;
this is the portion for the gods, a binding of waters, the essence of plants, and of clarified butter.
Bhaṭṭa: Śakra chose this drop of Soma;
the great rock became his body. (Bhaṭṭa: with the *abhi* [verse], PS 16.24.4).
He is the father of the calves, the lord of the cows;
he is the father of the great jars. He is the calf, the afterbirth, the fresh milk, and the first-pressed cream.
Curdled milk and ghee—these indeed are his seed.
You bear a full vessel of Soma;
you are Tvaṣṭṛ, the progenitor of forms and of cattle.
May these wombs be auspicious for you;
O Svadhiti, bestow upon us those [wombs] which are yonder—
the vigor of Indra, the two arms of Varuṇa.
The shoulders belong to the Aśvins; this hump belongs to the Maruts.
Those who are wise seers and those who are possessed of insight say that it was brought together by Bṛhaspati.
He bears the clarified butter; his seed is ghee.
They call him thousandfold nourishment, and they call him sacrifice.
The bull, clothed in the form of Indra—him they call sacrifice.
So may that auspicious gift come to us, O gods!
You, rich in milk, extend yourself to the divine tribes; they call you Indra, they call you Sarasvant.
He who, as a brahmin, offers up a bull, bestows a thousand with a single mouth;
Bṛhaspati and Savitṛ have bestowed the mind upon you.
From Tvaṣṭṛ and Vāyu your self has been brought hither; with my mind I offer you in the intermediate space;
heaven and earth have become your sacrificial grass.
The limbs of that bull who goes among the gods like Indra, bellowing loudly for the cattle.
May Brahmā praise [you] with auspiciousness.
May Anumati be at his sides; may Bhaga be at his two flanks.
Bhaṭṭa said that Mitra spoke of the two ankle-bones as "these two belong to me exclusively."
Bhaṭṭa says: "From this [body], the buttocks became mine;
the hips belonged to the Ādityas; and the thighs belonged to Bṛhaspati."
The tail of the god Vāta was [there]; with it he shakes the plants.
The breast was that of Jāmiśaṃsa (Bhatt.: Āsirjāmisaṃsasya).
The vessel of Soma was held;
they spoke of the feet of the one who had arisen when they fashioned the bull. PS 16,25.4.
The anus was that of Sinīvālī;
the gods, having assembled, declared the skin to be that of Sūryā— whatever [was made] from all [of them].
They fashioned a bull;
those Kuṣṭhikas gave the hooves to Saramā (Bhartṛhari’s reading: Saramāyai) and to the tortoises.
The Bhaṭṭas held his hooves and the contents of his stomach for the insects that live in dog-dung.
O Bhaṭṭa, from the Śaparttas,
protect us with your two horns; you ward off the enemy and strike him down with your eye.
He who is the lord of cows, the inviolable one, hears what is auspicious with his two ears;
he performs a hundred sacrifices and attains a hundredfold prosperity.
The fires do not burn him; all the gods hear him, protect him, and quicken him.
O Brahmin, he who offers up a bull as a sacrifice—
having given a bull to a Brahmin—
he makes his mind most excellent.
May he behold the prosperity of the inviolable cows within his own pen.
O Bhaṭṭa, may we have inviolable cows; may we have progeny; and may there also be bodily strength for us.
May all the gods grant their approval to this [sacrifice] for the giver of the bull; here is he who,
having drunk, possesses the power of Indra.
He bears wealth that brings consciousness;
he possesses this milch-cow, easy to milk, who has a calf forever.
He milks the wise one into his power before the dawning of day; tawny-hued, bestowing vigor from the sky,
the all-formed strength of Indra has come to us.
Bestowing offspring and wealth upon us, may we sit near the nourishment of riches.
We entrust this youth here to you.
Playing with them, move according to our will;
O fortunate ones, do not harm us by birth,
but attend to us with the increase of wealth.
May the sprinkling be joined here in this stall;
may the seed of the bull be joined.
O Upendra, this is your power.
This protective amulet,
a hero, is bound upon the hero.
Possessed of vigor, a slayer of rivals, a heroic hero, a protector, and most auspicious—
this jewel is a slayer of rivals and a source of excellent heroes.
May the powerful, vigorous, and conquering hero come forth, subduing and destroying the malevolent magic.
By means of this amulet, Indra slew Vṛtra.
By this the wise one overcame the Asuras;
by this he conquered both heaven and earth; by this he conquered the four quarters.
This is the Srāktya amulet,
the counter-turner, the protective amulet; it is a powerful amulet that crushes adversaries.
May he protect us from every side.
This Agni has said, and Soma has said this; Bṛhaspati, Savitṛ, and Indra have said this.
May those various gods, acting as our domestic priests, drive back the sorceries with their counter-spells.
May the two protective amulets ward off diseases; I place myself between heaven and earth,
as well as between day and the sun.
And may these gods, with you as their domestic priests, drive back the sorceries with counter-spells against this Brahmaṇaspati.
May those who wear the *srāktya* amulet as a protective charm be struck down by their own counter-spells (*pratisara*). 16.27.6. May they be afflicted.
Having ascended to heaven like the sun,
the controller subdues the *kṛtyā* with the *srāktya* amulet.
Like a wise seer,
I have conquered all hostile armies; I strike down the demons.
The spells that belong to the Aṅgirases, the spells that belong to the Asuras,
and the spells that have been fashioned by oneself—
And those which have been brought by others—
let both of these go away to the far distance, beyond the ninety navigable rivers.
May the gods— Indra, Viṣṇu, Savitṛ, Rudra, and Agni— bind this amulet and armor for him.
Prajāpati, Parameṣṭhin, Virāj, Vaiśvānara, and all the seers—
you are the supreme among herbs.
Like the ox among creatures,
like the tiger among beasts of prey— him whom we desired, him we have obtained.
They spoke of the counter-attack:
"He indeed becomes a tiger, and also a lion, and also a bull."
He who wears this jewel shines forth in all directions;
the *apsarases* do not strike him down.
Neither Gandharvas nor mortals [surpass him];
he who wears this amulet shines forth in all directions.
Kaśyapa created you;
Kaśyapa impelled you. Indra bore you among men. (Bhatt. reads *abhivas*.)
Bearing [it], he conquered for the one who seeks alliance.
The gods bound on the jewel that crushes rivals as armor, [saying], "O Bhaṭṭa, conquer with tears! (PS 16,28.4).
Whoever seeks to harm you with magical spells, whoever seeks to harm you with initiatory rites, or whoever seeks to harm you with sacrifices— [may he be struck down].
O Indra, strike him who is right before you; O Indra, with your hundred-knotted thunderbolt.
This indeed is the turning back.
May the victorious Sañjaya-jewel,
the auspicious protector, guard our progeny and wealth.
Without rivals for us from below, without rivals for us from above;
O Indra, without rivals for us from behind.
Place light at the forefront, O Hero.
Bhaṭṭa [says]: "The thick, formidable armor belonging to Indra and Agni—which all the gods together cannot pierce—[is before me]. (PS 16,28.7)
May that great [gem] protect your body on all sides, so that you may be long-lived and reach old age.
The divine amulet has ascended onto you.
For my well-being, enter this boundary-pillar, which protects the body and provides triple defense for the sake of vigor.
May Indra bestow manly vigor upon him;
O gods, enter into him together for long life, for a hundred autumns.
— May the long-lived Indra, the conqueror who is unconquered, the drinker of Soma, the bringer of fearlessness, the bull, bind the amulet for you, just as the venerable Jaradaṣṭi did.
May he protect you always,
by day and by night, on every side. (PS 16.28.11,
Anuvāka 5)
May Indra churn it, the churner;
may Śakra, the hero, the destroyer of forts, churn it, so that we may slay the army.
May it bind thousands of enemies; may the fetid rope,
binding them, make that army putrid— this one [or] that one.
Seeing the smoke of the fire,
let them harbor fear in their hearts;
let those called *paruṣa* make those enemies *paruṣa*.
The executioner slays them with his weapons;
let them be swiftly broken like arrows caught in a great net.
O Aśvattha tree, crush these; O Khadira, devour them!
Let them break instantly like a brittle reed.
Bound by the Great Net:
the atmosphere was the net,
and the vast quarters were the staffs of the net.
With that, Indra, having assailed the army, scattered the Dasyus.
Bhaṭṭa [says]: He scatters [the grains] with the verse, "O Indra, hero, great is your net, great... Bhaṭṭa [continues]: "...great is yours...
O hero, of him who is worth a thousand and possesses a hundredfold power."
With that, O Maghavan, bend down the enemies; [bend down] the enemies for eternal years.
Great is your net, O Great One.
Of Śakra, the lord of the swift steeds;
with that [weapon] Indra struck down a hundred, a thousand, and ten thousand of the Dasyus' attacking armies.
This great world was a net belonging to the Great Śakra;
by means of that net of Indra, I [have bound you].
I place all those darknesses upon them:
exhaustion, fierce agitation, affliction, and that which cannot be warded off.
With weariness, sloth, and delusion— with these I overwhelm them all.
Bhaṭṭa: "I deliver those to Death" (PS 16,29.9); "I deliver these to Death";
"these are bound by the nooses of Death"; "bound."
Those who are the cruel messengers of Death— Bhaṭṭa, from them I lead these [people] away, having bound them.
O messengers of death, bind these; O messengers of Yama, lead them away and hold them back!
Let more than a thousand be slain; let them trample these [enemies] underfoot, O mortal Bhava!
Bhaṭṭa says: Mortality and existence (PS 16,30.1) are the things to be proven;
raising a single net-staff, they go forth with vigor.
The Rudras [hold] the second, the Vasus the third, and one is raised up with the Ādityas;
the Viśvedevas are above.
Let them go forth, subduing by their might;
let the Aṅgirases go forth, striking down the army with their weapons in its midst.
I impel the lords of the forest, the products of the forest, the herbs, and the plants; the bipeds and the quadrupeds.
Just as he slew that army—
the Gandharvas, Apsarases, gods, serpents, Puṇyajanas, and ancestors— so [did he slay this].
I impel those seen and those unseen,
so that they may slay this army as it was seen;
these snares of death are now set.
Having stepped upon which you shall not be released—
let this peak strike that army by the thousands!
Bhaṭṭa: A thousandfold is the heated cauldron by fire;
this oblation is a winner of thousands.
And Bhava Pṛśnibāhu and Śarva— slay this army!
Let them fall into the very jaws of Death.
Indra [warded off] hunger, exhaustion, slaughter, and fear with his two eyes and his net.
"O Śarva, destroy this army!
Vanquished, let the enemies tremble; conquered, flee by means of the sacred word!"
Let not one among these, who have been driven away by Bṛhaspati, escape;
let their weapons fall down.
May they not be able to aim their arrow;
rather, let the arrows strike the vital organs of these many who are terrified.
May both Heaven and Earth, together with the intermediate space and the deities, cry out against them!
May they find neither a kinsman nor a support— may they not find a support, O Bhaṭṭa!
Striking one another, let them go unto death.
Should one read *vighnānā* or *'bhighnānā*?

(PS_16,30.11) The four quarters are the mares of the divine chariot; the sacrificial cakes are its [wheels]. According to Bhaṭṭa, the four mares are the hooves, and the intermediate space is the felloe.
The two worlds, heaven and earth, are the two sides; the seasons are the reins; speech is the chariot-pole. (Bhaṭṭa Udbhaṭa, *Paddhati-saṃgraha*, 16.31.1)
Bhaṭṭa [reads]: *parirukthiyam*.
In the wheel of day and night, the months are the spokes (*māsārā*). (Note: Bhaṭṭa reads *māsārā*, but see the critical apparatus.)
The year is the foundation;
Virāj is the pole, Agni is the front of the chariot, Indra is the left-side driver, and the Moon is the charioteer.
From here, conquer; conquer further; conquer completely; conquer! Svāhā!
From heaven, from earth, from the intermediate space, from the ocean—
From Agni the Madhukasha was born from the winds;
all creatures rejoice in their hearts at her, who is clothed in immortality.
With verses [of the Ṛgveda], O Bhaṭṭa,
men on earth perceive her activity, investigating it in various ways.
From Agni and Vāta the Madhukashā was indeed born; she is the fierce granddaughter of the Maruts,
possessing great and multiform milk.
And they say that you are the seed of the ocean; from where the honey-whip comes forth, bestowing gifts—
that is the vital breath, that is the immortal established therein.
She is the mother of the Ādityas, the daughter of the Vasus, the breath of all creatures, and the navel of immortality;
she is golden-hued, sweet as honey, and dripping with clarity.
Great splendor moves among mortals.
The gods produced a whip from honey;
its embryo became the omniform.
The mother nourishes him when he is born as a youth;
once born, he clothes himself in all the worlds.
Who knows them? And who has told us of them?
As for her two breasts, inexhaustible with a thousand streams, they yield nourishment without ceasing;
who knows them, and who has truly perceived them?
The jar of this heart, which holds the imperishable Soma—
may the wise Brahman rejoice therein. The great *hiṅ* sound, making its resonance, bestows vital strength.
She who goes with a loud cry,
yearning toward the three heats,
lowing her lowing, pours forth milk with her milks.
The waters sit upon her who is full;
the powerful bulls, the self-ruling ones, sit upon her.
They rain, they cause to rain—Bhatt. they rain, they rain.
May the waters grant that desire and vigor to you.
O Prajāpati, thunder is your voice;
as a bull, you cast forth your strength upon the earth.
For from Agni and Vāta the Madhukashā was born, the fierce granddaughter of the Maruts,
just as Soma [is prepared] at the morning pressing.
One becomes dear to the Aśvins;
thus, O Aśvins, may splendor be maintained within my own self.
Just as Soma becomes dear to Indra and Agni at the second pressing, even so, O Indra and Agni, may splendor come to me. […] PS_16,33.2
Just as Soma is dear to the Ṛbhus at the third pressing, even so, O Ṛbhus, may splendor be mine.
May it be sustained within me:
may I produce sweetness, may I conceive sweetness.
O Agni, rich in milk, I have come; unite me with splendor!
O Agni, unite me with splendor!
May I be united with offspring and united with long life;
may the gods know this of mine, and may Indra know it together with the seers.
"yad giriṣu" is the *pāñcarcikī* [verse]:
"Just as honey-makers collect honey upon the springtime..."
O Aśvins, may strength and vigor be maintained for me,
just as this honey is for the bee.
They anoint [him] at every moment;
even so, O Aśvins, may splendor and brilliance be maintained for me.
O Aśvins, lords of splendor, anoint me with the honey of the bee;
[make] my limbs full of sweetness.

From your two feet, from your two ankles, from your two calves, from your two knees, from your two thighs, from your two hips, and from your loins.

In the Residue are names and forms; in the Residue the world is placed;
