In that, all this is contained: whatever moves, breathes, and blinks.
Bhaṭṭa [says]:
"The breath, carrying water upwards like a water-carrier with a jar. (PS 16.101.9)
All see with the eye,
but not all know with the mind.
From the deficient, the full arises.
From the full, the deficient is drawn up;
the seer, the priest, knows that from which it is poured out.
Prajāpati moves within the womb, unseen; he is born in many ways.
With one half, he generated the entire world.
What was born from that which is its half?
That which stirs, moves, and stands; that which remains breathless yet breathing, and that which stands with closed eyes.
Bhaṭṭa reads *aprāṇaprāṇaṃ* ... *ceṣṭate*, with the proposed emendation:
*tad dādhāra pṛthivīṃ viśvarūpam*.

Having come together, that becomes one alone. That which is joined in front and that which is joined behind, that which is joined from all sides and that which is joined from every direction— [all this is one].
And where it goes to its setting—
that alone I consider the highest; beyond that, nothing whatsoever exists.
By truth he heats upward; by the Brahman he sees downward;
by the vital breath he breathes crosswise.
In whom the eldest is established.
Bhaṭṭa: Regarding this [verse] PS 16,102.6:
"He indeed would know those two fire-drills from which wealth is produced by friction."
That wise man should consider himself the eldest; he should know the knowledge and know the Brahmin as great.
In the beginning, he came into being footless.
He brought forth the light at the beginning;
having become four-footed, he, as the enjoyer, took all food unto himself.
Then he became an object of enjoyment and gave much food,
he who favored the god who possesses the higher realm.
One should worship the eternal;
they call him eternal, yet he is ever new even today.
Day and night are born from one another’s forms;
a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, and a hundred million.
An incalculable portion of one's own [merit] is deposited therein;
they destroy that very portion while he is looking on.
Therefore, this god shines forth for him. PS 16.103.1.
He saw a single [hair-tip] the size of a needle-point, yet it was not seen at all; thereafter, he embraced her more closely.
That deity is dear to me:
this auspicious, ageless, immortal [goddess] is in the house of the mortal.
He for whom it was made lies down;
he who made it is its consumer.
You are female; you are male.
You are a maiden or indeed a youth;
you are an old man who totters with a staff.
You are born and you exist, O you whose face is turned in every direction.
Is he the eldest, or is he the youngest? Is he the brother, or is he the father? The one God has entered into the mind.
He was born first, even within the womb; he moves not, yet everything moves within him,
for all beings are contained within him.
May that man, procreating by the *ṛta*,
go to all the ends while remaining even as he stands;
the speckled stone is placed in the midst of heaven.
Moving apart, filling the expanse of space,
he gazes upon all things with his powers,
between the eastern and the western sign.
Those who, whether now or in the past, speak around one who knows the Veda—
they all speak only of the Āditya.
They kindle the fire— the second, the threefold, the swan—
with a single verse by means of twelve fires.
In it the waters, in it the cows,
in it the plants are supported.
Seven fair-winged ones blow upon the arrow.
May this Vāyu, gathered by means of the Anuṣṭubh meter,
purify the mind upon the surface of the waters— him who is stretched out, spread abroad, and extended as a thread.
The seven seers are appointed within the body; they ever guard it with vigilance.
Seven waters go to the world of the sleeper.
Therein dwell the two gods who are wakeful, sleepless, and seated at the sacrificial session.
(Anuvāka 16)
O Bhava and Śarva, be gracious; come toward me, O lords of beings, O lords of cattle, homage be to you both!
Let not that which has been sent forth by me be scattered away.
Do not harm us, neither those with two feet nor those with four. Do not let dogs, jackals, or vultures devour our bodies.
And those black,
voracious flies and birds, O Paśupati—
let them not find us as their prey.
ŚS *vidanta*; Bhatt. *viyanta* PS 16,104.2:
For your roar, for your breath, and for those growths of yours, O Bhava, [we offer this].
Homage we pay to you, O Rudra,
thousand-eyed and immortal;
we pay homage to you from the front.
From the north and from the south, from the zenith and from the sky, from the zenith and from the intermediate space— to you, homage! (PS 16.104.4)
For your mouth, O Paśupati;
those which are your eyes, O Bhava; for the skin, for beauty, and for the act of seeing.
Homage to you who face westward; homage to your limbs, your belly, your tongue, and your mouth.
Homage to you for the teeth and for fragrance!
With the missile [armed] with the blue-crested one,
with the thousand-eyed steed—
May we not come into conflict with that Rudra, the slayer of travelers (or the slayer of Bhaṭṭas)—
may Bhava spare us on every side.
May Bhava spare us, as fire spares the waters;
may he not be angry with us—let there be homage to him!
Four times, eightfold, let there be homage to Bhava.
Ten times, O Paśupati, homage be to you! These five classes of creatures are distributed by you:
cattle, horses, humans, goats, and sheep.
The four quarters are yours; the sky is yours; O fierce one, this vast intermediate space is yours;
all this that possesses a self is yours.
Whatever moves upon the earth— this wide treasure-chest of yours is the container of wealth,
within which all these beings exist.
Be gracious to us, O Paśupati; homage be unto you!
May the jackals, the overpowering dogs, and the wailing, disheveled women go far away.
You bear a golden, green bow, O crested one,
that slays a thousand and kills a hundred.
The arrow of Rudra, the weapon of the god, flies abroad;
homage be to it from whichever direction it comes hither.
Bhaṭṭa: O fierce one, whoever approaches you to seek refuge while desiring to harm you, [is overcome]. PS 16,105.2. yo 'bhiyāto nilayate tvām ugra nicikīrṣati /
Thereafter, you apply that [remedy] like a tracker following the footprints of one who has been pierced.
Bhaṭṭa: "The two, Bhava and Rudra, joined together and in harmony, both fierce, move for the sake of heroic power. (PS 16,105.3)
The earth, the intermediate space, and the heavenly sky—these are their domains.
To them, to Bhavamatya, we pay homage;
homage be to you as you approach!
Homage be to you as you go away;
homage to you, O Rudra, as you stand and as you sit— homage to you.
Homage in the evening, homage in the morning; homage by night, homage by day—
to Bhava and to Śarva.
I have paid homage to both.
To Rudra, the thousand-eyed, the far-seeing, who stands in front discharging [his arrows] in many ways, the wise one— [to him I pay homage].
I would not enjoy the pleasure of the tongue while [the enemy] is devouring Śyāvāśva,
the dark, the black, the unblemished one who crushes [them], the one who praises [him],
the terrible chariot, and the long-haired one who strikes them down.
We acknowledge him from of old; let there be homage to him!
O Lord of Beasts, do not let the divine bolt strike us mortals; do not be angry with us— salutations to you!
Shake down a divine branch elsewhere than for us;
do not harm us, speak for us, choose for us, and do not be angry.
O Hunger,
may we not come into conflict with you;
may we not [come into conflict] with our horses, our cattle, or our men.
Do not covet our goats and sheep;
O fierce one, turn away elsewhere!
Slay the offspring of those who are hostile.
Bhaṭṭa: Of those whose weapon is fever and cough, it goes forth like the neighing of a stallion, O Priyārūṇas.
Bhaṭṭa [says]: "The word *krandah* is determined as being preceded by *abhi*;
let there be homage to him. (PS 16.106.2)
He who stands firm, supported in the intermediate space, crushing those who do not sacrifice and destroying the revilers of the gods.
To him be homage with ten Śakvarī verses! For you are the wild animals and the beasts dwelling in the forest. For you—
The birds, the winged fowls— O Paśupati, let them carry away your consumption into the waters; for you,
the celestial waters flow to increase your strength.
Porpoises, pythons,
*pulīkayas*, *jaṣas*, and fish— *Bhatta*, you hurl [your weapons] at those who are covered in dust.
Neither is there anything distant for you, nor is there anything hidden;
O Bhava, you behold the entire earth instantly.
O Rudra, do not strike us with fever nor with poison from the eastern ocean into the western one.
Do not consume us with divine fire; let this lightning strike elsewhere than upon us.
Bhava rules over heaven; Bhava rules over the earth.
He has filled the vast intermediate space;
no misfortune whatsoever reaches him here.
O King, be gracious to the sacrificer; for you have become the Lord of Animals. (Bhaṭṭa: prāpata PS 16,106.7) bhava rājan yajamānāya mṛḍa paśūnāṃ hi paśupatir babhūtha.
O Bhaṭṭa, you who have become one who has faith that "the gods exist," be gracious toward his four-footed and two-footed creatures.
Do not harm our great ones, nor our small ones; do not harm those who dwell at home, nor those who have gone abroad; do not harm our father, nor our mother.
O Rudra, do not harm our own bodies! [From the *Rudra* hymn, for those who are Elabakāras, who do not speak in accordance with the Saṃhitā.]
I have offered this homage to the large-mouthed dogs.
Homage to you, O Ghoṣiṇīs; homage to you, O Keśinīs.
Homage to those who are self-restrained;
homage to those who possess reverence!
Homage to you as you are being born!
Homage be to you who have been born;
homage to your young ones, to your hooves, to your form, O inviolable one— homage to you!
He who knows the seven downward slopes, who knows the seven distant realms,
and who knows the head of the sacrifice—
He should take hold of the barren cow:
"I know the seven slopes; I know the seven distances."
I know the head of the sacrifice and the Soma that is discerning within it—
by which [the head] the sky exists and by which the earth exists.
By which these waters are protected—
that cow of a thousand streams—
we address with a sacred prayer.
A hundred calves, a hundred milkers,
and a hundred guardians are upon her back—
those gods who breathe within her.
They know the cow to be one and the same:
she whose feet are the sacrifice, whose eyes are milk, whose life-breath is the *svadhā* offering, and who dwells in the great earth.
The barren cow, the consort of Parjanya,
approaches the gods with a sacred prayer;
Agni has entered into you.
Soma is under your control; O auspicious one, Parjanya is your udder,
and the lightning-flashes are your teats under your control.
You milk the waters first; the fertile fields, the others, at will; you milk the third, the kingdom.
O you who abide in truth, when you are invoked by the Ādityas, you come under my control with food and milk.
Indra caused you to drink the Soma from a thousand vessels under his control.
Bhaṭṭa says that because of the removal of the *tvā*,
when [the suffix] *air* follows *anūcīndra*, from that [form] *ayirāṭ* arises,
and then the *ṛṣabha* was invoked.
Therefore, the enraged slayer of Vṛtra brought milk— namely, cow’s milk— under his control;
for the enraged Lord of Wealth [brought it under his control] as well.
He brought milk under your control;
today that very thing, O Nāka, protects within three vessels.
The divine cow brought that Soma in three vessels to where Atharvan was consecrated.
He sat upon the golden sacrificial grass;
for he has come together with Soma and with every living creature that has feet.
The barren cow has lowed in the ocean,
bearing the *ṛc*s and the *sāmans*;
for she has come together with the sun.
With her whole eye,
the barren cow has ascended the ocean together with the Gandharvas and the Kalis.
For she has come together with the wind and with all winged birds;
the barren cow has looked across the ocean.
Bearing auspicious lights,
the auspicious ones, the Cow, the Impeller, and likewise Self-existence, came together.
Where Atharvan, consecrated,
sat upon a golden sacrificial grass-mat covered with gold.
When you stood, O observer of the cosmic order, the horse, having become the ocean,
leaped upon you according to your will.
The barren cow is the mother of the Rājanya; the barren cow is your mother, O Svadhā.
From the barren cow was born the weapon, [the sacrifice].
From that, the mind was born.
The drop rose upward from the summit of Brahman.
From that you were born in Vaśa;
from that the Hotṛ was born.
May the Gāthās be from your mouth.
Strength is yours from the *uṣṇih* meters;
the sacrifice was born from your belly;
from your breasts the rays came forth by your will.
Your birth was from the two *īrma*s,
and from the two *sakthi*s [is] your power (*vaśa*),
O Bhaṭṭa; [it was] from the two *śakti*s.
From his intestines the *atrā* plants were born,
and from his belly the creepers;
for the belly belongs to Varuṇa.
"You entered into his control;
then Brahmā summoned you."
For he indeed knew your eye;
all those who were in the womb trembled at his birth from the vital breaths.
Bhaṭṭa said: "She has indeed given birth; they call her 'the will' (vaśā). Bhaṭṭa said:
"She has given birth by means of the sacred formulation (brahman); moreover, this is her kinship."
He alone brings together the battles; he who is the sole ruler of this [world].
Sacrifices became the means of crossing over.
The cow became the eye of the waters;
the cow received the sun,
and the cow sustained the sacrifice.
The rice entered into the barren cow together with the Brahman;
they call the barren cow itself immortality.
They worship death as their own power;
by this power all this came to be— the gods,
humans, asuras, ancestors, and seers.
He who knows thus should accept the barren cow;
for in this way, the sacrifice yields everything to the giver without failing.
Bhaṭṭa: "They flashed forth after him.
(PS 16,109.7) Three tongues of Varuṇa flash within his mouth.
Among them, she who shines in the midst is the barren cow (vaśā), difficult to receive;
the seed of the vaśā became fourfold.
One quarter is water, one quarter is the immortal,
one quarter is the sacrifice, and one quarter is the cattle.
He who knows thus may accept the barren cow.
The Sky is the Cow, the Earth is the Cow,
Viṣṇu is the Cow, and Prajāpati is the Cow; they drank the milk of the Cow.
The Sādhyas and those who are the Vasus:
having drunk the milk of a cow,
the Sādhyas and those who are the Vasus [attain their goal].
These [beings] wait upon her milk at the summit of the sun;
some milk this Soma from her.
Some worship with clarified butter;
those who gave a barren cow to one who knows thus have gone from heaven to the third heaven.
Having given a barren cow to the Brahmins, one enjoys all the worlds. (Bhaṭṭa: Having given, one enjoys all the worlds.)
For in her is established the *ṛta*,
as well as the sacred word (*brahman*) and ascetic heat (*tapas*);
upon her, the gods subsist.
By her will men [exist], and by her will all this has come to be,
as far as the sun shines.
Section 17.
Whoever may know the one Brahman through its performance, he indeed may speak with greatness today—
He whose joints are the ritual preparations and whose spine is the *ṛc* verses.
The Vedic hymns are his body hairs,
the sacrificial grass is his spread-out mat,
and the Yajus formulae are said to be his heart.
When the host of guests looks upon the guests, he gazes upon the sacrificial ground for the gods. When he greets them, he enters the consecration;
when he asks for water, he leads forward the waters.
The waters that are brought forth for the sacrifice are those very same waters;
the libation that they bring is that very same [libation]; the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma that is bound is that very same [animal];
the dug-out earth that they bring is the two sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*).

When they prepare dwellings, they are thereby preparing the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* sheds. When they spread out the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), that is the *barhis* itself. When they bring forth the cushions and pillows, those are the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
When they bring the upper bedding, by that he wins the heavenly world.
When they bring ointment, that is indeed clarified butter (ājya).
When they call for the one who has prepared the food, they indeed call for the preparer of the oblation (haviṣkṛt).
When rice and barley are poured out, they are sown as mere stalks.
The mortar and pestle, the two pressing-stones, the winnowing-basket,
the strainer, the husks, and the dregs [are all cast away].
The *sruc* is the ladle, the *mekṣaṇa* is the stirring-spoon, the *āyavana* is the water for mixing, and the *droṇakalaśa* and *kumbhī* are the vessels for pressing.
Bhaṭṭa: The waters for pressing are the *droṇakalaśa* (PS 16,112.1).
This very black antelope skin serves as the *vāyavya* vessels.
The host of guests makes this [skin] the sacrificer or the Brāhmaṇa; [thus it is] the sacrificer-Brāhmaṇa.
When he looks at the things to be brought forward, saying, "Let this be more, let that be more," and when he says,
"Bring forth more," by that he increases both his offspring and his cattle;
by that he makes his vital breath more abundant.
In that he asks a question, he thereby wins desire; for when asked, one asks for what one desires.
In that he sprinkles water, he thereby wins the waters.
Whatever oblations he offers and whatever sacrificial vessels he sets down— of those which have been set down, the guest offers into himself with the sound of the *sruk* ladle,
with the *vaṣaṭ* call, with the *sruc* ladle, with his hand, and into the pillar of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Therefore, one should not eat from someone who hates, nor should one eat the food of someone who hates; nor from one who is being scrutinized, nor from one who is currently being scrutinized.
Indeed, he whose food people eat has consumed all evil;
yet he too has not consumed all evil.
The food of one whose [guests] do not eat is not consumed.
Those who bring offerings follow the stride of Prajāpati.
For him who brings offerings, this sacrifice is extended as that of Prajāpati himself.
Or rather, he who brings [the oblation] is always like Sutasoma, with the pressing-stones joined and the strainer moistened;
he whose sacrificial rite has been undertaken and whose excellence is spread abroad—
he who serves the guests is the Āhavanīya fire.
That which is the means of preparing food is the Dakṣiṇāgni;
that which is in the dwelling is the Gārhapatya. Indeed, he consumes both what is sacrificed and what is offered.
He who eats before the guest eats up his offspring and his cattle.
He who eats before his guest consumes the vigor and the milk of the household.
A learned man (śrotriya) is indeed such a guest.
Therefore, one should not eat before [the guest]; one should eat only when [the guest] has eaten—that is the vow.
It is for the non-interruption of the sacrifice, for the protection of the sacrifice, and for the integrity of the sacrifice. When he pours out milk and offers it...
Whatever one obtains by sacrificing with the fully successful Agniṣṭoma, that much he obtains by this [rite]. In that he pours out clarified butter and offers it,
[he obtains] as much as by the fully successful Sāhna sacrifice.
Whatever he offers after sprinkling it with honey,
[it is successful] as far as the *atirātra* sacrifice;
… whatever meat he offers after sprinkling it.

Whatever one obtains by performing a prosperous sacrifice lasting twelve days, that much he obtains by this [rite]. When he pours out water and offers it, it is for the procreation of offspring; he lives long, reaches a full lifespan, and does not die before old age—he who acts thus.
He knows. For him, Vāta utters the sound *hiṅ*, and Savitṛ praises him for prosperity.
Bṛhaspati chants the *udgītha* with vigor; Tvaṣṭṛ responds with nourishment; the Viśvedevas are the *nidhana*.
Prosperity in offspring and cattle comes to him who knows this;
at his rising, the sun utters the *hiṅ* sound for him.
The time of the gathering of cattle is the *prastāva*, midday is the *udgītha*, the afternoon is the *pratihāra*, and the setting sun is the *nidhana*.
Therefore, when he becomes a cloud, he utters the *hiṅ* sound;
flashing with lightning, he performs the *prastāva*; thundering, he sings the *udgītha*; raining, he performs the *pratihāra*; and lifting up [the rain], he performs the *nidhana*.
Bhaṭṭa: He takes up the year...
(he looks toward the guests and utters "hiṅ"). See 1d PS_16,115.3.
He addresses [the guest], he praises him, he asks for water, he sings the *udgītha*, he brings [food] near, he presents it, and the *ucchiṣṭa* is the *nidhana*.
He who knows this becomes the *nidhana* of prosperity, offspring, and cattle. PS_16,115.4 (115)
These very guests, whether dear or not dear, are indeed the officiating priests who cause one to go to the heavenly world;
for when he calls the attendant and causes him to announce [the oblation].
That which he promises and that which he causes to be heard in response;
when the attendants enter the dwellings,
they are indeed the *camasādhvaryu*s.
Not even one among them was their Hotṛ.
That which he offers in the morning is indeed the morning libation (prātaḥsavana).
That which he offers at midday is indeed the midday pressing;
that which he offers in the evening is [the third pressing].
That is indeed the third pressing (tṛtīyasavana).
When the host of guests, having served the guests, asks for a seat— that is, having served them, he sits down— that is indeed the ritual bath (avabhṛtha) he enters.
Bhaṭṭa [says]: He causes [the sacrificer] to share; when he distributes the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), he thereby causes it to be shared;
when he performs [the rites], he thereby concludes the sacrifice (*udavasyati*). (PS 16.116.7–8)
Invited, he eats upon the earth;
invited, he eats that which is of manifold forms upon the earth;
it burns upon the earth, it shines upon the earth.
He who knows thus attains the world of heaven. He, being invited, partakes [of the draught] in the intermediate space;
he is invited to that which is multiform in the intermediate space.
He burns in the intermediate space; he shines in the intermediate space.
(…) He, being invited, partakes [of the offering] in heaven.
Invoked therein is that which is multiform in heaven;
it burns in heaven and shines in heaven.
Invited among the gods, he partakes;
invited therein is that which is multiform among the gods.
It glows among the gods; it shines among the gods.
(…) Having been invited among the worlds, he partakes; having been invited, he partakes of whatever is multiform in those worlds.
He shines among the worlds, he blazes among the worlds,
and he attains the heavenly world— he who knows thus. When, sitting facing the east, he scatters [the grain].
When he offers while seated facing south, he cuts [the sacrificial portion] for the sacrifice and for the gods.
When he offers while seated facing south,
he cuts [the sacrificial portion] for Yama and for the ancestors.
When he, sitting facing westward, pours out [the oblation] for Varuṇa, the dweller in the waters, he cuts it off.
Bhaṭṭa [says]: He cuts himself off from Varuṇa, who dwells in the waters, when he offers while sitting facing north;
and he cuts himself off from King Soma and the Seven Seers when he makes the offering.
Bhaṭṭa: [From] the seers:
"If, having made his lap [his seat], he sits and offers [the oblation] to Vāyu and to the intermediate space, he cuts himself off. (PS 16,118.4–5)
When he offers while standing upright, he cuts off [the portion] for Dyaus and Āditya.
Regarding one whom he might desire: "May he become worse off in himself, in his offspring, in his cattle, in his house, and in his wealth"—[he should offer thus].
For him who offers thus, having offered thus, he should offer again in this very manner;
then indeed he becomes worse off in himself, in his cattle, his houses, and his wealth.
This is the expiation for one who desires:
"May he not become better off, nor superior in himself, in offspring, in cattle, in houses, or in wealth.
For such a person, one should offer this oblation.
If he should thus offer [the oblation] in this very manner without having first offered it,
then he becomes neither better nor worse in himself, nor in his offspring, cattle, house, or wealth;
he should perform this and that— this is the expiation.

If one should desire, "May he become more prosperous, better off in himself, in offspring, in cattle, in houses, and in wealth," for him one should offer the oblation in this manner; having offered it in this manner, one should subsequently offer it in this very same way.
At that very moment, he becomes more prosperous and superior in himself, in his offspring, in his cattle, in his house, and in his wealth—
thinking "he shall do this and that"— this is the expiation for when a grain of rice spills while being pounded.
Year after year, he who chooses this becomes short-lived.
When it is made of iron,
it makes one devoted to the ancestors as deities.
Whatever flows forth— the milk of houses and the milk of cattle—
that which he sprinkles.
If one sprinkles water upon the milk of houses and cattle, the master of the house dies.
If the *āyavanī* [ladle] breaks,
the master of the house dies.
If the ladle breaks,
the mistress of the house dies; if the cooking-pot cracks, [the same occurs].
Both the giver and the receiver suffer total ruin.
When one turns [the hair] toward the east,
he cuts himself off from the sacrifice and from the gods.
In that he turns [the hair] upward toward the south,
he cuts it for Yama and for the ancestors; in that he turns it upward toward the west...
He seizes for Varuṇa those who sit within the waters.
Bhaṭṭa [says]: "To Varuṇa, the dweller in the waters" (PS 16.121.3);
"When he turns it upward, [it is] for Soma the King and for the Seven Seers; [if he does not do so,] he cuts himself off" (PS 16.121.4).
Whatever he pulls out from its continuous placement,
fear comes upon him from every direction;
this is why he spreads the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) facing eastward.
When he spreads the sacrificial grass (barhis) pointing toward the south,
he cuts it for Yama and for the ancestors.
In that he spreads the sacrificial grass facing westward,
he performs what has not been done before.
In that he spreads the sacrificial grass facing northward...
If one cuts [the handle] for King Soma or for the Seven Seers, it harms him.
If one makes the handle of the vessel in front [of the bowl],
a hemorrhoid arises in the mouth of the recipient.
In that he makes the handle of the vessel on the south side,
he cuts it off for Yama and for the ancestors.
In that he makes the handle of the vessel on the west side...
If she makes the handle of the vessel face northward, the arrowhead reaches the recipient;
she cuts herself off from King Soma and the Seven Seers.
In that he becomes bright, he attains the very dear abode of the Ādityas. He who should consume the bright [Soma]—
With the words, "I eat thee with the beloved abode of the Ādityas," he should eat it;
for if he were to eat it with any other abode,
he would cut himself off from the Ādityas.
When it has been husked, it becomes the beloved of all the gods... He who should eat what has been husked...
With the beloved abode of all the gods [...
he eats it;
