(…) what is your liver and what your two kidneys.
Your intestines and your bowels;
your spleen and your pancreas.
Your two flanks and your belly,
that which is your marrow and your bones.
That which is my flesh and that which is my blood;
those two which are your arms and those two which are your shoulders.
And that which is your shoulder and your hump... those which are your shoulders and your neck.
Those which are the ribs and those which are the ribs of the sides;
those two thighs and the two knee-caps of yours.
Those which are your hips and that which is your buttocks;
that which is your tail and those which are your hairs.
That which is your udder and those which are your teats;
those which are your shanks and those which are your hocks.
And those which are the *ṛtsarās*, they are the hooves; (*Bhatt.* reads *hṛtsarā*...
May your hide at the hundred-porridge [sacrifice], O inviolable cow, and your hairs,
yield curd for the giver.
Milk, clarified butter, and honey—
this breast of yours is curd,
this is clarified butter, this is honey.
O Goddess Śataudanā, may this [offering] milk for you all your desires;
may the two cakes be your two breasts.
Having made those two wings anointed with clarified butter,
O Goddess, carry the donor to heaven.
Whatever grains or husks are in the mortar, in the pestle, on the hide, or in the winnowing basket—
whatever the wind, Mātariśvan, has scattered for me.
May Agni, as the Hotṛ priest, make that well-offered;
I set down the divine waters, honey-sweet and dripping with ghee, separately in the hands of the Brahmins.
Whatever desire I fulfill for you by sprinkling this [water] upon you,
may that be ours; may we be masters of riches.

Prajāpati and Parameṣṭhin are the two horns; Indra is the head; Agni is the forehead; Yama is the back of the neck; King Soma is the brain; Truth is the eye; Righteousness is the ears; the out-breath and in-breath are the nostrils. Bhatt. [notes]: the eyes.
The sky is the upper jaw, the earth the lower;
Agni is the mouth, lightning the tongue,
the Maruts the teeth, and Pavamāna the breath.
The wind is the universe, the throat is the heavenly world;
Kṛṣṇadram is the support, the Vikeśyas are the necks,
Revatī is the vertebrae, and the Kṛttikās are the shoulders.
The *gharma* is the shoulder, the *vah* the breast, the *śyena* the belly, and the atmosphere the flanks;
Mitra and Varuṇa are the two shoulders,
and Tvaṣṭṛ and Aryaman the two forearms.
Mahādeva is the forearms; Bṛhaspati is the hump; the *bṛhatī* meters are the vertebrae; the wives of the gods are the ribs; the *upasad* rites are the side-ribs;
Indrāṇī is the anus; Vāta is the tail; and Pavamāna is the tail-hair.
The priesthood and the nobility are the hips; strength is the thighs;
Dhātṛ and Savitṛ are the two knee-bones;
the Gandharvas and Apsarases are the shanks.
The ankle-bones are Aditi;
the hooves are the mind; the heart is the intellect; the liver is the dark complexion; the bile is the sacred observance; and the pericardium is the vow.
Hunger is the belly; food is the rectum (Bhaṭṭa);
the mountains are the lungs; the divine folk are the anus; human beings are the entrails; the waters are the intestines; and the stomach is the abdomen.
Other people are the *ūbadhya*; the *rakṣas* are the blood;
anger is the two kidneys; wrath is the testicles; progeny is the penis;
the ocean is the bladder; and the river is the urethra.
The thundering cloud is the udder; the lords of rain are the teats;
the all-pervading one is the hide; the herbs are the body hair; the stars are the form; the cloud is the fat; the marrow is the *nidhana*.
He who knows this becomes the end (the source) of prosperity, offspring, and cattle.
Indra stands facing the east; Yama stands facing the south; Dhātṛ stands facing the west; Savitṛ stands facing the north.
Soma, having reached the grass, is *rājāvṛtta*; Ānanda is *rājāvṛtrahā*.
Being observed in Mitra, he is *yujyamāna*; as *vaiśvadeva*, he is *yukta*; as Prajāpati, he is *vimukta*; [as] everything, he is *sarva*.
This, indeed, is the form of the cow;
cattle possessing form attend upon him who knows thus.
Bhaṭṭa: Those possessing form were created by Brahmā through toil and austerity; they are supported by wealth at the end of the Veda.
Enveloped by truth, clothed in splendor, surrounded by fame, invested with self-power (*svadhā*),
covered by faith (*śraddhā*), guarded by consecration (*dīkṣā*),
established in sacrifice— *loka* is the finale (*nidhana*).
The *chandases* are the form; the *aṅgirasas* are the heat; the Brahman is the path-finder;
the Brāhmaṇa is the overlord.
For a Kṣatriya who seizes that Brahmin’s cow and defeats the Brāhmaṇa, truthfulness,
vigor, and auspicious merit depart from him.
Vitality, splendor, endurance, and strength;
speech, the sense-faculties, prosperity, and righteousness;
the priesthood, the nobility, the realm, and the commoners.
Radiance and fame, splendor and wealth; longevity and beauty, name and renown;
milk and sap, food and the eating of food.
The out-breath and the in-breath, the eye and the ear;
the *ṛta* and the *satya*, the sacrifice and the charitable work, as well as offspring and cattle—all these depart from the Kṣatriya who seizes the Brahmin’s cow. (141)
This very one is the terrible *brahmagavī*, the poison of evil,
a magical spell (*kṛtyā*) enveloped in *kulvaja*— [or] brought from *kulvaja*. Within her are all cruel things and all deaths.
In her are all terrors and all killings of men; she, being seized as the cow of a Brahmin by one who treats a Brahmin with violence,
draws him toward death like a tethering post.
For that [cow] is indeed a host of a hundredfold weapons,
for she is the dwelling place of the oppressor of Brahmins;
therefore, the cow belongs to the Brahmins.
Invincible to the discerning,
Vaiśvānara is the raised chant (udgītha),
while Mahādeva is the one who looks on.
The thunderbolt runs, the weapon rushes,
uprooting the hooves;
sharp-edged and keen, it gazes about.
Death, uttering the sound *hiṅ*,
thunders toward the one who bellows—
the two Brahman-cows of the oppressor of Brahmins.
The fierce goddess, tossing about the tail, is total ruin; she who makes the ears ring is consumption; being milked, she is the urinary disease; when milked, she is the headache.
Sedir stands near; Bhatta says that when there is mutual conflict, [the victim] is seized while the arrow-head is being fixed to the mouth [of the bow]. PS 16.143.1.
The *ṛti* being struck is misfortune; the *ṛtu* being struck is beneficial.
Falling with the poison of sin, it falls as darkness. Following after the vital breaths, the Brahman-cow destroys the one who injures the Brahman. (PS 16,143.2)
Enmity was being torn asunder; the portion of the grandson was being divided; the weapon of the gods was being taken away; the intellect was set aside; Destruction was laid low.
When the intellect is being carried away, evil is being deposited; when evil is being deposited, harshness is being deposited;
when harshness is being deposited, lack of progeny is ordained. (PS 16.144.1)
The Gharma is being placed around;
Vaiśvānara has been put on.
The poison is being offered forth; Takman has been offered forth.
The earth, being uprooted by its very foundation, has been overturned;
sin, being cooked, has reached its full maturity;
and the venomous serpent, being well-restrained, has been extracted, rendered unconscious by the fragrance.
Non-existence is being offered; supreme existence is offered.
Śarva is enraged while being crushed; [all] is being crushed;
Śimidā is being crushed. (PS 16.144.4)
Affliction is that which is being eaten; it is cut away when it has been eaten.

The student (*brahmacārī*) cuts off from this world and from yonder world the one who violates the sacred law (*brahmajyā*). *ārtir aśyamānā vīkartosītā aśitā lokāc chinatti brahmacārī brahmajyam asmāc cāmuṣmāc ca //* *Bhatt. asitā PS_16,144.5 (144)*
Its striking is sorcery; its expectation is a spell;
its entrails are a hidden charm; it is turned away, driven off.
Agni, having become a consumer of raw flesh, enters the Brahmin’s cow and devours the oppressor of Brahmins;
he cuts away all his limbs and roots,
destroys his paternal kinsmen, and causes his maternal kinsmen to perish.
The Brahmagavī, when not given away again, purifies all the kinsmen of a Kṣatriya who have been involved in a marriage.
Bhaṭṭa says:
[The one who knows] all this makes him homeless, without cattle, and without offspring; he becomes without support, unable to sustain himself from one stage to the next, and perishes.
Bhaṭṭa: Furthermore, for one who knows thus, if a Kṣatriya seizes the cow of a Brāhmaṇa,
his slaughter will surely come quickly.
The vultures raise a clamor;
the long-haired women dance around his cremation pyre.
Striking their chests with their hands and committing a sin against the descendant of Ilu—
[this occurs] in his dwellings.
The wolves make a pack;
they quickly question him:
"What was that which was there? Is this it, father? (PS 16.145.5)
Cut it! Cut it away! Cut it out!
Burn it up! Burn it up!
O Āṅgirasī, [burn] him who seizes [us].
Cause the oppressor of Brahmins to perish!
For you are called Vaiśvadevī, a sorcery born of the clan that has been turned back.
Burning, fiercely burning, the thunderbolt of Brahman,
having become death with razor-sharp edges, has pursued [them];
you seize the splendor of those who conquer.
Having taken away one's sacrifices, charitable works,
and blessings, you bestow them upon the one who has conquered in that other world.
Bhaṭṭa says: "O inviolable cow, grant [this];
be a path-maker against the Brahmin's curse."
O Bhaṭṭa, become a path, a missile, a target, and a source of sin for the sinner; O Agni, strike off the head of the one who harms the Brahmin and has committed an offense.
May Agni burn the silver that you have offered, the evil deed of the one who harms the gods and bestows no bounty.
Bhaṭṭa! Tear apart the god-hater; tear him asunder, cut him, cut him to pieces! Bhaṭṭa!
Having torn him apart, hack him, hack him to pieces, mince him, mince him thoroughly, burn him up, burn him, consume him!
O Goddess, O inviolable one, burn up the oppressor of Brahman from the very root; whatever misfortune is in your head, [burn it away].
That which is stuck in the hair or placed upon the forehead—
may this Apāmārga, the universal remedy, wipe it away.
Whatever ill fortune is in your eyebrows, or what has been placed in your ears and eyes...
Whatever misfortune is in your mouth, in your nose, in your speech, or in your lips...
Whatever misfortune is placed in your teeth,
on your tongue, or in your jaw...
That misfortune which has been placed in your mind, in your intention, and in your vital breath...
Whatever misfortune is in your jaws, situated in your throat and in your lungs—
Whatever misfortune is in your shoulders, in your neck, in your ribs, or in your spine...
Whatever misfortune is in your two arms,
in your shoulders, or in your armpits...
Whatever misfortune is in your two arms, following after the elbows and the forearms—
Bhatt. [reads] *kalpuṣīr*.
(…) Whatever misfortune is in your hands, following along the fingers of your palms...
(…) Whatever misfortune resides in your back,
or is placed upon your hips and buttocks—
(…) whatever ill fortune was placed upon your chest, or that which was fixed upon your sides and breasts.
Bhaṭṭa: On both sides...
Whatever misfortune is in your heart...
Along the navel and down the flanks...
That misfortune which is in your spleen (*plīhan*).
Or that which is in the liver and the kidneys;
(... // see 16.147.1cd PS_16,148.4 That which is in your intestines and the entrails.
Misfortune is located in the belly; (... what misfortune is in your bladder... (see PS_16,148.5)
It is placed upon the rectum and the bladder.
(…) That misfortune which you cast off—
Or whatever [misfortune] is in the thighs or in the testicles;
whatever misfortune is in your hips.
The benefit for *avacā* and *lūśa*.
That misfortune of yours which is in the ashes (*bhasadi*), O Bhasati.
That which is placed upon the thighs and knees... (see 16.147.1cd) ...that misfortune (*daurbhāgya*) of yours which is in the shanks.
It is placed upon the two thick heels.
(…) Whatever misfortune is in your ankles...
Along the toes of the feet... [as in 16.147.1cd] ...that misfortune which is in your joints.
In the flesh, in the bones, in the marrow—whatever misfortune belongs to you...
PS_16,149.2) ...whatever misfortune belongs to you.
That which is established in each limb, or that which resides in the body hairs, (...
Whatever misfortune is yours in the dice,
in the casting,
or upon the gaming board...
Whatever misfortune is yours among your livestock, or that which is fixed upon your plowing and your thunderbolt...
That misfortune of yours which is the slaughter of an embryo,
and that state of yours which is childlessness—
That which was ordained for you by the Pitṛsadyas, and also that which is your honor...
Whatever evil fortune is yours, and whatever lack of cattle you have—
this [remedy] is the universal healer for that.
May the Apāmārga plant wipe away that sin which arose against the gods, [committed] by men afflicted by cold and reaching up to their necks.
May these waters carry away that impurity; may they purify me with their hundred-streamed filter. Bathe away the impurity and every stain.
Having cast away evil upon black clothing,
having left behind the turning point, destruction, and the nooses of death,
come toward the sun, the light, and Agni.
Rising up from the great ocean, being released from distress and from evil, may our mind and our life-span return to us again.
May the Paṇis and the Yātudhānas not harm us!
We have wiped away our own blemish and the curse.
May luster be bestowed upon me;
may splendor be bestowed upon me.
May out-breath and in-breath not forsake me.
May I attain the full span of life.
"Brahma was born" is one verse:
"Brahma has risen up, shining, the atmosphere and the sky; with the immortal, Brahma has shaken off death."
May Brahmā, the direct overseer of good deeds,
drive away from us blemish and darkness.
May the spreading, extended [grass-blades] facing westward serve as the strewing.
We see them spread out;
[Bhaṭṭa asks: "What do we see? Those which are placed in the waters of the ocean."
For the Asuras, it is made of iron.
The golden-winged bird has ascended to heaven with his radiance;
those who wish to harm you as you fly up to heaven—
Strike it down with your heat, O Jātavedas;
for you are formidable, rise to heaven with your flame, O Sūrya, being free from fear.
The illusory Asuras who roam about marked with iron nets and made of iron fetters— those I deliver over to you for destruction, O Jātavedas!
O thousand-edged thunderbolt, go forth crushing our rivals.
The thousand-backed one, the lord of the gods, comes; the Gharma,
shining by the cosmic order (ṛta), beholds immortality.
O golden-hued divine Sūrya, you,
the glowing cauldron of heat, traverse the ends of heaven with your lightning-flash.
The lightnings, whose tongues are fire, flash forth.
Golden-hued and immortal within the waters, in the midst of the ocean,
is the lightning hurled by Rudra, the thunderer;
may that bolt of Vaiśvānara spare us.
Blazing with lightning, Agni goes to the heart where the fearsome tigers dwell in the waters;
thundering, Rudra comes with the strides of Viṣṇu.
Driving away enemies and scattering adversaries, may he make the quarters free of rivals for me;
clothed in the waters, he moves through the mid-air.
The kindled Agni, the celestial bestower of heat,
Vaiśvānara, with his cooling form, goes as the eagle of the waters upon the back of heaven.
Vaiśvānara goes around the ocean, the bright Gharma, shining and radiant with splendor;
driving away my enemies, burning up my rivals.
The wise Āditya has ascended to the sky;
Vaiśvānara heats the mid-air, and Agni, kindled and born of fervor, heats the celestial realm.
They press the Soma for him; they train themselves.
Shining, he clothes himself in immortality as his garment.
These two, not wavering, have sped forth.
He goes toward his two forms, the cool and the thin, and the two terrifying ones;
clothing himself in many forms, he makes his bodies turn away into the secret depths.
As the five-spoked wheel revolves,
all the worlds mount it; yet its axle, though bearing a heavy burden, does not burn.
From of old it is not severed; it is of ancient kinship.
He who is heated by the five heats shines forth; they follow him, who possesses a thousand abodes.
O Sūrya, seven bay horses carry you; O Āditya, through the threefold power of sacred prayer as your mouth,
you shine forth, you shine, and you shine again.
The immortal Gharma rises within the waters;
it is the slayer of Vṛtra, the vanguard of the bay steeds— the unassailable bodies of Sūrya.
The Gharma is behind us, and the Gharma is before us;
we cast it against the hater with iron teeth.
Vaiśvānara, clothed in cold and heat.
May it destroy all my rivals who hate me.
The Gharma, the sole hero through the sacred word (brahman), cooks the seasons with the seasons.
Purifying himself, kindled with fuel, the Brahman heats you with prayer and with splendor. The Brahman was born first.
That which was being born took on a uniform form;
it did not split, nor does it split. That [form], conceiving itself as a father, spoke out. (Bhatt. [Is it *aṃhamānaṃ*? )
His channels are stretched out, spread wide, and extended;
he brought forth the existent from the non-existent.
He who begot him is indeed his sustainer.
Prajāpati, being in harmony with his offspring, establishes the three lights; he is not one who is merely cooked. Prajāpati moves within the womb.
Being born, he is manifested in many ways;
the wise behold his station,
and in him all worlds are established.
In whom gods, ancestors, and humans are supported like spokes in the hub—
I ask you about the flower of the waters.
Wherein that [world] was established by means of illusion.
Bhaṭṭa [says]: "That wherein the flower of the waters is placed by Māyā, well-placed in the secret cave" (PS 16.152.1).
He who indeed knows that directly, he would know the great Brāhmaṇa;
it is a gem placed within three threads, finding its own light.
Let him go upward, crosswise, or among the people, knowing his way; as a man, procreating by the *ṛta*,
let him go forth to all the ends this very day.
May Āditya, together with Jātavedas, burn away everything throughout the night as he ascends from the earth to heaven by means of Agni.
May he anoint me with long life;
may he endow me with splendor. The Gharma, thousandfold, is kindled by the fuel-stick.
May he make all the quarters my rivals;
may Sūrya Vaiśvānara, the tawny one, slay all my rivals.
May the heated Gharma burn up my rivals and those who hate me;
may the Āditya grant [victory] over the enemies.
May Vaiśvānara, the bull, rising like the sun, burn away those who attack us,
our rivals, and our enemies.
Rising for me, may the bright Āditya,
the Sun, destroy the adversaries.
The bright, well-winged, golden Brahman.
The shining, eternal light has spread across the sky;
may the golden-winged, swift, and crushing bird slay our rivals with his great weapon.
May Hari, the fair-winged one, the auspicious day, the dispeller of fear, the golden-hued, the difficult to overcome, and the swift—
may Sūrya [drive] all my rivals away.
May Āditya strike with his rays; may he,
the bright one rising, encompassing the great purpose, ordain day and night as he goes forth.
"May Vaiśvānara Sūrya go forth today, burning all my rivals," [and] "Rising today, O thou of Mitra-like luster," [these constitute] one [verse].
You bear splendor, ascetic heat, bliss, prosperity, majesty, and stability from your very mouth;
being encompassed by them, you go forth everywhere as the embodiment of glory.
Your truth and fame are unfailing and exalted; you,
the observer of the holy life, traverse both worlds, in whom the gods become of one mind.
He supported this earth and yonder sky;
may he fulfill his teacher through ascetic fervor.
The teacher, initiating the religious student...
He makes a germ within;
for three nights he bears it in his belly.
When it is born, the gods come together to behold it.
The ancestors, humans, divine beings, and Gandharvas— all of them follow this student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*).
Thirty-three, three hundred, and six thousand [gods] [follow him].
By means of his ascetic heat (tapas), he satisfies all the gods.
This earth is the fuel-stick, the sky is the second; moreover, he fills the intermediate space with fuel.
The student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*), girded with the sacrificial cord and carrying the firewood,
fills the worlds through exertion and austerity;
he was born before the *brahman* as the *brahmacārī*.
Clothed in heat, he stood above austerity; from that was born the Brāhmaṇa, the Brahman as the eldest,
together with all the gods and immortality.
The student of sacred knowledge, kindled with fuel, clothed in black, consecrated, and long-bearded—
he goes instantly from the eastern ocean to the western ocean.
Having repeatedly stirred the worlds,
the Brahmachārī, generating the waters of sacred knowledge, [established] the world and Prajāpati.
Having become the embryo within the womb of immortality, he became Indra and struck down the Asuras— [he who is] Parameṣṭhin, the Virāj.
The first student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) brought forth this earth, the ground, and the sky;
having made these their sacred formulation (brahman), they worship them with fuel-sticks.
In them all the worlds are established. The Teacher fashioned both atmospheres; he, whose eye is that [truth], carved out the vast and deep earth and heaven.
The student protects them with austerity;
the gods revel in their shared feast.
One is near, the other is far.
Two treasures are deposited in the secret cave of the Brāhmaṇa; the student of sacred knowledge protects them through austerity,
and the knower of Brahman makes them his own entirely.
One [Agni] is on this side of the back of heaven,
the other is here on earth; these two Agnis, joined together, are between the two worlds of space.
Upon those two rest the firm rays;
the student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) stands upon them through his ascetic fervor (tapas).
Roaring, the ruddy one with white horns—Varuṇa—roars.
The one with the large tail has stretched himself along the earth;
as a student of sacred knowledge, he pours his seed upon the summit of the earth.
By that the four quarters live.
Parjanya, Death, Varuṇa, Soma, the plants, and milk— these are its forms.
The clouds were the courageous ones;
by them they brought this [light] to heaven—
from the fire, from the sun, and from the moon.
The student of sacred knowledge places the fuel-stick in the waters within the wind;
their flames move separately through the clouds.
For them, clarified butter is the man, rain is the horse;
having become the teacher, Varuṇa makes the ghee his own alone at home.
Whatever Prajāpati desired,
that the student (brahmacārī) offered up from himself as his own friend (mitra).
The teacher is a celibate student;
the celibate student is Prajāpati;
Prajāpati shines forth as the sovereign ruler.
Indra became the sovereign Virāj;
through celibacy and austerity,
the king protects his kingdom.
The teacher desires a student through celibacy;
a maiden [desires a husband] through celibacy.
A young woman finds a husband;
through the practice of celibacy, the ox seeks fodder and the horse desires grass.
By means of celibacy and austerity,
the gods conquered death;
indeed, Indra [conquered it] by means of celibacy.
—He brought down the immortal nectar from heaven.
The plants are the past and the future;
day and night are the forest trees.
The year together with the seasons—
these are the domestic animals born as celibate students, belonging both to the earth and to heaven.
Those that are wild and those that are domestic,
those birds that are wingless and those that have wings—
they are all born as practitioners of the holy life (brahmacārin).
Each of the lords of creatures bears the vital breaths within himself;
Brahman protects them all.
It was brought by a female religious student.
The Vedic student bears the shining Brahman that has been brought;
in him all the gods have gathered together.
Accompanied by the Bhaṭṭas,
that tawny, reddish-brown man, having bathed, shines greatly upon the earth. (PS 16.155.3)
This is the portion set apart for the gods; it moves unclimbed and radiant. In it are all cattle, and in it are all sacrifices.
In that [fire], food [is offered] together with the deities.
Bhaṭṭa’s misprint: *tasiṇṇaṃ* (PS 16,155.4).
Generating the out-breath and in-breath from the beginning, and generating the diffused breath, sight, hearing, sacred knowledge, and intelligence.
Bestow upon us the most excellent speech and glory. Food, semen, blood, and the belly— these are the [necessary] arrangements.
A celibate student stood upon the surface of the water, performing austerities in the midst of the ocean. (PS 16.155.6,
Anuvāka 22)
Truth, the great, the formidable cosmic order, consecration, asceticism, sacred formulation, and sacrifice— these sustain the earth.
May she, the mistress of what has been and what is to be, the Earth, create for us a wide and unconfined space among men in the midst of the world.
She who possesses highlands, lowlands, and level plains, and who bears herbs of manifold powers—
may that Earth spread out for us, may she be propitious for us.
In whom the ocean and the Sindhu, in whom the waters, and in whom the gods found the falsehood;
she who bears in many ways the moving breath— read *prāṇat* with K.
May that earth grant us [a share] in cattle, horses, and food—
she upon whom the men of old strode forth,
and upon whom the gods overcame the Asuras.
May that Earth, upon whom this whole trembling world lives, grant us the first draught.
Upon whom the four quarters of the earth are established.
May the Earth grant us fortune and splendor— she in whom the settled peoples were produced, and who is the source of cattle, horses, and birds. PS_17.1.5
The all-sustaining, the bearer of wealth, the foundation, the golden-breasted, the resting place of the world—
the Earth bears Agni Vaiśvānara.
May Indra, the bull, bestow wealth upon us.
In her, the waters flow together in equal measure,
day and night, without fail.
May that earth, yielding many streams, milk forth milk for us; may she also sprinkle us with splendor—
she whom those who are ever vigilant protect at all times.
O gods, may the earth, the ground, yield for us her dear honey through heedfulness;
and may she likewise sprinkle us with splendor.
That which was upon the waters at the beginning of the ocean, which the wise pursue through their creative powers (māyā),
and in which the heart [rests] in the highest heaven.
By truth is the nectar of the earth encompassed;
may that earth bestow upon me brilliance and strength within the kingdom.
[The earth] which the Aśvins measured out...
That upon which Viṣṇu strode forth,
which Indra, the Lord of Śacī, made for himself free of enemies.
May that earth release for us milk, as a mother for her son;
may those mountains and snowy peaks [grant us the same].
"O Earth, may you be pleasant and auspicious for us. The brown, the black, the ruddy, the multiform—
the firm ground, the earth, protected by Indra."
Unconquered, unslain, unhurt, I have ascended upon the earth.
Bhaṭṭa Ajītahata (PS 17.2.1):
That which is your center, O Earth, and that which is your navel, and those strengths of yours that have come into being as bodies; [with these we worship you].
Bestow those [blessings] upon us; flow for our benefit. The earth is the mother, I am the son of the earth;
Parjanya is the father—may he indeed protect us.
On that earth where they enclose the altar,
on which the creators of all things perform the sacrifice,
and on that ground where the sacrificial posts are measured out.
The pure [waters] rise upward before the oblation;
may that Earth, ever increasing, cause us to prosper. O Earth, whoever should hate us or who should attack us—[may she hold him back].
O Earth, deliver him who seeks to harm us with thought or weapon to one who has acted against us from before;
for mortals born of you move about upon you.
You support bipeds and quadrupeds;
upon you, O Earth, rest these five classes of men, for whom there is immortal light among mortals.
The rising sun spreads himself out with his rays.
May they milk for us all our offspring together;
O Earth, bestow upon me the honey of speech.
May we always follow after the Mother of plants, the all-encompassing, the firm earth, the Pṛthivī held by the cosmic order— she who is auspicious and pleasant.
Great is your dwelling place; you have become great.
Great is your surge, your movement, and your trembling.
Indra protects you with his great heroic power.
O Earth, inspire us with delight at the sight of you, as if at the sight of gold;
Agni is upon the earth, Agni is in the plants.
The waters bear Agni; Agni is in the stones;
Agni is within men;
and there are Agnis in cows and horses.
Agni shines from heaven;
the vast mid-air belongs to Agni, the god;
mortals kindle Agni.
The bearer of oblations, lover of clarified butter—
may Agnivāsas, the Earth, and Asitajñu make me radiant and disciplined.
Upon the earth, they offer to the gods the sacrifice, the well-prepared oblation. (Bhaṭṭikāvya)
Upon the earth mortals live by means of their own inherent power and food;
may that earth bestow upon us breath and long life.
May the earth not bring upon me the sight of old age.
O Earth, that fragrance of yours which has come into being, which the plants and the waters bear—
That which the Gandharvas and Apsarases bear, which they have partaken of, that is yours; it deserves cattle and horses.
By that, make us fragrant;
let no one at all hate us.
That fragrance of yours which has entered the lotus—
That fragrance which the immortals gathered first on earth at the wedding of Sūryā—
with that, make us fragrant.
May no one whatsoever be hostile toward us.
O Earth, that fortune and splendor of yours which resides among men, among women, and among men— may it be ours.
He who is in the brides and those desiring brides;
he who is in the cattle, in the horses, in the wild beasts, and even in the elephants.
Whatever splendor is in the maiden and in the earth, with that unite us;
let no one whatsoever hate us.
The earth is rock, stone, and dust—
the earth that is gathered and sustained, upon which grow trees and forest lords.
They stand firm forever;
we address the earth, whose breast is gold, as she is firmly held.
Whether rising up, or sitting, or standing, or stepping forward with the right and left feet.
May we not suffer distress upon the earth.
I address the wide-spreading earth, the patient ground that has been magnified by the sacred word (*brahman*).
Bearing strength and nourishment, I settle down upon you, O Earth, as a portion of food, as clarified butter.
Pure waters flow for me from my body.
That which has overcome me with what is unpleasant, that we deposit within the filter;
with the filter, I purify the earth upward.
Bearing treasures in many ways, she dwells in secret as wealth.
May the Earth grant us jewels and gold;
may the Goddess, the giver of wealth, bestowing riches upon us, grant them with a gracious mind.
Those quarters of yours that are eastern, those that are northern, those of yours, O Earth, that are below and those that are behind—
may they be pleasant for me as I move about.
Do not fall upon me while I am resting in this world;
do not push me from behind nor from the front;
O Earth, grant me well-being.
Drive away the more excellent [path]; let not the waylayers find me as long as I behold you.
O Earth, with the sun as your companion,
may my sight not fail me for as many years as there are even-numbered years ahead.
Whatever root of yours I dig up, O Earth, let that grow back again; do not disclose your vital parts, O you who are free from predators.
May I not pierce your heart,
O Earth, when lying down I turn over from my right side toward the left.
When we, lying on our backs, press against you from the side while you face us, do not harm us there, O Earth.
O Earth, you are the refuge of all;
yours are summer, the rains, autumn, winter, the cool season, and spring.
The seasons have been ordained for you as years;
may day and night and the earth yield milk for us—
she who drives away the serpent and is free from wild beasts.
In whom the fires were placed within the waters;
she who, choosing Indra as her lord, drove away the Dasyus, the revilers of the gods, as the earth [crushed] Vṛtra.
I have offered [this] to Śakra, the bull, the vigorous one;
may he assign to us from the earth whatever wealth we desire.
May Bhaga impel [it] after [us].
May Indra go as the leader,
in whom the Sadas and the Havirdhāna sheds are established, and in whom the sacrificial post is erected.
In which the Brahmins who know the Yajus offer worship with the Ṛg and Sāman verses,
and in which the officiating priests are joined together.
The Soma for Indra to drink;
may that Earth, being well-disposed, bestow great favor upon us at the sacrifice through this sacrificial fee.
In whom the ancient seers who created beings, the seven ordainers, sang forth the cows by means of the sacrificial session.
Together with sacrifice and austerity,
may she bestow upon us cattle of every form;
may Savitṛ grant me long life.
To that Earth, whose food is rice and barley, and upon whom these five peoples dwell, who is the wife of Parjanya.
Homage be to her; she prospers through the rain.
In her, mortal people belonging to the clan of Vīlva sing and dance.
May that earth, upon which there is shouting and upon which the drum resounds,
drive away our rivals— our rivals.
May he who hates us make him lower;
in whatever city made by the gods, in whatever field they exert themselves.
May Prajāpati make the earth, which contains all embryos, pleasant for us in every direction;
she who bears many people of diverse speech.
May the Earth, like a cow that does not kick, yield for us a thousand streams of wealth, according to the various dwellings of manifold beings,
as steady as a fixed milch-cow.
The serpent that is yours, the scorpion with the stinging bite, born in winter, the restless one that lies in its lair— the worm that moves upon the earth during the rainy season.
May that [path] of yours, moving and gliding, move toward us; with that which is auspicious, be gracious to us. Those paths of yours which lead in many ways to the people...
May we conquer that path which leads to the tracks of the chariot and the course of the mind,
along which both the good and the evil travel—
that path which is free from enemies and thieves.
Bearing [the body] slowly, supporting the heavy, and enduring the destruction of both good and evil;
The earth, in harmony with the boar, yields itself for the sake of the wild boar, the beast;
those wild animals and deer that are established in the forest.
Lions, tigers, and man-eaters roam about;
O Earth, drive away from us the wolf, the jackal, misfortune, the ṛkṣīkā, and the rākṣasa.
The Gandharvas and Apsarases,
those who roam about, the Kimīdins,
all the Piśācas, and the Rakṣasas—
Drive them away from us, O Earth!
Those two-footed winged creatures that fly together—
the swans, the eagles, the birds, the fowls— [drive them away].
In which the wind Mātariśvan moves, creating the realms of space and shaking the trees—
the flame blows along with the wind’s forward rush and its backward blast.
Upon that earth, day and night were established as black and ruddy;
the earth, the broad world, was covered by rain.
May she grant us [this] with auspiciousness,
in every beloved abode.
May both Heaven and Earth for me—
The intermediate space is my wide expanse;
Agni, Sūrya, the waters, and all the gods have bestowed wisdom upon me.
I am the enduring one, named Uttara upon the earth;
I am the subduer, the all-conquering.
O Goddess, you who endure all things, reaching from hope to hope;
O Goddess, you who were first created by the gods and have spread abroad through your greatness.
Welfare entered into you at that time; you did not conceive of the four quarters—
the villages and the forests.
O Goddess Earth, among those assemblies that exist upon the ground, may I rise up with honeyed speech.
What I shall speak, let that be honeyed; what I behold, let the pressers purify me with it.
I am radiant and impetuous against those whom I strike down, the turbulent ones.
Like a horse shaking off dust, he milked out that people who were settled upon the earth; then he was born,
the guardian of the world, encompassing the Madras.
The seizer of the lords of the forest and of the plants—
peaceful, fragrant, pleasant, with udders of mead, and full of milk.
May the Earth speak for us;
may the Earth, together with her milk,
place me within her, O Mother.
Well-established by Bhadrā;
being in agreement with you by day,
place me in prosperity and well-being.
Her whom Viśvakarman sought with oblation, in whom the fires were established within the waters—
therein was placed a vessel for enjoyment, hidden in secret.
— she was present with her manifest enjoyments and accompanied by her mothers;
you are the sower for people,
Aditi, the cow of plenty, possessing all forms.
Whatever is deficient in you, may Prajāpati, in harmony with all creatures, fill that full for you. (PS 17.6.10,
Anuvāka 1)
In which limb does his austerity abide? In which limb is his *ṛta* placed?
Where does his vow and where does his faith abide?
In which limb is its truth established?
Where is Brahman, where do the waters abide, and in which limb are the quarters of space established?
Which limb do they both follow in common day and night, being in agreement?
In which limb does his earth abide?
In which limb does the intermediate space abide?
In which limb does the established heaven abide?
In which limb does that which is above the heaven abide?
From which limb does his fire blaze? From which limb does Mātariśvan blow?
From which limb does the moon measure itself out?
Measuring out a great limb of the Skambha: where does Agni blaze upward, seeking his goal;
where does Mātariśvan blow, seeking his goal?
Tell me of that pillar toward which they go, veiled, seeking [it]; what indeed is it?
Where do the two young women of different forms go, seeking [it]?
Day and night flow together, meeting at that place where the waters, seeking their goal, come together;
[therein is] the Supporter.
Where do the half-months go? Where do the months go, in harmony with the year?
Where do the seasons go, and where do the seasonal deities go?
The Pillar (skambha) … upon which Prajāpati, having fixed the aggregates,
supported all the worlds.
Tell me of that Pillar: what indeed is it?
That which Prajāpati created as the highest, the lowest, and the middle, endowed with all forms.
To what extent did Skambha enter therein?
And that which he did not enter—where did that become?
To what extent did Skambha enter into the existent?
How much will remain in his expectation?
Since he has divided one single limb into a thousand parts,
how much of the Skambha has entered therein?
Wherein the worlds and the treasuries exist,
wherein wise people know Brahman, and wherein both the unreal and the real are contained within.
Tell me of that Pillar: what indeed is it?
Upon which, having exerted its fervor, it sustains the supreme *ṛta*.
Wherein there is the vow and faith,
wherein the waters of Brahman are concentrated—
that is Skambha. (…)" PS_17,8.2
In whom the earth, the intermediate space,
and the sky are deposited; in whom fire, the moon, and the sun abide.
The winds stand fixed upon the pillar of him whose [support] are the thirty-three gods.
All [the gods] are concentrated in the limbs;
[they enter] the Skambha,
where the seers who create beings [dwell].

The Ṛgveda, Sāmaveda, and Yajurveda are the great [earth]; the One-Seer in whom they are fixed—[I praise] Skambha. (…)* *Note: The ellipsis indicates the continuation of the verse as found in the *Paippalāda Saṃhitā*. The term "mahī" here refers to the earth, which serves as the foundation for the Vedas.*
He from whom the four quarters stand as well-sustained channels,
in whom the sacrifice has exerted its power.
The Pillar (…) where both immortality and death,
and the Puruṣa, are contained.
The ocean is its channels; tell me of that Skambha—what indeed is it? Those who know Brahman within the person [know this].
They know him along with the Skambha—
both he who knows Parameṣṭhin and he who knows Prajāpati.
Those who know the Brāhmaṇa as the eldest, they know Skambha thoroughly;
he whose head is Vaiśvānara.
The eye became the Aṅgirasas; [the text reads] *cacakṣur*, but this is likely a misprint for *cakṣur*. It became the Aṅgirasas.
Tell me, which one indeed is that Skambha, whose limbs are the Yātus?
Bhaṭṭa: Who is he of whom they say that Brahmā is his mouth and the honey-stalk is his tongue?
Whose upper part they call Virāj,
the Skambha—
(…) from whom I have carved out the Ṛg-verses.
From whom they drew forth the Yajus;
whose body hairs are the meters (chandas).
Tell me of that Support: what indeed is it?
People know it as the supreme, standing upon the branch of non-existence.
But those who worship his branch, the lower ones, think themselves to be superior, where both the Ādityas and the Rudras [reside].
And the Vasus are concentrated;
tell me of that Skambha—what indeed is he?
He upon whom the thirty-three gods [depend].
They always guard a treasure;
who today knows that treasure which the gods protect?
Where the gods who know Brahman worship Brahman as the eldest—
whosoever, indeed, knows that Brahman as such.
Those who know Brahman indeed know him.
Those gods named the "Great Ones" were born from non-being.
People say that one part of Skambha is non-existent,
where Skambha, bringing forth [creation], dwells.
He turned out the Purāṇa.
They know that one limb of Skambha as being according to the Purāṇa.
Wherein the thirty-three gods took possession of the limbs and members;
those indeed are the thirty-three gods.
Some knowers of Brahman know him as Hiraṇyagarbha, the supreme,
whom people know as the unsurpassable.
In the beginning, Skambha poured forth that gold within the world;
in Skambha are the worlds, in Skambha is austerity.
Upon the Skambha is the Truth established;
we know you, the Skambha,
as Indra, in whom everything is contained.
In Indra are the worlds, in Indra is heat, in Indra is the Truth established;
we know you, O Indra, face to face.
Everything is contained within the Skambha.
Before the sun, before the dawn, I call aloud by name with a name.
That which first came into being together with that [world] attained self-sovereignty;
there is no other being superior to it.
Salutation to that supreme Brahman, whose earth is the limit and whose belly is the mid-air, and who made heaven his head. PS_17,10.3
He whose eye is the sun, whose moon is ever renewed,
and who made fire his mouth.
Homage to that eldest Brahman,
whose out-breath and in-breath are the wind, and whose eyes were the Aṅgirases.
Salutation to that supreme Brahman, the wise one, who created the earth and the quarters. PS_17,10.5
He who, born from the toil of asceticism,
has pervaded all the worlds,
and who made the Soma his own alone.
Homage to that eldest Brahman!
Skambha has supported the earth and yonder sky; Skambha has supported the wide mid-air.
The Pillar has supported the six wide quarters; the Pillar has entered this entire world. How is it that the wind does not cause it to waver?
Why does the mind not find delight?
Why do the waters always move forward, seeking the truth?
Bhaṭṭa reads *caṅkramiti*, but it should be emended to *caṅkramati*.
"A great Yakṣa in the midst of the world. (PS 17.10.8)
Upon the surface of the waters, ascetic heat has spread;
upon it rest all those gods who are like branches around the trunk of a tree.
To whom [the gods] always offer tribute with their hands, feet, speech, ears, and eyes; to whom the gods [offer tribute].
They bestow the immeasurable upon the measured;
tell me, what indeed is that *skambha*?
Darkness has been dispelled from it.
He is turned away from evil;
in him are all the lights that are in Prajāpati.
He who knows the golden reed standing in the water—
he indeed is the secret Prajāpati.
He does not pass beyond Prajāpati,
nor does he pass beyond Parameṣṭhin; and there, too, our choice is established.
That which is the eldest, beyond which nothing surpasses— truly, that exists beyond the earth; truly,
that exists beyond the sky.
The worlds are indeed woven into that in which these creatures are woven. (PS 17.11.4,
Anuvāka 2)
He licks within the vessel, difficult to behold, seeking what is ill-placed.
(Selva 2019, 56; Bhatt. duḥśe durni°)
O Uruṇḍā, Abhicaṅkramā, Vakmakā, and Bastyavāsinī—
may all of you, together with the Bhaṇvās, [be present].
We know your names;
as many as you have been born,
so many are these [beings] who are ever following after us.
I [conquer] Karṇā, Dṛṣadvatī, Urūṅgī, Keśinī, Krakum,
Khaḍūrī, and Ambarīṣyā.
We ever destroy the followers of evil.
The seventeenth lesson:
[He should avoid] a woman with pale speech, with teeth like ploughshares, and who utters indistinct sounds.
We declare all those unpleasant ones to be yours;
perish from here, O Sadānvās,
you who cause him to gnash his teeth while he lies down!
At night they desire the sick man;
moreover, while people are asleep,
they lick from their mouths and snatch from their hands.
Those [missiles] appropriate for those who possess teeth—
we cause them to perish from here as they fall, being scattered.
"Those who always follow after the scent of others—
I shall pierce them with my sword,
like a bull with its sharp horns."
Together with the Sadānvās and the Sādānveyas, both women and men, may you,
powerful through power, prevail together with them.
I strike down the adversaries and the demons.
Bhaṭṭa: [He should strike] those with four fangs, pot-like testicles, long hair, and blood on their faces. PS 17,12.6.
We destroy the rats that smell of bottle-gourd, those of ill-omen,
born upon the stalks and on the hair.
From you, we drive away the weeping Rodākā; we destroy all ill-named female spirits who always follow after us.
Those whose offspring cry out as they are born, who burn within the forest, and who lie upon the trees— [may their power be destroyed].
(…) // see 8cd PS_17,12.9 When wind, clouds,
lightning, and rain arise, the agent [is perceived].
The Śālā spirits desire to act quickly;
we shall always destroy all the Durṇāmīs, the Santokās, and the Sadānvās.
Those things which arise from grain sown in a field after it has been rained upon, and which are produced through cultivation.
Therefore, those women who are foul-smelling, always harsh, and whose feet are cracked shall perish.
Those men who are foul-smelling, always rough, and whose feet are cracked [shall likewise perish].
O Śacīpati, being struck by that thunderbolt, you were rendered stainless;
arise and run forth!
There shall be no shrinking back here;
Indra shall simultaneously shatter the wombs and the eggs of you all.
O Indra, slay Sthūlaśaṅkhā; crush Durṇaśī and Kuhā; [slay] the Arāyī and the Śakadhūmyā.
We always destroy the Sadānvās—
[the goddess] who strikes down Āsutām, Nagnahva, and Ajamāyu.
We destroy the piercing Viṭiṭiṅgas and the ever-following Sadānvas;
you shall subdue him whose son [you pursue].
O you who are full of strength and ever-flowing,
make the parched grain moist;
when you are satiated with the juice, [then let it be so].
— from [him], you pour down the surā.
Having drunk of it, I am now exhausted;
my head reels and I lie prostrate.
We destroy those ever-attacking ones that corrupt food—
those who are free from disease yet emit smoke-colored excrement.
Let them go quickly to the trees; then let the ill-intentioned Arāyīs seize the house.
Among them, one was Acchavākā, one was Śaṅkhāvankā, one was Vanekṛkur,
and one was Kanikradā.
We know all your names together; as many as you are born, so many are they.
May those who constantly pursue [us] perish from here.
I cast forth this powerful, all-conquering hall.
We invoke the ever-following herb for victory,
O you of fearsome aspect, difficult to look upon!
O naked one, O Bhaṇvu, O Sadānvā! Against Dhṛājī, Tviṣī, and the pure Agni— what do you desire here, O Arāyī?
Do not sing out toward the smoke; I shall always praise Sadānvā.
One is Kaṅkī, one is Prakhidā.
Seeking what do these ill-named *arāyī* demons, who resort to tranquility, roam at night— the *rāyīs* that cause miscarriage and sterility?
We cause those to perish from here:
the Apakrathā, the Abhiśrayā,
the Ānṛtyantī, and the Kutūhalā.
The *kusūlī*, the *rathabhañjanī*, and the *trikūkvā* born from the threshing floor—
these we cause to perish from here.
Those who, with disheveled hair, intoxicated, and with terrible eyes,
have torn out the heads of one another.
O Brahmaṇaspati, cast those who dwell as if possessing a canopy, the Sadānvas, beyond the embryos.
May Agni drive away from here those whose manifold fragrance reaches a man on the road.
The Jātavedas and Sadānvās—
those who seek to devour the person while he is being burned and rendered empty in the fire.
You are called "the one torn out," you who are always pursued by the tip of the fist;
we drive those away from here.
Those who, accustomed to the threshing floor, eat the dry grain like mares or she-donkeys eating chaff.
We destroy the *sadānvās* who devour the embryos, one after another,
in their full force.
The cows accustomed to the body of a woman, like the Rohiṇīs—
those we cause to vanish from here.
Those which arise from the fathers— the Indrajās, the Sadānvās—
[drive] away what has been brought as if it were a debt.
We give them back again:
those that eat raw flesh, those that eat cruel things, and those that eat what lacks the scent of fire.
"O Sadānvas, eat this corpse that has been cast away;
the corpse is the exclusive domain of custom."
What indeed do you desire in the halls?
Those who are maidens, those who are old, those who are young, and those who are always with their husbands.
Let all the horned female scorpions go away; let the noble milch-cow creep forth, and let the stingy Arāyīs depart from here.
From them Rudra emitted a radiance that slays travelers; let those [radiances], being discharged, strike [the enemy] with lightning.
O Śakra, O Indra, with your faultless thunderbolt, release them;
O Indra, thresh out their husks.
May Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, destroy those devouring old women who eat the young boys.
The goddess who drives away all *rakṣas*—
those which belong to the *dāsīs* of the *asuras*,
and those which have been fashioned for human beings.
May both these kinds go away to the far distance, beyond the ninety navigable rivers, they whose sound is heard when they have come together.
Like a pack of wolves,
she was snatching away the gifts that were being offered to her.
We destroy those ever-attacking yakṣas which, according to their respective stations, surge forth during the night at evening.
May Agni, the all-conquering, drive away all those *ṛkṣīkāḥ* and *kalīlāndas*, as well as all the *rakṣas* demons.
The *pulīkayas* are born in the waters;
their guardian alone knows from whence they were born, for they are always accompanied by the *sadānvas*.
We cause those to perish from here:
the shadow of the teacher, the one to be honored,
the child, the longing, and the echo.
We destroy all the daughters of Caṇḍa, the Sadānvās, who are exceedingly foolish, fickle, and made of tūla-cotton.
One who talks excessively, one without a chin, one with pendulous breasts, one with missing toes, one with teeth like those of a porpoise, and one without a nose.
We always destroy the ever-following ones—
the loud-voiced, the barking,
the leaping, the lowing, and the small.
We destroy the stingy speech, the restless one, and those who always follow after it. (PS 17.15.10, Anuvāka 3)
"I give," he should say,
and he granted her to the Brahmins who were begging for the cow.
That [gift] is "possessing offspring" (prajāvat), meaning "possessing descendants" (apatyavat);
he exchanges it for offspring, and he bestows it well along with cattle.
He who does not wish to give a cow to the ancestral seers when they beg for one, as if it were the cow of the gods—
his [bones] shall be shattered by a trap.
With a woman who has a protruding hip, one's waist is crushed;
with a woman who is a eunuch, the house is consumed by fire; with a woman who is one-eyed, one's own property is lost.
From the foundation of the deep red,
one finds the Lord of Cattle;
likewise is the knowledge regarding the barren cow.
For you are called "the one who pierces from afar," he who pierces her ears cuts himself off from the gods.
Thinking "I am making a mark," he makes himself smaller;
from his standing upon her feet.
One finds what is called "dissolution";
through lack of mindfulness, those [senses] wither away which one smells with the mouth.
Since the crow has defiled the hair of this truthful cow while she was with her owner,
therefore the colts die.
And a predatory wolf slays her calves;
when someone cuts off her young for some kind of enjoyment.
Then the young children die; consumption (yakṣman) seizes them because of her [the earth]’s swelling.
This is for the purpose of her swelling.
The female slave mixes it with dung;
from that, even a beautiful form is produced.
Therefore,
she who is born as a cow, being born from one whose sin has not yet been expiated, brings forth the gods together with the Brahmins.
Therefore, this [wealth] is to be given to the Brahmins;
regarding this, they say: "It is the protection of one's own [self] for those who come seeking it."
The cow was created by the gods for them;
they said that he who treats her with hostility shall suffer the defeat of Brahman.
He who does not wish to give her to those who ask for her, being of priestly lineage,
is cut off from the gods.
And [it is] for the wrath of the Brahmins. He whose enjoyment of a cow is under the control of another—
if he should desire another [cow], then he [is at fault].
One might harm [the earth], or if the lord of the cows (the king) has been asked for [land] but does not wish to give it—
just as if a treasure were buried [there].
Likewise, the barren cow belongs to the Brāhmaṇas;
they come for her whenever anyone is born.
This comes back to them when Brahmins attack the barren cow;
just as another might conquer these [enemies].
Thus is its non-cessation;
even if it remains unrecognized for three years, one should indeed practice it.
O Nārada, a Brāhmaṇa who then says of her, "She is barren," shall come to ruin.
To him who has laid down the treasure of the gods,
both Bhava and Śarva circumambulate and discharge their arrows.
He lies ensnared from afar;
he does not wish to give what has been asked for, and his desire is not fulfilled.
He who desires to act without having given her [her due],
