By that same [power] with which Agni took this earth’s right hand,
by that I take your hand.
Do not be distressed; [be] with me.
Dhātṛ has taken your hand; Savitṛ has taken your hand.
Bhaga has taken your hand;
Aryaman has taken your hand.
You are a wife by sacred law.
"I am your householder; let this woman be my wife to be cherished.
Bṛhaspati has given her to me."
With me as your husband, live a hundred autumns, blessed with offspring.
Tvaṣṭṛ has fashioned this garment for your beauty.
By the command of Bṛhaspati, the sage among poets,
may Savitṛ and Bhaga clothe this woman with it, for the sake of progeny, as [they clothed] Sūryā.
May the houses envelop you with splendor and fortune; put on this radiant body,
like Uṣas in the sight of the Sun.
Indra and Agni, Heaven and Earth, Pūṣan,
Mitra and Varuṇa, Bhaga, both Aśvins,
Bṛhaspati, the Maruts, the Brahman, and Soma.
May they cause this woman to increase through progeny.
Bṛhaspati was the first to fashion the hair upon the head of Sūryā.
O Aśvins, with this we adorn this woman together with her husband.
This is that form which the young woman has assumed.
I seek with my mind the wife who wanders;
I shall pursue her with the Navagva companions.
I indeed shall be that in whom her form resides; perceiving it, I know the nest of the mind.
I do not eat what is stolen by the mind; I have been released from it.
Loosening for myself the noose of Varuṇa— this noose of Varuṇa I untie,
with which Savitṛ, the very gracious one, bound you.
I make wide space here for you, O bride, and an easy path for you together with your husband.
Raise yourselves up; you shall slay the Rakṣas.
Place this woman in a state of well-being;
the wise Dhātṛ has found a husband for her.
May King Bhaga go before her, knowing the way.
Bhaga fashioned the four feet; Bhaga fashioned the four hoof-tips;
Tvaṣṭṛ shaped the fetlocks from the middle.
May she be auspicious for us;
with this choice oblation of clarified butter, may she be desired for the sake of progeny.
For the sake of cattle and for sight,
may we kindle Agni together—
him who possesses beautiful *kiṃśuka* wood, whose vehicle is multiform.
O Sūryā, ascend the golden-hued, well-rolling, well-wheeled chariot to the world of immortality;
make for your husbands a pleasant bridal procession.
Do not harm the young girl on the path prepared by the gods;
[open] the door of the divine hall.
We make the path for the bride pleasant.
Let the sacred word (*brahman*) be joined at the rear, the sacred word at the front; the sacred word is at the end, in the middle, and on every side.
Having entered the inviolable city of the gods,
may you, auspicious and gracious, shine forth in the world of your husband. (PS 18.6.12,
Anuvāka 1)
For you they first drove Sūryā around, together with her bridal procession;
give the wife back to her husbands.
O Agni, together with offspring!
Agni has given back the wife,
along with life and splendor.
May he who is her husband live a long life for a hundred autumns.
Soma’s wife was the first.
The Gandharva is your other husband; Agni is your third husband;
the one born of man is your fourth.
Soma gave it to the Gandharva;
the Gandharva gave it to Agni; he has bestowed both wealth and sons.
Agni [has come] for me, and also this [earth].
O Aśvins, possessors of abundant wealth, your benevolence has come to us; desires have settled within our hearts.
O Gopā, O Śubhaspati, may we attain that which is not yet manifest, the beloved dwelling-place of Aryaman.
May she, rejoicing with a gracious mind—
Bestow upon us wealth consisting of all-heroic sons, worthy of our speech;
O Lords of Splendor, provide an easy passage, a good ford, and excellent water for drinking; strike down the obstacle that stands in the way and destroy evil intent.
Drive away the demons, strike down the evil thought;
O Lords of Splendor, come from afar to us. O Agni, as our leader, go forth conquering the demons.
As one who knows the field, drive away the adversaries first.
Whatever herbs there are, whatever rivers, whatever fields, and whatever forests—
May they, O bride, protect you, who are possessed of offspring, from demons for the sake of your husband.
We have come upon this path.
It is auspicious, a vehicle of well-being;
where the hero does not suffer harm, he acquires wealth from others.
Listen well to this from me, O men: by which blessing a husband and wife obtain what is desirable—
those Gandharvas and divine Apsarases [who dwell] in the sky.
Upon these trees they have now taken their stand; may they be pleasant for this bride,
and may they not harm the bridal procession as it is being led away.
The consumption-diseases that follow people when they go after the bride’s moon-bright bridal procession— may the worshipful gods drive them back again.
Let them lead [the bride] back to where they came from; let not those who sit around, seeking to obstruct,
find the couple.
Having crossed over the difficult path by means of the Sugata,
may the enemies flee far away.
I illuminate the vehicle with sacred prayer and with houses.
With a non-terrible eye, with a friendly one— with that friendly eye,
the multiform [face] which is bound upon him.
May Savitṛ make that pleasant for her husbands;
this auspicious woman has come home—
the Creator has found this world for her.
May Aryaman, Bhaga, both Aśvins,
and Prajāpati increase her with progeny. This womanly field has come here, possessed of a soul.
Sow your seed in her;
may she bring forth offspring for you from her wombs, bearing the vigorous seed of the bull.
Establish yourself here like Virāj, like Viṣṇu, O Sarasvatī; may you multiply like dūrvā grass, O Indra.
May it be within the good favor of Bhaga.
May your wave rise up at the yoke-pin; may the waters release the thongs.
May the two inviolable ones, free from malice and sin, come to the swelling [embryo];
may she be of gentle aspect, not slaying her offspring, and auspicious.
Auspicious, very kind, easy to manage in the home, possessing offspring, bearing heroic sons, and desiring her husband—
serve this Gārhapatya fire.
O Bhaṭṭa,
may you be free from the slayer of brothers-in-law and free from the slayer of husbands;
be gracious, kind toward our cattle, and possessed of noble heroes.
A mother of heroes, desiring her husband's brother, may we dwell with you in comfort, being well-disposed toward one another.
Arise from here; desiring what have you come here?
But I, O Nirṛti, am the conqueror from my own home; you have come with empty hopes. Arise, O enemy, fly away, and do not linger!
When this bride has worshipped the former fire, the Gārhapatya, then,
O woman, [worship] for Sarasvatī.
And pay homage to the ancestors.
Bring this skin as armor to spread beneath this woman.
O Sinīvālī, let her give birth;
may she abide in the favor of Bhaga.
Spread out the balbaja grass.
Upon the red hide,
having sat down there, may she of good offspring serve this Agni.
The balbaja grass that you lay down and the skin that you spread out—
may she of good offspring mount it.
The maiden who finds a husband—
climb up upon the skin, sit down near the fire;
this god slays all the Rakṣasas.
O auspicious one, sit down near this Agni;
O wife, adorn yourself here before the gods.
Let offspring be born from the lap of this mother.
Animals of various forms are being born;
here, procreate offspring for this husband.
May this son of yours be preeminent in excellence.
Auspicious, a bringer across [to safety], gracious to the husband and bringing welfare to the father-in-law, pleasant to the mother-in-law—may we enter these houses. (Bhaṭṭa:
may we enter this house.)
May she be rich in offspring and reach old age. This bride is highly auspicious;
come together and behold her.
Having bestowed good fortune upon her,
O young women who are ill-disposed, depart with misfortune! (PS 18.9.8)
And those here who are even aged—
grant them indeed splendor; then go away to your home.
Sūryā Sāvitrī ascended the litter, which has a golden covering and bears all forms.
For the sake of great good fortune,
ascend the bed with a well-disposed mind; here, procreate offspring for this husband of yours.
Like Indrāṇī, well-awakened and awakening, you, O Uṣas, have woken up as a fierce light. In the beginning, the gods descended upon their wife.
They have touched their bodies with [your] body;
like the sun, O woman of every form, by your greatness, may you be auspicious for your husband, bringing offspring.
Arise from here, for she has a husband; with reverence and songs I praise Viśvāvasu.
Seek a kinswoman who sits among the fathers and is well-disposed.
That is your portion by birth; know it to be so:
those Apsarases who rejoice in communal revelry between the oblation-holder and the sun.
They are your birthplace; go toward them.
I pay homage to you, O Gandharva, according to the season.
Homage to the mind of the Gandharva!
Homage to Bhāmā and to Cakṣus we pay;
O Viśvāvasu, homage to you with this sacred prayer (brahman).
Go away to your other wives, the Apsarases!
O King, may we be well-disposed;
we have brought back the Gandharva from here. That god has gone to the highest dwelling place. He has gone.
We have come, extending our lifespan.
O Father and Mother, unite at the proper time; may you both become the source of seed.
O mortal man, mount this woman; may you two produce offspring here, rejoicing together.
May Prajāpati bring forth progeny for you both.
May Aryaman anoint [us] equally with day and night;
may we, free from ill fortune, enter this world of the husband.
Be auspicious to our bipeds, be auspicious to our quadrupeds.
O Pūṣan, send forth that most auspicious woman upon whom men sow their seed, who,
longing for us, shall spread her thighs apart.
Upon her we would gladly bestow our seed.
Place your hand upon her thigh; embrace your wife with a well-disposed mind.
Produce offspring here and prosper with wealth;
may Savitṛ grant you a long life. That portion of the sacred word which they have given us from the two brides—
The garment for the bride and the cloth—
O Bṛhaspati and Indra, acting in agreement with the priest, grant these together.
This bridal garment, given by the gods together with Vanu, is the robe for this bride;
he who gives it to a wise Brahmin.
He indeed strikes down the demons who dwell upon the same bed;
awakening from a pleasant womb, laughing and exulting with great joy.
May you two carry us across to good cattle, good sons, and a good home,
while the radiant dawns shine forth for our living.
Clothed in new [garments], fragrant and well-attired,
I, living, have risen toward the shining dawns.
O Bhaṭṭa, may they shine forth;
may I fly away from the egg like a bird,
away from every sin.
May the beautifying Heaven and Earth, who are near with their benevolence and possess great ordinances, and the seven flowing rivers, [protect us].
May they release us from distress.
Bhaṭṭa [says]:
To Sūryā, to the gods, and to Mitra and Varuṇa.
To those who [perceive] the existent with clear insight,
to them I have paid homage—
those who [know] even without conscious attachment.
Before the clavicles are pierced,
may Maghavan, the possessor of many riches, join the joint together; he shall restore what has been torn asunder.
Bhaṭṭa:
May the one who restores [the light] for Purūvasu drive away our darkness; may it shine away from us that which is blue, tawny, and even red.
I cast that burning, speckled [sorcery] upon this pillar.
As many sorceries as there are on the undergarment—
As many snares as belong to King Varuṇa— those failures and misfortunes from the snares—
I fasten them all upon this post.
Whatever ends, however many fringes and woven cloths, and whatever threads there are— this garment that has been woven by the wives.
May those longing maidens, as they go from the world of the fathers to their husband, touch him gently.
They have released the consecration; Svāhā!
Released by Bṛhaspati, all the gods have sustained it.
Whatever luster has entered into the cows— with that we unite this [woman].
Released by Bṛhaspati.
The All-Gods have sustained it;
that brilliance which has entered into the cows—
with that we unite this [earth].
Released by Bṛhaspati,
the Viśvedevas sustained it; the milk entered into the cows.
That we now join this together;
released by Bṛhaspati,
all the gods have upheld it.
Whatever glory has entered the cows, with that we unite this [earth].
Released by Bṛhaspati.
The All-Gods have sustained it;
since Bhaga has entered into the cows, with that we unite this [earth].
That daughter of yours who, with disheveled hair, wept much— by her weeping she brought about evil.
May Agni and Savitṛ release you from that sin,
[committed] when those long-haired people [acted].
In your house they have danced together, causing evil with their weeping.
When the sisters, when the young women,
have danced together in your house,
making mischief with their weeping.
(…) that these two, the husband and wife,
have both removed evil at their wedding.
Causing harm with their roar...
that which [is done] to your offspring and your cattle.
Or whatever sin has been committed by evildoers within the houses, may Agni deliver you from that transgression.
And may Savitṛ release her.
This woman, scattering the grains, speaks thus: "I am a noble lady."
May my husband be long-lived;
may my ancestors prosper.
O Indra, drive these two together here.
Like a pair of cakravāka birds, may this couple,
possessing offspring and being well-established,
enjoy a long life.
Whatever [was done] on the throne (āsandyām), on the pillow (upadhāne), or on the seat (upavāsane) according to Bhaṭṭa, or whatever rite (kṛtyām) they performed at the wedding;
We place that [evil] into the bathwater:
whatever ill-deed and whatever stain there is in the wedding and in the bridal procession.
Upon the woolen blanket of Saṃbhala,
we wipe away our evil;
having deposited our impurity upon Saṃbhala.
We have cast away our misfortune upon the woolen blanket; we have become pure and worthy of sacrifice.
May they prolong our lifespans.
That body of mine which is most dear has become afraid of my garment;
before that [body], O Lord of the Forest, you stand.
Gird yourself; may we not suffer harm.
This artificial comb, which has a hundred teeth—may it remove the impurity from her hair.
Wipe away the disease from the head.
From limb after limb, you must lay down the consumption (*yakṣma*) from her. Away! Away!
Let this impurity not reach the earth, nor the gods, let it not reach the sky, nor the intermediate space; let it not reach the waters, O Agni.
May you not fall into the power of Yama nor into that of all the ancestors.
I bind you with the milk of the earth; I bind you with the milk of the plants.
I bind you together with offspring and wealth;
thus bound, win this prize.
I am he, you are she.
I am heaven, you are earth; I am mind, you are speech;
let us two come together here.
"Let us two procreate offspring!
Our wives desire sons, and the bounteous givers desire sons."
May we, being unharmed, abide with those fathers who behold the bride, for the sake of great victory in the contest for booty.
They have come to this bridal procession; they have come for this bride,
his wife.
May they grant a skin rich in offspring;
may she who formerly came here acting as a girth-belt,
having bestowed upon her both progeny and wealth in this world— having bestowed them— [grant it].
Let them carry her along the path of one who has not yet gone;
this Virāj, possessing good offspring, has emerged victorious.
Wake up, O you who are well-awakened, being awakened!
For long life lasting a hundred autumns,
go forth to the house with a well-disposed mind; may Savitṛ grant you a long life.
I loosen your tether, I loosen your reins, and I loosen your yokes and the fastenings;
may you be unharmed in this light.
Be auspicious toward the master of the house;
be pleasant to your parents-in-law, pleasant to your husband, and pleasant to the household.
Be pleasant for this entire people; be pleasant and nourishing for these [people].
(PS 18.14.7) (Anuvāka 2)
Arise, O steed who art within the waters; enter this kingdom, which is full of prosperity— thou,
the ruddy one who has brought forth this entire universe.
May he carry you, well-supported, to the kingdom.
May he fulfill [our desires]. O strength, come forth! That which is within the waters, ascend to the clans that have their origin in you.
Bringing Soma, the waters, the plants, and the cattle— both four-footed and two-footed— may you cause them to enter here.
O fierce Maruts, sons of Pṛśni!
With Indra as your ally, crush the enemies.
O bounteous Maruts, may your ruddy steed hear you— O you who are thrice-seven, you who delight in sweet joy.
The red one grew; the red one ascended to the lap of the mothers of all beings. Grasped by them, he found the six wide expanses.
Beholding a path, he has brought the kingdom here for you.
Rohita has brought the kingdom to you here; he has cast away the adversaries, and fearlessness has come to you.
For you, O Heaven and Earth, may the two wealthy worlds milk out your desire here with the *śakvarī* verses.
Rohita brought forth heaven and earth.
The Supreme Lord stretched out that thread; thereon rested the Unborn One-footed,
who by his might made firm heaven and earth.
Bhaṭṭa [comments]: Rohita made firm heaven and earth; by him the self was supported, by him the vault of heaven.
PS 18.15.6: Rohita made firm heaven and earth; by him the self was supported, by him the vault of heaven.
By him the atmosphere was measured out and the regions;
by him the gods found immortality.
The ruddy one reached toward the omniform.
Bringing together both the ascending and the descending growths,
having ascended to heaven with great majesty,
may your kingdom be anointed with milk and ghee.
Those roots of thine that grow forth, those that shoot up, and those with which thou fillest heaven and the mid-air—
increasing through the power of the sacred word (brahman) and their sap, [may they prosper].
Be watchful in the realm of Viśi, in the domain of Rohita.
O Bhaṭṭa Viśi, those clans of yours that arose from ascetic heat have come here following the calf, the Gāyatrī.
May they enter you with a benevolent mind;
those mothers, he, the red calf, approaches.
The red one has stood erect upon the vault of heaven.
Generating all forms, the youthful sage Agni shines forth with sharp light;
he has established his beloved things in the third realm.
The thousand-horned bull, Jātavedas,
invoked with clarified butter, whose back is laden with Soma, the hero of heroes— may he not abandon me; I, seeking protection, shall not forsake you.
Bestow upon me the nourishment of cattle and the nourishment of heroes!
Rohita is the progenitor and the mouth of the sacrifice;
for Rohita I offer with speech, with hearing, and with mind.
The gods go toward the Rohita with well-disposed minds; may he cause me to ascend with ascents for the sake of companionship.
Rohita has distributed the sacrifice to Viśvakarman.
Therefore, these splendors have come near me;
I shall proclaim your navel in the midst of the world's foundation.
The Bṛhatī and the Paṅkti have ascended unto you.
O All-Knowing One, the *kakubh* has mounted you with splendor;
the *uṣṇih* syllable and the *vaṣaṭ* call have mounted you;
the ruddy horse has mounted you along with the seed.
This one clothes himself in the womb of the earth; this one clothes himself in heaven; this one clothes himself in the intermediate space; this one clothes himself in the summit of the sun.
He has fully attained his own worlds.
O Lord of Speech, may the earth be pleasant for us; may our womb and our bed be pleasant and very gracious.
Bhaṭṭa [inserts *syonā* in brackets]:
"Right here let our vital breath be secure; may Agni, as the Supreme Lord (*parameṣṭhin*), endow you with splendor. (PS 18.16.7)
O Lord of Speech, the five seasons belonging to Viśvakarman who have come forth...
(see 7c)
(…) may the ruddy one bestow splendor upon us.
O Lord of Speech, grant us good cheer and a well-disposed mind; settle our cattle in the cow-pen and our offspring in their wombs.
Right here let our breath be with you as a friend; you, O Parameṣṭhin, I enclose with splendor.
May the god Savitṛ and Agni enclose you.
With splendor, O Mitra and Varuṇa, rise up against you;
driving away all hostilities, ascend—
make this kingdom full of prosperity.
When the spotted deer and the ruddy steed draw you on the chariot,
you go forth in splendor, releasing the waters.
Therefore, O Lord of Prayer (Brahmaṇaspati), cause this supreme ascent to rise for us;
Rohiṇī follows the will of Rohita.
The wise one, the well-winged, the lofty, the radiant—
through her may we win all forms of booty;
through her may we overcome the hostile armies.
This is the constant dwelling of Rohiṇī, the red one;
that is the path along which the speckled doe goes.
To her, the Gandharvas and the Kaśyapas lead her up.
The wise protect it with vigilance.
The immortal, tawny horses of the Sun, bearing banners, always draw his easy-moving chariot.
The ghee-drinking, radiant Rohita,
the god, has entered the speckled heaven;
he who is the red bull with sharp horns.
He has encompassed Agni and he has encompassed Sūrya—
he who supports both the earth and the sky;
from him the gods release their creations.
The Rohita has ascended to heaven from the great ocean;
the Rohita has climbed all the plants.
Measure out for us the milk-laden, ghee-rich cow of the gods, she who is never-failing;
let Indra drink the Soma, and let there be peace.
May Agni offer praise; drive away the adversaries.
Kindled with fuel, Agni is being enkindled, increased by ghee, and offered with ghee.
May Agni, the overcomer, the all-conqueror, slay those who are my rivals;
may he strike them down and burn them up.
The fire that attacks us—
the flesh-eating fire— with that fire we burn our rivals away.
O Agni, cast our rival beneath us; O Bṛhaspati, cause him who seeks to harm us to tremble;
O Indra and Agni, Mitra and Varuṇa!
Let them fall low, not contending with one another;
strike them down, O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, as they descend.
Then, O Agni, by means of your splendors, I seize my rivals.
O divine Sūrya, as you rise...
Make my rivals low;
strike them down with a stone so that they do not rise again.
May they go to the lowest darkness.
Vatsa, the bull of the Virāj, whose back is radiant, has ascended the firmament, the abode of inspired thoughts.
They worship the sun with ghee; may they cause the calf, who is Brahman, to grow by means of Brahman.
Ascend to heaven and ascend to earth.
Ascend the kingdom and ascend wealth;
ascend progeny and ascend immortality.
With the Rohita, touch thy body.
The gods who, as sustainers of the realm,
move around the sun—
with them Rohita is in harmony for you.
May he, being well-disposed, establish the kingdom for you.
The sacrifices, purified by sacred prayer, carry you upward;
the bay steeds carry you along the path.
Thou shinest across the ocean,
over the flood. Rohita, upon whom heaven and earth rest,
is the winner of wealth, the winner of cattle, the winner of all, the winner of battle.
I shall proclaim to you his thousand and seven treasures, his navel within the expanse of the world.
O Bhaṭṭa, they call you Yaśas; you go along the intermediate directions and the quarters,
the glory of cattle and of men.
Famous upon the lap of the earth and Aditi,
I am as beautiful as Savitṛ; being there, you know me here.
Being here, he sees those;
from here they see the radiant Sun, the wise one, in heaven.
A god worships a god;
he moves within the ocean;
they kindle the same fire.
The wise know him as the Supreme;
"below the other" and "beyond"—this is one [verse].
PS 16.67.7 is repeated: "She became one-footed, two-footed, four-footed, eight-footed, and nine-footed."
The fivefold sequence of the world consists of a thousand syllables;
from it the oceans flow forth.
Ascending to heaven, the immortal one has protected my speech.
The sacrifices, purified by prayer, carry you upward;
the bay steeds carry you as you drink the clarified butter.
O immortal one, know this of yours.
That which is your ascent to heaven,
that which is your dwelling-place in the highest firmament—
Sūrya [reaches] the sky, Sūrya [reaches] the earth.
The sun gazes across the waters;
the sun, the sole eye of all that exists,
has ascended to the great heaven.
The wide [spaces] were the enclosing sticks; the earth was fashioned as the sacrificial altar;
there he established these two fires.
Rohita [produced] both snow and heat;
having brought forth snow and heat, he fashioned the sacrificial posts and the mountains.
The two fires, the rain and the clarified butter, have sacrificed for the ruddy one who finds the light;
[the two fires] of the ruddy one who finds the light.
By Brahmā, Agni was concentrated;
from him came heat, from him came frost, and from him sacrifice was born.
Agni, kindled by the *brahman*,
increased by the *brahman*, and offered to with the *brahman*—
these two fires, inflamed by the *brahman*, perform the sacrifice.
Of Rohita, the finder of light:
one is established in the waters, the other is established in truth.
(…) That which the wind fans, that which Indra and Brahmaṇaspati [fan]—
The two fires, kindled by Brahmā, sacrifice for the ruddy one who finds the light.
Having fashioned the earth as the sacrificial altar,
having made heaven the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
and having made the sun that fire;
Rohita made the universe possessed of a self by means of rain as his oblation;
rain is the oblation, and the heat is Agni.
The earth was fashioned as the sacrificial altar;
there Agni [Bhatta] fashioned these mountains; there he raised them up with his songs.
Having fashioned the heights with his songs,
Rohita said to the earth:
"Let all this be born from you."
That which has been and that which is to be—
that was the first sacrifice; it was born as both the past and the future.
Therefore, indeed, in this sacrifice,
whatever shines here—
all this was brought forth by the seer Rohita.
His bright rays, the observers of men, rise up shining in the sky toward the sun.
Of the one of great vows, the bountiful;
the knower of the directions, shining with light by his radiance, the well-winged, swift one flying over the ocean.
Let us praise Sūrya, the guardian of the world, who illuminates all the quarters with his rays.
O Bhaṭṭa, all [these things]:
that you go swiftly from east to west by your own power,
and by your creative might you have fashioned the two days of diverse forms.
O Āditya, that is your greatness, that is your great glory,
that you alone are born encompassing the entire world.
[I praise] the wise one, the deliverer, the radiant one.
He whom the many green ones carry,
whom Atri brought up to heaven through praise—
may we behold you as you encompass the race.
Let them not deceive you as you encompass the racecourse;
swiftly pass over the difficult path by way that is easy to travel, O Sūrya, reaching both heaven and the goddess earth.
As you travel, measuring out day and night,
may there be well-being for your chariot, O Sūrya, by which you swiftly traverse both ends of the world.
Mount that which your green, most swift steeds draw; mount it easily, O horse-like one.
O Sūrya, [mount] the easy-to-ascend chariot, the radiant one.
Mount the pleasant,
well-yoked steed, whom your many bay horses— the most excellent carriers— draw: whether they be a hundred horses or seven.
The seven sun-steeds, golden-skinned, have been yoked to the great chariot for him to travel.
Śukra was released beyond the dust;
shaking off the darkness, the god ascended to heaven.
With his lofty banner, the gods have come.
He has dispelled the darkness and has resorted to the light; the divine, strong-winged, mighty one has looked out from the darkness— suparṇaḥ (according to Bhaṭṭa).
The son of Aditi, [pervading] all worlds;
rising, you extend your rays and behold all creatures.
O Bhaṭṭa, you behold both oceans; by your power you shine forth, encompassing all worlds as you blaze.
Moving by means of their creative power (*māyā*) from east to west, these two children go around the ocean of lotuses;
one of them clothes himself in all the worlds.
Others, the bay horses, carry you along with golden ornaments;
Atri sustained you in heaven so that Sūryā might be made into a wife.
Well-sustained, heating and having become light, he moves along, looking down upon both ends. He flows toward both limits.
Like a calf with its two mothers,
surely even those gods knew this Brahman before this time.
That which rests along the ocean, Sūrya desires to win; his path is stretched out, vast.
He who is both before and behind—
that [state] he attains through his impetuous powers;
therefore, he does not shrink away from it.
Therefore, they do not obtain a share of the nectar of the gods. *ud u tyam jātavedasam*... [etc.]
The banners bear the god Sūrya so that everyone may behold him. Those [lights] have departed like thieves.
The stars go forth with the nights for the sun that beholds all;
his banners have become visible.
His rays extend out among the people like shining fires;
he is the one who carries us across, visible to all.
O Sūrya, you are the maker of light; shining brightly, you illuminate the entire universe.
Facing the clans of the gods, facing the human races, you rise up. Bhaṭṭa Rocana. (Or: *rocanam*) PS 18.22.3.
Turning back toward all, so that the light may be seen— O Purifier, with that eye wherewith you look upon the active people.
O Varuṇa, you behold;
you traverse the wide sky and the broad mid-region,
measuring out the day with your nights.
Beholding all births, O Sun!
O divine Sūrya, seven bay horses carry you on your chariot.
To the one with flaming locks, the far-seeing;
he has yoked the seven bright mares, the daughters of the Sun’s chariot.
With those self-yoked [powers] he goes;
do you come toward me, sprinkling my songs with splendor.
Like milch-cows toward their calf,
those beautiful ones flow,
mingling with splendor and dear [to us].
Like a mother for her newborn child,
may she bring fame and prosperity to our hearts, as if with a thunderbolt, bringing us success.
May my life be dear as ghee.
Rohita, the ascetic, has ascended to heaven by means of his austerity;
he returns to his source and is born again.
He became the sovereign lord of the gods—
he who belongs to all people, who has faces on every side, hands on every side, and who reaches out to all directions.
Bhaṭṭa emends to *-thaḥ*:
He bears [the world] together with his two arms, together with his wings; the one god, generating heaven and earth. (PS 18.23.3)
The one-footed has stepped out further than the two-footed; the two-footed follows after the three-footed.
Indeed, the three-footed has stepped out further than the six-footed.
They sit together upon his body as a single foot; when, unwearied, setting out with his bay steeds,
you assume your radiant form in heaven.
Rising as the banner, overcoming the regions,
O Āditya, you shine across all slopes.
Truly, you are great, O Sūrya.
O Āditya, you are great;
great is your greatness, for you, O Āditya, are truly great.
You shine in heaven, you shine in the intermediate space; O Pataṅga, you shine upon the earth, you shine within the waters.
You have pervaded both oceans with your radiance.
A god, you are a god, a mighty buffalo, a finder of heaven.
From this side and from beyond the expanse, across the middle of the path, the swift, wise bird flies on its flight.
Viṣṇu, conscious and standing firm through his might, overcomes all that moves by means of his banner. Blazing and sharpening his body, he is keen.
Stepping onto the stage,
bestowing gifts upon the heights, luminous, winged, mighty, and bestowing vital strength, he has pervaded all the quarters, making them fit.
Variegated, wise, a buffalo, a fair-winged bird,
illuminating the two worlds and the mid-air,
the sun clothes himself in day and night.
Transcending all heroic powers, he goes forth.
The wondrous banner of the gods, the radiant face, the light-bringing Sūrya rises toward the quarters of space.
The Sun, the radiant one, has dispelled all darkness and overcome all difficulties with his splendors.
Bhaṭṭa: *viśvātārī*. PS 18.24.1:
The wondrous host of the gods has risen, the eye of Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni.
The Sun, the soul of all that moves and stands, has filled the heaven, the earth, and the mid-air;
he is the ruddy, fair-winged bird flying aloft.
May we behold you, Savitṛ, shining in the midst of heaven, whom they call the Sun,
that eternal light which Atri discovered.
Fleeing on the back of the sky, seeking protection in fear, I approach Suparṇa, the son of Aditi.
(Bhaṭṭa reads *yāma*; Śaunaka Saṃhitā reads *yāmi*).
O Sūrya, prolong our long life;
may we not suffer harm, but remain in your favor as you ordain days and nights.
Creating the earthly realm,
O divine Sūrya, you establish a new friendship with us at every moment.
The two wings of this golden swan Hari, as he flies toward heaven, extend across the sky for a thousand days.
Placing all the gods within his breast,
he goes beholding all beings;
Rohita became the world.
In the beginning, Prajāpati was Rohita;
Rohita is the mouth of sacrifices;
Rohita is called light.
Having become Rohita,
he brought forth what was to be; Rohita is the mouth of sacrifices.
Rohita brought the light;
Rohita became Time; Rohita heated the sky intensely.
The ruddy one, with his rays, shall traverse the earth and the ocean;
he traverses all the quarters.
Rohita is the sovereign lord of heaven;
may he guard the sky, the ocean, the earth, and all the worlds.
He bears [the world] and releases the ray like a garland;
he spreads out and raises up his rays, the great ray.
The Sun beholds that which is beyond the beyond; from the forenoon onwards, he surveys the entire universe with his lofty form.
Golden, green-hued, and rising as a banner,
the bright and tireless one ascends the lofty heights; the bright mortal, ascending, performs heroic deeds.
The divine, well-winged, mighty bull, swift as the wind,
who shines over all the worlds.
Bhaṭṭa:
[The bull] goes beyond one [side], clothing himself in another; the buffalo, fashioning himself according to the cosmic order, moves between day and night.
Desiring protection, we invoke Sūrya, who dwells in the mid-air, the finder of the path,
the great bull of the earth for the one who implores him.
The path-finder, whose eye is undeceived, has encompassed all;
beholding everything, the benevolent one worthy of sacrifice—may he grant us protection with his auspicious form. (PS 18.25.4)
His greatness extends around the earth and the ocean,
shining with light; he encompasses the sky and the intermediate space,
in harmony with day and night.
May he extend our unharmed life-force to us.
Agni has been awakened by the fuel of the people,
facing the Dawn as she approaches like a milch-cow.
Like young falcons rising up to the branch,
their rays shoot forth toward the firmament;
the youthful mother bears the child within her womb.
The cave bears it and does not give it to the father; O people, you do not perceive his face,
though you see him placed before you within the fire-wood.
O young woman, you carry this boy; the queen has given birth to him. For the embryo, vast as he is, has grown through many autumns.
I saw him who was born when his mother gave birth to him—
he whose three paths are of one accord while he exists as one,
for whom the hosts of gods bring tribute.
For him, that heaven, earth, and the intermediate space stand in secret, united with wealth;
nine [worlds] are protected by the divine host from heaven.
There are nine intermediate spaces and these nine worlds;
that in which all this is woven crosswise and lengthwise—
there is nothing else whatsoever beyond it.
There is nothing before him, nor after; there was nothing that existed, nor is there anything yet to be.
He has a thousand feet, a single head, and a dual nature.
He indeed encompasses all this that has come to be.
Those birds who flew away one by one— desiring to harm the Soma, they fell down, held fast by the serpent.
Who knows their father and mother? Who knows their origin, and who knows their self? By whom is the wind impelled when it blows forth?
Those who bestowed the five converging directions, those gods who disregarded the oblation—
what were they, the leaders of the waters?
One of them clothes this earth; one has encompassed the intermediate space;
he who is the disposer bestows the sky upon them.
One among them protects all the directions.
(PS 18.26.4, Anuvāka 4)
In the beginning, it was indeed the Vrātya who existed here;
being himself in a state of wandering, he set Prajāpati in motion.
Bhaṭṭa says: That Prajāpati beheld Suparṇa within himself;
that became one, and that became a mark.
That became the Great; that became the Eldest; that became austerity; that became truth; that became Brahman; by that, he was procreated.
He grew; he became great; he became Mahādeva; he became Īśāna;
he attained the lordship over the gods.
He became the one who shares a single vow with the gods. He took on the form of a cow; that became the bow of Indra.
Its belly is blue, its back is red.
"By the black [color] he covers his hostile rival;
by the red [color] he pierces the one who hates him," so say the exponents of sacred knowledge.
He moved forth toward the eastern direction.
The *bṛhat*, the *rathantara*, the Viśve Devas, and the Ādityas followed after him.
He who knows this becomes the beloved abode of the *bṛhat*, the *rathantara*, the Viśve Devas, and the Ādityas.
He who reviles a Vrātya knowing this cuts himself off from the Bṛhat and the Rathantara, from the Viśvedevas and the Ādityas.
In his eastern direction—
Faith is the harlot, Mitra the bard; knowledge is the garment, day the turban, night the hair, the two green ones the ear-rings, and the glittering gem the amulet.
Past and future are the two attendants, mind is the crossroads, and Mātariśvan the wind.
Pavamāna and Vipathavāha are the two horses, Vāta is the charioteer, and Reṣman is the whip;
Fame and Glory are the two precursors. Fame goes before him and Glory goes before him—he who knows this.
He moved out toward the southern direction;
after him, the Yajñāyajñīya and the Vāmadevya [sāmans], as well as the sacrifice and the cattle, moved out.
He [became] the essence of the Yajñāyajñīya, the Vāmadevya, the sacrifice, and the cattle.
For the Yajñāyajñiya, for the Vāmadevya, for the sacrifice, and for cattle...
In its southern direction:
saline soil, a harlot, a mantra, and a Māgadha... (see 2bc)
Day and night were his attendants.
He moved forth toward the western direction;
after him Vairūpa, Vairāja, and King Varuṇa moved forth.
And of Vairūpa, and of Vairāja, and of King Varuṇa, and of the Waters... / And for Vairūpa, and for Vairāja, and for King Varuṇa, and for the Waters...
// In his western direction.
Irā, Puṃścalī, Hasa, and Māgadha are the attendants;
Paurṇamāsī and Amāvāsyā are the two side-attendants.
He set out toward the northern direction.
Soma the King and the seven seers followed after that Śyaita and Naudhasa.
He who knows thus comes to possess the beloved abode of the Śyaita, the Naudhasa, Soma the King, and the seven seers.
He who reviles a Vrātya knowing this cuts himself off from the Śyaita, the Naudhasa, King Soma, and the Seven Seers.
In his northern direction—
Lightning is the harlot; thunder is the bard; consciousness is the garment; day is the turban; night is the hair; the two green [halves] are the side-locks; the flame is the jewel;
both what is heard and what is renowned are the attendants; and the mind is the crossroads.
Mātariśvan and Pavamāna are the two who carry him along the paths;
Vāta is the charioteer and Reṣman is the whip. Fame and glory are the two precursors;
fame goes before him and glory goes before him—he who knows thus.
He stood upright for a year.
The gods said to him, "Vrātya, why do you stand? He replied, "Let them bring me a throne."
Therefore, they brought together a throne for him;
of that throne, spring and summer were the two front feet, and the rainy season and autumn were the two rear feet.
The Bṛhat and the Rathantara were its two longitudinal beams,
and the Yajñāyajñiya and the Vāmadevya were its two cross-beams;
the Ṛg-verses were the longitudinal threads and the Yajus-formulas were the transverse threads.
The Vedas were his spread-out seat, the Brahman was his cushion, and the Sāmans were his reclining support; he sat down,
and his intentions became his attendants.
The divine folk, the attendants, the Apsarases as wives, and all beings are his followers.
All beings go toward him and he becomes dear to all beings, who knows thus. (PS 18.29.1)
For him, they made the two months of spring the guardians of the eastern direction, and the Bṛhat and Rathantara [sāmans] the executors;
thus the two months of spring guard him from the eastern direction.
For him who knows thus and performs the Bṛhat and Rathantara [sāmans],
they made the two summer months the guardians of the southern quarter.
The Yajñāyajñīya and the Vāmadevya are the two performers;
during the two summer months, the Yajñāyajñīya and the Vāmadevya protect him from the southern direction.
For him, they made the two months of the rainy season the guardians from the western quarter, and Vairūpa and Vairāja the performers of the ritual;
these two months of the rainy season guard him from the western quarter.
And Vairūpa and Vairāja...
from that northern direction,
they made Śyeta and Naudhasa the two protectors for the two months of autumn, and [Vairūpa and Vairāja] the two reciters of the *anuṣṭubh*.
The autumn months protect him from the northern direction with the Śyaita and the Naidhasa [Sāmans].
For him, from the fixed direction...
They made the two winter months the guardians, and the earth and Agni the executors;
the two winter months guard him from the fixed quarter (the north),
as do the earth and Agni.

Therefore, they made the two months of the dewy season the guardians of the upward direction, and the sky and the sun its supporters. These two months of the dewy season guard him from the upward direction.
Heaven and the sun stand by him who knows thus.
For him, they made Bhava the archer the one who stands behind from the intermediate region of the east.
May Bhava, the archer, stand by him from the intermediate region of the east—
[he who knows thus stands firm]—
for him [from the intermediate region of the south].
They made Śarva the archer [the performer]. Śarva the archer [attacked him] from the intermediate region of the south...
For him, they made Rudra the archer [the supervisor] from the western intermediate region;
Rudra, the archer, [protected] him from the western intermediate region.
(…) From that intermediate region of the north,
they made Paśupati the archer (the performer).
Paśupati [gave] this archer from the intermediate region of the north...
from that fixed intermediate region.
They made the fierce god, the archer, the performer [of the rite].
The fierce god, the archer, [placed him] from the fixed intermediate region...
From that intermediate direction above,
they made Mahādeva the archer (the performer); Mahādeva, the archer, [established him] from that intermediate direction above.
The performer (…) [see 1d PS_18,31.6].
For him, from all the intermediate regions,
they made Īśāna the archer the performer.
Īśāna, the archer, stands behind him from all intermediate directions for one who knows thus;
he moved out toward the fixed direction.
The earth, the fire, the herbs, the trees, the shrubs, and the forest plants followed after him;
for he was indeed [the essence] of the earth, the fire, the herbs, and the trees.
He who knows thus becomes the beloved abode of the creepers, the trees, the plants, and the forest-dwellers;
he indeed cuts himself off from the earth, from Agni, from the herbs,
from the trees, from the creepers, and from the forest-dwellers.
He who reviles a Vrātya who knows thus departed toward the upward direction; after him,
both *ṛta* and *satya*, as well as the sun and the moon, departed.
And indeed, he [is] of *ṛta* and of truth, of the sun and of the moon;
and indeed, he [is] for *ṛta* and for truth, for the sun and for the moon.
He moved forth along the great quarter.
The *ṛcs*, the *sāmans*, the *yajus* formulas, and the *brahman* moved toward him.
He is indeed the beloved abode of the *ṛcs*, the *sāmans*, the *yajus* formulas, and the *brahman*;
he is [the beloved abode] of the *ṛcs*, the *sāmans*, the *yajus* formulas, and the *brahman*.
He moved toward the northern direction;
after him, the *itihāsa*, the *purāṇa*, the *gāthās*, and the *nārāśaṃsīs* followed.
Indeed, he became the beloved [abode] of the *itihāsa*, the *purāṇa*, the *gāthās*, and the *nārāśaṃsīs*.
And for the sake of history (*itihāsa*), for the sake of ancient lore (*purāṇa*), for the sake of songs (*gāthā*), and for the sake of hymns in praise of men (*nārāśaṃsī*)...
He moved forth toward the supreme quarter;
after him the seasons and the seasonal phenomena, the worlds and the worldly phenomena, moved forth.
He is indeed the beloved abode of the seasons, of the seasonal phenomena, of the worlds, and of worldly things.
He is deprived of the seasons, of the seasonal phenomena, of the worlds, and of worldly things—he who [acts otherwise].
He moved forth along the direction that is not downward; from there, he thought that he would not return.
Virāj followed after him, as did all the gods and all the deities.
Indeed, he is dear to Virāj, to all the gods, and to all the deities.
And indeed, he cuts himself off from Virāj, from all the gods, and from all the deities [who acts thus].
He set out toward an unspecified direction, thinking that he would not return from there.
After him, the *dakṣiṇāgni*, the *gārhapatya*, the *āhavanīya*, the sacrifice, and the sacrificer followed.
Indeed, he [the sacrificer] was the beloved abode of the *dakṣiṇāgni*, the *gārhapatya*, the *āhavanīya*, the sacrifice, and the sacrificer.
He indeed cut himself off from the Dakṣiṇāgni, the Gārhapatya, the Āhavanīya, the sacrifice, and the sacrificer.
He moved away through the intermediate directions;
Diti, Caditi, Iḍā, and Indrāṇī followed him as he moved away.
He indeed [is dear] to Diti and Aditi, to Iḍā and Indrāṇī;
he indeed [cuts off] for Diti and Aditi, for Iḍā and Indrāṇī.
He moved forth through the quarters.
Prajāpati, Parameṣṭhin, the father, and the grandfather followed after him.
He who knows thus becomes the beloved abode of Prajāpati, Parameṣṭhin, the father, and the grandfather.
He who reviles a Vrātya who knows this cuts himself off from Prajāpati, from Parameṣṭhin, from his father, and from his grandfather. (PS 18.32.9,
Anuvāka 5)
That greatness, having become a mountain with a peak, reached the end of the earth and became the ocean.
Prajāpati and Parameṣṭhin, as well as water, faith, and rain, followed it by turning around it.
Sacrifice, the worlds, food, and the eating of food, having become these, surrounded it on all sides.
The waters go to him, the rain goes to him, faith goes to him,
consecration goes to him, the sacrifice goes to him, the world goes to him, food goes to him, and the eating of food goes to him— whoever knows this thus.
He delighted in that; from him, as he was delighting, the Rājanya was born.
He rose up toward the Viśas, their kinsmen, food, and the eating of food.
He who knows thus becomes the beloved abode of the Viśas, of their kinsmen, of food, and of the eating of food.
He who reviles a Vrātya knowing this cuts himself off from the Vedas, from his kinsmen, and from food and the eating of food. PS_18,34.1 (34)
He moved out among the people;
after him the assembly, the council, the army, and the heroes moved out.
Indeed, he is the beloved of the assembly, the council, the army, and the heroes.
He who knows thus becomes a *dhāman*.
He who reviles a *vrātya* who knows thus cuts himself off from the assembly (*sabhā*), from the council (*samiti*), from the army (*senā*), and from the liquor (*surā*).
Bhaṭṭa [notes]: *vidvāsaṃ* is a misprint for *vidvāṃsam*. PS 18,35.1 (35):
If a learned Vrātya should come as a guest to the house of a king, he should honor him as superior to himself; thus he does not harm his kingdom.
In that way it does not harm the Kṣatriya, nor does it harm the Brahmin.
Thereupon, the Brahman and the Kṣatra both stood up; they said, "Into whom shall we enter?"
Prajāpati said to them: "Bṛhaspati has entered the Brahman; Indra has entered the Kṣatra.
Thereupon, indeed, Bṛhaspati entered the Brahman and Indra entered the Kṣatra.
This earth is indeed Bṛhaspati, and yonder sky is Indra.
This fire here is indeed the *brahman*, and yonder sun is the *kṣatra*.
The *kṣatra* goes to him who knows the sun as the *kṣatra*, heaven as Indra, and Indra [himself]; he becomes one who possesses the power of Indra.
The *brahman* goes to him who knows this; he becomes one who possesses the splendor of the *brahman*.

He who knows Agni, Brahmā, Bṛhaspati, and the Earth—[to him] a Vrātya guest who possesses such knowledge should, when the fires have been drawn out but the Agnihotra has not yet been offered, rise up toward him in person and say: [18.36.1] (36) ... [he should say].
"Vrātya, where have you stayed?"—"In water," says the Vrātya. "Vrātya, let them satisfy [you]," [says the priest].
When he says, "Vrātya, where have you stayed?", by that he secures for himself the paths traveled by the gods.
When he says, "Vrātya, water," by that he secures for himself the waters.
When he says, "O Vrātyas, may you satisfy [me]," he thereby unites his breath with the rainy season.
Before the offering of the Agnihotra, he should perform it in a whisper.
"O Vrātya, may it be as is dear to you;
O Vrātya, may it be as is your desire;
O Vrātya, may it be according to your will."
When he says, "O Vrātya, as is dear to you, so let it be," he thereby secures what is dear; he becomes dear to what is dear, and what is dear comes to him who knows thus.

As it is said: "O Vrātya, let it be for you according to your desire. By this, he obtains exactly what he desires; his desire becomes fulfilled at every turn, and fulfillment comes to him who knows thus.
When he says, "O Vrātya, as is your will, so let it be," by that he obtains will itself; he who knows this becomes the master of his will, and will comes to him. PS_18,37.5 (37)

If, while the *agnihotra* has been established, a *vrātya* guest who knows this should come to one's house, he should rise toward him in person and say, "O *vrātya*, give me leave; I shall sacrifice. If he gives leave, he should sacrifice; if he does not give leave, he should not sacrifice.
Bhaṭṭa [says]:
"He who, not being authorized by a Vrātya who knows thus, offers [the oblation],
does not recognize the path leading to the gods, nor the path leading to the fathers."
He who offers an oblation without being permitted by a Vrātya who knows this cuts himself off from the gods; his offering becomes as if unoffered.
He who, having been permitted by such a Vrātya, offers the sacrifice, discerns the path leading to the gods and the path leading to the fathers.
For him in whose house a Vrātya, knowing this, dwells for one night as a guest, his abode remains in this world and his offerings become effective.
He wins for himself those worlds on earth that are meritorious.
If a learned Vrātya stays as a guest in one's house on the second night,
he thereby wins for himself those meritorious worlds that are in the intermediate space.
When a learned Vrātya stays as a guest in his house for the third night,
he thereby wins for himself those meritorious worlds that are in heaven.
If a learned Vrātya stays as a guest in one's house on the fourth night,
by means of him he wins all the worlds of merit.
If a learned Vrātya stays as a guest in one's house on the fifth night,
by him he wins the worlds from afar.
If a learned Vrātya stays as a guest in one's house for an unlimited number of nights,
by him he wins unlimited worlds.
If a non-Vrātya who calls himself a Vrātya should come to one's house as a guest, bearing his name...
One should draw him [the water] and not fail to draw it;
Bhaṭṭa says "one should draw.
Saying, "I ask for water for this deity," one should ask that person for the water.
"I envelop this deity," with these words he should envelop it;
for him who knows thus, what is offered and sacrificed becomes offered and sacrificed in that very deity.
When [the fire] moved forth toward the eastern direction...
Having become Indra, they moved forth, making the mind the eater of food;
he who knows this eats food by means of the mind as the eater of food.
As for that which they moved forth toward the southern direction...

Becoming the host of Maruts, they moved forth, having made wrath the eater of food; he who knows this eats food by means of wrath as the eater of food. When [he] moved forth along the western direction...
Having become Varuṇa, he moved along, making the waters the eaters of food; he who knows this eats food with the waters that are eaters of food. When he moved along toward the northern direction...
King Soma, having become the seven seers, moved along after [the oblation], making the oblation his food;
he eats food through the oblation and food, he who knows thus.
When he moved along toward the fixed quarter...
Having become Viṣṇu, he moved forth, making Virāj the eater of food;
he who knows thus eats food through Virāj, the eater of food.
That which moved forth along the upward direction...
Having become Bṛhaspati, he moved along after [the sacrifice], having made the *vaṣaṭ*-call the eater of food.
By means of the *vaṣaṭ*-call as the eater of food, he eats food—he who knows thus.
When he moved along after the cattle...
Having become Rudra, he moved along after [the creatures], making the plants his food;
he who knows this eats food with the plants that provide food.
That which moved along after the gods—
Having become the Ruler, he moved along, making strength his food;
by means of that strength-food, he eats food—he who knows thus.
That which moved along after human beings...
Having become fire, he moved forth, making the *svāhākāra* the eater of food. By means of the *svāhākāra*, the eater of food, [he eats food]—he who knows thus. That which moved after the ancestors...

Having become Yama and having made himself a consumer of food with the utterance *svadhā*, he moved along; by means of that utterance *svadhā* and that consumption of food, he who knows thus eats food.
That which the creatures followed as he moved along...
Having become Prajāpati, he moved along after making breath the eater of food;
by means of breath as the eater of food, he eats food—he who knows thus.
That which he moved along through the intermediate directions...
Having become wind, he moved along after it, making the wind his consumer of food; by means of that wind as a consumer of food, he eats food—so it is for one who knows thus.
As for that which moved along after the quarters...
Having become the Supreme Lord (*parameṣṭhin*), Brahmā moved forth after making himself the eater of food;
he who knows thus eats food by means of the Brahman that is the eater of food.
His [vital breaths] are seven out-breaths (*prāṇa*), seven in-breaths (*apāna*), and seven diffused breaths (*vyāna*).
That first vital breath of his, named Ūrdhva, is this Agni;
that second vital breath of his, named Proḍha, is yonder Āditya;
that third vital breath of his, named Abhyūḍha, is yonder Candramas.
His fourth vital breath, named Vibhu, is this Pavamāna;
his fifth vital breath, named Aparimita, is these domestic animals;
his sixth vital breath, named Priya, is these creatures.
That which is his seventh breath, named *yoni*, is these waters;
that which is his first *apāna* is the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*).
Its second downward breath is the Aṣṭakā;
its third downward breath is the New Moon (Amāvāsyā);
its fourth downward breath is Faith (Śraddhā).
That which is his fifth downward breath is the consecration;
that which is his sixth downward breath is the sacrifice; that which is his seventh downward breath is...
That is the *vaṣaṭ*-call;
it is his first diffused breath (*vyāna*);
it is this earth.
That which is its second diffused breath (vyāna) is the intermediate space;
that which is its third diffused breath is the sky.
That which is its fourth diffused breath (vyāna) are the lunar mansions (nakṣatra);
that which is its fifth diffused breath are the seasons (ṛtu).
That which is its sixth vyāna is the seasons;
that which is its seventh vyāna is the year.
"The gods go around the common goal"—
this refers to how the seasons indeed go around the year;
"when they enter into the Āditya."
They enter into both the full moon and the new moon;
that single form of theirs is immortality, namely the oblation itself. "Increasing through austerity in every form"—this refers to day and night.
That which is his right ear is this Agni; that which is the left is this Pavamāna.
That which is his right eye is yonder Āditya; that which is the left is yonder Candramas.
Diti and Aditi are the two skull-bones of the head; the year is the head; day and night are the two nostrils.
Averse to the night, facing toward the day—homage to the Vrātya!

The bull of the waters has been released; the celestial fires have been released.

Shattering, crushing, grinding, utterly destroying, the fire that blinds the eyes, the fire that steals the mind, the fire that digs up, the fire that burns away, the fire that corrupts the self, the fire that corrupts the body.
I release this [water] upon them; do not pour it down upon me. With them I release it upon him who hates us and whom we hate.
You are the foremost of the waters; I release you into the ocean.
Those fires which are in the waters, them I release: Mroka, Khani, Tanūdūṣi.
That fire of yours, O Waters, which has entered within, that which is terrible in you—that is this very one.
With the power of Indra, he should consecrate [the sacrificer]; the Waters are stainless; let them drive away defilement from us.
O Waters, sprinkle away my sin;
carry off my evil dream.
Behold me with a gracious eye, O Waters; touch my body and my voice with auspiciousness.
We invoke the auspicious fires that dwell in the waters; O goddesses, bestow upon me sovereignty and splendor!
O you who are free from ill-will, full of vigor, full of sweetness is my speech; you are full of sweetness.
May I utter speech that is full of sweetness; may I not be deprived of speech.
Unassailable is my protector; unassailable is my protection.
May my ears hear well; may my ears hear what is auspicious. May I hear an auspicious report. May both Upaśruti and Anuśruti not desert me.
The eye of Suparṇa, the eternal light;
you are the sacrificial strew of the seers. Homage to the divine sacrificial strew!
May I be the head of riches, may I be the head of my equals.
May Ruja and Māvena not desert me;
may Urva and Camasa not desert me;
may Vimoka and Ārdrapavi not desert me.
May Ārdradānu and Mātariśvan not abandon me;
may Mūrdhan and Vidharma not abandon me;
may Dhartṛ and Dharuṇa not abandon me.
May Mṛdha and Vaimṛdha not abandon me!
Bṛhaspati is my self, named Nṛmaṇas;
do not abandon me, who am undecaying of heart! May my heart be free from distress.
Vast is my pasture; I am an ocean by my supporting power.
May I be the center of riches, may I be the center of my peers.
You are a good seat, a bringer of prosperity, immortal among mortals.
Let not the out-breath (*prāṇa*) abandon me and depart; let not the in-breath (*apāna*) abandon me and depart.
May Sūrya protect me from the day, Agni from the earth, Vāyu from the intermediate space, Yama from human beings, and Sarasvatī from earthly creatures.
May out-breath and in-breath not forsake me; may I not perish among the people.
May I attain well-being this day from both the dawn and the evening; may I, with my whole troop, reach all the waters.
You are well-being; you are the ray; you are the bestower of life; bestow life upon me.
Thou art auspicious; thou art a ray;
thou art the bestower of splendor; bestow splendor upon me.
Thou art auspicious; thou art a ray; thou art the bestower of brilliance; bestow brilliance upon me.
May the Sun, the bestower of luster, grant me luster; you are power, bestow power upon me;
you are luster, bestow luster upon me.
You are the Śakvarī verses; may cattle attend upon me. O Mitra and Varuṇa, grant me out-breath and in-breath;
may Agni bestow skill upon me.

May I, as a friend, turn my friend toward me through our bond of friendship,
having traveled even across the vast ocean;
may the wise one take up the grandson of his father.
Gazing further upon the earth,
your friend does not desire this friendship, that she who shares the same mark should become one of different form.
The heroic sons of the Asura, the upholders of heaven, looked far and wide around.
Truly, those immortals desire this from you.
Of this one mortal who has abandoned his body,
may your mind be fixed upon our mind;
as a husband, you shall enter the body of your wife.
What we have never done before, how could we now speak untruth while professing the truth?
The Gandharva is in the waters, and there is the watery maiden.
That is our kinship, our highest birth.
Even in the womb, the god Tvaṣṭṛ, the progenitor, the impeller, who possesses all forms, made us a husband and wife.
No one violates his sacred laws; both Earth and Heaven know them.
Who today yokes to the pole the oxen of Order?
The vigorous ones, the formidable, the difficult to overcome, with arrows in their mouths,
who take away one's wealth yet bring joy— only he who fulfills their service shall live.
Who knows of this first day? Who has seen it? Who here can declare it? Great is the ordinance of Mitra and Varuṇa.
When will you speak, O driver, to lead the men across? Desire for Yama has come upon me,
his sister, so that we may lie together in the same womb.
Like a wife yielding her body to her husband, I would even draw them apart like two chariot wheels.
These do not stand still, nor do they close their eyes.
Those who move here as the spies of the gods—
O you who strike me down, go away with another, and further drive him away like the wheels of a chariot.
May he honor him with nights and days;
may he repeatedly extend the eye of the sun;
[he is] the pair of heaven and earth, the kinsmen.
May Yami separate from Yama’s unbrotherly union. Indeed,
may those later generations come, when kinsmen shall commit acts unbecoming to kin.
Press your arm close to the bull;
O fortunate one, seek another man as your husband.
What would a brother be, if he leaves one without a protector?
How much more so when my sister Nirṛti should approach? Driven by desire, I murmur this much;
O Bhaṭṭa, unite my body fully with your body.
Indeed, I would never unite my body with your body;
they call it an evil thing for one to approach his own sister.
Arrange your pleasures with another than me.
"Your brother does not desire this, O fortunate one. "I am not your protector here, O Yamī; surely I shall not unite with your body."
This is not a union for my mind or heart,
that I, as a brother, should lie upon the bed of my sister. Alas, alas, you are such a one, O Yama!
We have not found your mind or your heart;
surely another woman embraces you, as a creeper clings to a tree or a girth-rope encircles a yoked horse.
Either you shall desire his mind, or he shall desire yours; then establish with him a most auspicious agreement. The seers have discerned the three meters.
The many-formed, beautiful to behold, all-seeing— the winds, the waters, and the plants—
all these are placed within a single world.
The bull has milked for the bull the milks of heaven by his own milking; the mighty one, the undeceivable son of Aditi,
knows all through his wisdom, even as Varuṇa does.
He, the worthy of sacrifice, sacrifices during the sacrificial seasons.
May the Gandharva women and the water-nymphs protect our mind on every side within the roar of the river.
May Aditi protect us in the midst of what is desired;
may our eldest brother speak forth first. He indeed is auspicious, possessing food and glory.
The light-bringing Dawn has shone for Manu, when they, according to the will of those who desire,
brought forth Agni as the Hotṛ priest for the sacrificial assembly.
Then the falcon, released at the sacrifice, brought down that far-reaching, all-seeing drop;
when the Aryan tribes chose the wonder-worker.
Then the sage brought forth Agni as the Hotṛ-priest.
O Agni, you are ever delightful to one who thrives like a pasture, performing well the rites for man through his oblations.
O Bhaṭṭa Manuṣa, or you who are like a Brahmin, being tranquil and worthy of praise, come with many [attendants] to the laudable strength of the one who offers the hymn.

Rouse up your two parents like a lover; the beloved one desires to worship them and sends forth his longing from his heart. As the bearer of the oblation, he speaks; the sacrificer performs his work with skill.
The Asura thunders; he trembles before your hymns, O Agni. That mortal who attains your favor, O Son of Strength, he becomes renowned far and wide.
Bestowing nourishment, borne by his horses, he,
the radiant and mighty one, adorns the days.
Hear us, O Agni, in our common dwelling place.
Yoke the swift chariot of immortality;
O son of Veda, bring both heaven and earth to us.
May no one among the gods be excluded; may you be present here.
O Agni, worthy of worship, when this divine assembly occurs among the gods, it is a sacrifice offered by the sacrificer.
And when you, O self-dependent one, distribute treasures, grant us here our share of wealth.
Agni has looked upon the forefront of the dawns.
Day after day, Jātavedas is the first;
he has extended himself toward the many rays of the sun and toward heaven and earth.
Agni, the first Jātavedas, has looked along the forefront of the dawns, along the days,
and along the many rays of the sun.
He has extended across heaven and earth;
heaven and earth, as the first, by the cosmic order (*ṛta*) become responsive in their outpouring.
The god, making mortals strive toward their task,
sits down as the Hotṛ-priest facing his own vital breaths;
the god, encompassing the gods by means of the cosmic order (ṛta).
May he, the first one who perceives, carry our oblation—
the smoke-bannered, bright with fuel, the delightful, eternal Hotṛ-priest who is most skilled in sacrifice through his voice.
I worship you two for my prosperity, O waters that drip with ghee;
O Heaven and Earth, hear my prayer, O two worlds,
when the gods came to the world of the living.
May the two parents here satisfy us with honey;
the immortal nectar of the god is that which belongs to the cow.
Born from this, they have sustained the two wide worlds.
May all the gods approve that sacrificial formula of yours, whereby the dappled cow yields the heavenly ghee and water. What has the King seized from us? What of his [is it]?
We have indeed performed a difficult vow; who knows [the truth]?
For even Mitra, though he has provoked the gods to anger, there is a song of praise like that of those who go to battle, and there is also the prize.
Therein is the name of the immortal,
accompanied by its characteristic sign, whereby she who is of diverse forms becomes well-disposed; he who is mindful of Yama becomes well-disposed.
O lofty Agni, protect him without negligence—
he in whom the gods rejoice at the assembly,
and who they sustain in the seat of Vivasvat.
They placed light in the sun and nights in the moon; that radiance moves unceasingly around them,
in which the gods move together in their thought.
We do not know these [deeds] of his that are behind our backs; may Mitra, Aditi, and the god Savitṛ declare us sinless to Varuṇa in this matter.
O friends, let us instruct a sacred prayer for Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt;
let us praise him who is most heroic and bold.
For you are renowned by your might as the slayer of Vṛtra through the slaying of Vṛtra;
O hero, with your bounties you surpass the liberal patrons.
Like a steed, you traverse the earth;
let the great winds blow here upon the ground. May Mitra and Varuṇa, being anointed, protect us here.
Like fire in the forest, he has spread forth his flame.
Praise the famous one, the king of men who sits upon the chariot-seat— the terrible, fierce, and striking one.
Be gracious to the singer, O Rudra, when you are praised; let your other missile strike down someone besides us.
Those seeking the gods invoke Sarasvatī.
When the sacrifice is being performed, they invoke Sarasvatī;
the doers of good deeds invoke Sarasvatī— may Sarasvatī grant what is desirable to the donor.
Bhaṭṭa [says]: "The Sarasvatī whom the ancestors invoke,
as they approach the sacrifice from the south."
Having approached, rejoice upon this sacred grass; bestow upon us food free from disease. O Sarasvatī, you who have traveled on the same chariot—
O Goddess, rejoicing with the *ukthas* and the *svadhās* along with the ancestors,
bestow here upon the sacrificer a portion of the *iḍā* worth a thousandfold, an abundance of wealth.
May the lower, the higher, and the middle Soma-loving Fathers arise—
those who have gone to the spirit-world, who are harmless and knowers of the Eternal Law (Ṛta).
May those fathers protect us in our invocations.
I have found the benevolent fathers, and the descendant, and the wide stride of Viṣṇu.
Those who sit upon the sacrificial grass and partake of the pressed food with the *svadhā* call— may they be the most eager to come here.
"This for the fathers," [is] one [verse].
Mātali with the Kavis, Yama with the Aṅgirases, Bṛhaspati growing strong with the Ṛks.
Those whom the gods have strengthened, and those gods who rejoice in the *svāhā*-call and the *svadhā*-offering—
this [Soma] is indeed sweet and this is honeyed.
Truly, this [Soma] is intense in flavor,
and so too is he; indeed, no one at all can withstand Indra when he has drunk of it in battles.
Having departed along the great downward slopes,
he has spied out the path for many;
he has gone to Vivasvat’s son, the gathering place of men.
Worship King Yama with an oblation.
Yama was the first to find our path; this pasture-land is not to be taken away from us.
Where our ancient fathers have passed away, those who were born following their own paths— hither come, O fathers seated upon the sacrificial grass, with your help!
We have prepared these oblations for you; please accept them.
Come to us with most auspicious protection, and then bestow upon us well-being, health, and freedom from harm.
Sitting down to the south, with knees bent,
do you all, O Pitṛs, favor this sacrifice; do not harm us by anything whatsoever.
Whatever offense we may commit as human beings— Tvaṣṭṛ prepares the bridal procession for his daughter,
and to this all the world comes together.
Yama’s mother, being carried away,
the great wife of Vivasvat, vanished. Go forth, go forth by the ancient paths!
Where your former fathers have departed, where both kings rejoice in the *svadhā* offering—
there you shall see Yama and the god Varuṇa.
Depart, go away, and creep far from here; for the fathers have prepared this world for us,
distinguished by days, waters, and nights— by days, indeed.
Yama grants him a dwelling place.
Desiring you, we set you down; desiring you, we kindle you.
Desiring them, bring the desiring ancestors here to eat the oblation;
we establish you, O radiant one.
May we kindle the radiant ones.
O radiant one, bring the radiant ancestors here to eat the oblation.
Section 10.
The Aṅgirases are our fathers, the Navagvas, the Atharvans, and the Bhṛgus, who are worthy of the Soma;
may we abide in the good will of those who are worthy of sacrifice.
O auspicious one, may we be in a state of well-being!
O Yama, come here with the Angirases worthy of sacrifice; rejoice here with the Vairūpas!
I invoke Vivasvat, who is your father,
that he may sit down upon the sacrificial grass at this sacrifice.
Bhaṭṭa [recites]:
"O Yama, sit down upon this sacrificial grass, in harmony with the Aṅgiras ancestors. (PS 18,63.2)
The mantras recited by the seers bring you here;
O King, rejoice in this oblation.
Press the Soma for Yama.
Offer the oblation to Yama;
let the sacrifice go to Yama, with Agni as its well-prepared messenger.
Offer the oblation rich in ghee to Yama and step forward;
may he lead us among the living. (Bhaṭṭa Yama)
O long-lived one, as you proceed,
offer to King Yama the most honey-sweet oblation.
Homage to these seers, the ancestors, the ancient makers of the path!
It flies forth with the *trikadruka* vessels.
The six wide ones are but one great [Vāk];
the Triṣṭubh, Gāyatrī, and all the meters— these are all established in Yama.
Do not burn him up, O Agni; do not consume him; do not scorch his skin, his eye, or his body.
When you have made him cooked, O Jātavedas—
"Then send him forth to the ancestors!
O Jātavedas, when you have made him cooked,
then deliver him over to the ancestors."
When he goes to the world of the departed, then he becomes subject to the will of the gods;
let his eye go to the sun.
O self, go to the wind, to heaven, and to earth according to the cosmic order;
or go to the waters, if it is beneficial for you there.
Establish yourself within the plants with your bodies.
The goat is the portion of your heat; heat that, let your flame heat that, let your radiance heat that.
O Jātavedas, with those auspicious bodies of yours, carry him to the world of the righteous.
O Jātavedas, with those purifying flames of yours...
The cruel parts of the body are moving about;
may they follow the goat as it goes and be joined together with those other most auspicious parts. Make it cooked.
Release him again, O Agni, to the fathers— he who, offered by you, moves with the *svadhā* offerings;
clothed in life, let the remnant approach.
May you unite with a body full of splendor. Run past the two dogs, the sons of Saramā,
the four-eyed brindled ones, by the straight path.
Then approach the benevolent ancestors who rejoice in the shared banquet with Yama—
those two dogs of yours, O Yama, who are the guardians.
The two four-eyed ones who guard the path, the observers of men—
with those two, O King, do thou surround him;
bestow upon him well-being and freedom from disease.
"Urūṇasau" is one [verse].
Soma purifies itself for some; others worship clarified butter. (PS 10.9.10 = PS_18,64.6)
May she go even to those from whom honey flows, who possess offspring,
and who were formerly followers of the Cosmic Order.
Born of Truth, seeking Truth,
O Yama, go also to the ascetic ancestors, those born of austerity.
Those who are invincible through austerity,
those who have gone to heaven through austerity,
and those who have performed great austerity— [to them].
May he go even to those very ones—
the seers of a thousand paths who protect the sun.
O Yama, go also to the sages performing austerities, those born of austerity,
and to those who fight in great battles.
May he go even to those heroes who sacrifice their own bodies, or to those who bestow a thousand-fold sacrificial fees.
Be pleasant to him, O Earth— thornless, a peaceful dwelling;
grant him wide-spreading protection.

Bhaṭṭa: Widely renowned, in the unconfined, vast world of earth, he is glorified. PS 18,65.2: In the unconfined, vast world of earth, he is glorified. Bhaṭṭa: [In the] unobstructed, broad world, he is magnified.
Those *svadhā*-offerings which you have prepared for the living, may they be dripping with sweetness for you.
I invoke you with reverence.
Delighting in this house, come hither; unite with the ancestors and whatever has been given. May gentle, strengthening breezes blow upon you.
May the Maruts, the water-carriers, bring you hither, emerging from the waters, making it cool with their goat-skin.
"May Varṣeṇa come with his hair;
I have called upon life for the sake of life, for wisdom, for skill, and for living."
Let your mind go to its own limbs; then run toward the ancestors as well.
Let your mind not go to the Asuras.
Do not take delight in your limbs;
let nothing of your body be lost here. May the tree not press upon you.
O great goddess Earth,
having found a place among the fathers under the sovereignty of Yama, do thou swell.
That limb of yours which has been cast away, your out-breath and your in-breath that have departed; and those fathers who, having come together, dwell in one nest— [all these we restore for you].
Let them set down fodder upon fodder for him.
Living beings have shut him out from his homes; drive him out from this village.
O Death, you are the messenger of Yama; being wise, you have sent the vital breaths to the fathers—
those *dasyus* who have entered among the ancestors.
Those who move about with their faces turned toward their kinsmen, eating what is not offered; those who move among *parāpur* and *nipura*—
may the gods blow them away from this sacrifice.
May the fathers descend here; may they make for us a pleasant seat and prolong our life.
May we be able to worship them with oblation.
Living long through many abundant autumns—
[I take] that cow of yours which I praise,
or that milk-rice of yours.
Therefore, that man who lives here without fear is the lord of this people.
Cross over to Aśvāvatī, she who is most gracious.
Or let him cross over the Ṛkṣīkā more swiftly;
he who has struck you down, though he deserves to be slain, let him be so— let him not find any other portion of fortune.
Yama is beyond, Vivasvat is below;
beyond that, I see nothing else.
Upon Yama my sacrifice has been established.
Vivasvān spread himself out over the earth.
They concealed the immortal one from mortals; having fashioned Suparṇī, they bestowed her upon Vivasvān.
And she brought the two Aśvins, whatever it was that they were; Saraṇyū abandoned the two pairs.
Those who were buried and those who were scattered—
O Agni, bring here all those ancestors who have been cremated and those who have not yet been cremated, so that they may eat the oblation.
Those ancestors who are here, and those who are not here,
whom we know and whom we do not know— you know them, O Jātavedas, if they exist.
May they enjoy the well-performed sacrifice with their own offerings.
O Agni, let heat be auspicious; do not let heat burn me, nor let heat burn my body.
Let your vigor be in the forests;
let that which you sustain be upon the earth. I grant him this dwelling place.
He who has come here to me— if he has indeed arrived— Yama, the wise one, has declared this in reply:
"Let him stand here by my side for the sake of wealth."
We measure out a measure of love,
so that it may not diminish further.
(Bhaṭṭa reads *māsatai*)
Not before a hundred autumns have passed.
